Do you work or are you a student?

I'm working at the moment — I've been working for a logistics company in Tashkent for just over three years. It's my first proper job after university, and I've grown into it far more than I expected. It gets pretty full-on during the busy season, but the team are a decent bunch and I'm never bored. I did consider a master's, but for now I'm happy earning.

blocks.text: I'm still a student — I'm in my third year of economics at the university here. I'd never planned to study it, to be honest; I applied on a whim after a careers talk. It's turned out to be a good fit, though. The workload is relentless, and I'm forever snowed under with reading, but I'd rather be doing this than sitting in an office at twenty.

Both, actually — I'm doing a part-time master's while working four days a week. I've been juggling the two since last September and it's exhausting but worth it. My employer covers half the fees, which helps enormously. Had I not found a company willing to be flexible, I'd have had to choose, and I suspect the studying would have gone out of the window. It's a means to an end for now.

blocks.text: What work do you do? / What subjects are you studying?

I work in digital marketing — mostly running campaigns for small businesses that can't afford a big agency. Day to day it's writing copy, staring at numbers and talking clients round when they want something unrealistic. I've been doing it for four years and I've picked up a fair bit of design along the way. It's not glamorous, but there's always something new, which suits my short attention span.

annotations.text: I've been doing it for four years

blocks.text: I'm reading economics, with statistics and a bit of law on the side. The maths was a steep learning curve at first — I'd only done the basics at school before I arrived, so the first term was brutal. If I hadn't got a tutor in the second month, I'd have dropped out, genuinely. Now the modelling is the part I enjoy most. Law is the one module I could do without.

blocks.text: Why did you choose that job?

Honestly, it chose me as much as I chose it. I'd always been curious about how brands persuade people long before I realised it was an actual career. A family friend put in a good word for me at an agency, and that got me a foot in the door. I've never regretted it — it's creative work that still pays the bills, which is a rare combination.

annotations.text: I'd always been curious about how brands

blocks.text: There wasn't much of a plan, if I'm honest. I'd been applying for anything and everything after graduation, and this was the first place that said yes. If the interview had been a week later, I'd have taken a job in a bank instead — I'd already been offered one. It turned out to be a blessing in disguise, though. Sometimes you just fall into the right thing.

blocks.text: Why did you choose to study that subject?

Family pressure, mostly — that's the honest answer. My father is an engineer and he'd been dropping hints about the technical university since I was about twelve. I wasn't exactly dead set against it, so I was happy to go along with it. Had my parents pushed me any harder, I think I'd have rebelled out of pure spite. As it is, the subject has really grown on me.

annotations.text: been dropping hints about the technical university since I was about twelve.

blocks.text: Purely with an eye on the job market, I'm afraid — there's not much romance in it. Everyone kept telling me accountancy would always be in demand, and I've found that to be true so far; friends with history degrees are still looking. If I'd followed my heart, I'd have studied literature and been broke by now. It wasn't inspiring, but it was sensible.

blocks.text: I do, most days — which I know makes me lucky. I've been looking forward to Mondays lately, which sounds absurd, but we've just started a project I actually care about. My manager gives me a free hand, and that matters far more to me than money. I've worked in places where you're watched every minute, and it sucks the life out of you.

blocks.text: Mixed feelings, if I'm honest. The work itself is interesting and I've learned an enormous amount in two years, but the hours are punishing and I barely see my family. Had I known how much overtime was involved, I might have thought twice about signing. I'm not about to walk out — jobs like this don't grow on trees — but I wouldn't say I'm living the dream either.
Is there anything you dislike about your job?

The commute, without question. I've spent close to two hours a day on the road for the past year and it's slowly wearing me down. By the time I got home last night, I'd missed my daughter's bedtime again. The job itself I have no complaints about; it's the dead time that gets to me. Two days a week from home and I'd have nothing left to moan about.

blocks.text: Office politics, mainly. There's a lot of quiet jockeying for position, and I've never been much good at that game. I've been keeping my head down and letting the work speak for itself, which doesn't always pay off. If I'd been more willing to play along at the start, I'd have been promoted a year ago. Otherwise, I genuinely like the place.

blocks.text: What do you like about your studies?

The independence, above all. Nobody chases you, so I've had to learn to manage my own time, which is probably the most useful thing university has taught me. I've also been getting to know people from all over the country, which you simply don't get in a small town. Some of the lecturers are genuinely at the top of their field, and that rubs off on you.

blocks.text: The lab work, mainly — I like anything hands-on. I'd assumed the whole degree would be lectures and note-taking before I started, so the practical modules came as a relief. You only get to grips with something once you've broken it and fixed it yourself. Had the course been purely theoretical, I doubt I'd have lasted a year. The third-year placement is the bit everyone raves about.

blocks.text: What do you dislike about your studies?

How far removed it is from real life, mainly. I've sat through entire modules that I can't imagine ever using. I'd expected far more contact with actual companies before I enrolled, and there's almost none. A lot of it is learning by rote — you memorise it, you repeat it in the exam, you forget it a week later. That feels like a waste.

blocks.text: The sheer volume, honestly. I've been running on four or five hours of sleep since the exam period began, and everyone around me looks equally rough. If I'd chosen a lighter course, I'd have had time for a social life, but I'll stick it out.

blocks.text: What was your dream job when you were young?

A pilot, like half the boys in my class. I'd been collecting model aeroplanes for years before I discovered you needed perfect eyesight, which put an end to that. I've kept a bit of the obsession, though — I still get a kick out of the moment a plane leaves the ground. Looking back, it was the uniform and the travelling that appealed to me, not the flying.

blocks.text: A surgeon — my grandmother was a nurse and I hero-worshipped her. By the age of ten I'd already announced it to the entire family, and they still remind me. If I'd been any good at chemistry, I'd have gone for it, but I wasn't, and there's no getting round that. I still think medicine is the one job where you genuinely make a difference.

blocks.text: Have you changed your mind on your dream job?

Completely, yes. That childhood idea has long since fallen by the wayside — I found out what the training actually entailed and lost my nerve. I've become far more interested in the day-to-day reality of a job than the title. Had I stuck with the original plan, I'd probably be halfway through medical school and thoroughly miserable. Now I just want work that doesn't take over my life.

I've always been drawn to work where you build something people actually use — as a child that meant architecture, now it's software. I've been writing code since I was about fifteen, so in a sense I never really switched. My parents still think I'll come to my senses and become a doctor.

blocks.text: 13 questions · two or three model answers each — pick the one that is true for you
Please describe your hometown a little.
— You are from a small town

I'm from Margilan, a fairly small place in the Fergana Valley, and I've lived there my whole life apart from three years at university. It's quiet, low-rise, and almost everything is within walking distance. There's a real close-knit community feel to it. Had I been born in Tashkent instead, I think I'd have grown up a much less patient person.

annotations.text: life apart from three years at university.

blocks.text: — You are from a big city

Tashkent, so it's a proper capital — sprawling, noisy and growing outwards every year. They've been building new metro lines and apartment blocks non-stop since about 2018. I live in a quiet district in the north, though, so I get the amenities without all the hustle and bustle. By the time I finished school, half the streets I knew as a child had disappeared.

annotations.text: They've been building new metro lines and apartment blocks non-stop since about 2018.
By the time I finished school, half the streets I knew as a child had

blocks.text: What is your town well-known for?
— Your town has a famous product

Silk, mainly. Margilan is renowned for its hand-woven atlas fabric, and weavers have been using more or less the same looms for centuries. That one industry has really put the town on the map: it's brought in visitors from all over Asia, which you'd never expect from a place that size. There's even a small museum devoted to it now.

annotations.text: using more or less the same looms for centuries.
it's brought in visitors from all over Asia,

blocks.text: Honestly, not a great deal — it's not exactly a hidden gem waiting to be discovered. We're a bit in the middle of nowhere, and if you asked most Uzbeks they'd mention the cotton fields and nothing else. If the government had invested in the old fortress twenty years ago, we'd have had a proper tourist trade by now. As it is, the town has always been a place people drive through.

annotations.text: If the government had invested in the old fortress twenty years
ago, we'd have had a proper tourist trade by now.

blocks.text: — Yes, you are very fond of it

I'm very fond of it, yes. I've been complaining about the summers here for as long as I can remember, but I wouldn't swap it. The pace of life suits me — nobody's in a rush, and you can't walk to the bazaar without bumping into three people you know. If I'd grown up somewhere anonymous, I'd have missed out on that completely. It has its faults, but it grows on you.

annotations.text: I've been complaining about the summers here for as long as I can
somewhere anonymous, I'd have missed out on that completely.

blocks.text: Mixed feelings, if I'm honest. The people are lovely, but it can be stifling — everyone knows your business, and the traffic gets on my nerves every single morning. I'd been looking for an excuse to leave for ages before the job in the capital came up. That said, I've never managed to feel properly at home anywhere else.

annotations.text: looking for an excuse to leave for ages
never managed to feel properly at home anywhere else.

blocks.text: Is that a big city or a small place?
— You live in a big city

It's big — around three million people, which by Central Asian standards is enormous. It's grown well beyond what the old ring road was designed for, so rush hour is genuinely painful. On the plus side you're spoilt for choice when it comes to restaurants and concerts. If the metro hadn't been extended, I'd have given up driving altogether.

annotations.text: grown well beyond what the old ring road was designed for,
If the metro hadn't been extended, I'd have given up driving altogether.

blocks.text: — You live in a small town

Definitely a small place — about forty thousand people, so it's more of a large village really. It's sleepy compared with the capital, and the peace and quiet takes some getting used to if you've lived in a city. But I've been walking home at midnight without a second thought since I was fifteen, and nobody I know has ever bothered locking a front door.

annotations.text: I've been walking home at midnight without a second thought
nobody I know has ever bothered locking a front door.

blocks.text: How long have you been living there?

All my life, essentially — I've been living in the same neighbourhood for twenty-two years now, in the house my grandfather built. I've only ever spent one long stretch away, when I was studying in Tashkent. So I'm born and bred here, and I suppose I've put down roots without ever really deciding to, which is either lovely or slightly alarming depending on my mood.

annotations.text: I've been living in the same neighbourhood for twenty-two years
I've only ever spent one long stretch away,

blocks.text: Only about eighteen months, actually. I'd been putting the move off for years because I didn't want to leave my parents, and then a job came up I couldn't turn down. It took me a while to find my feet, and I still get lost occasionally, but the city has started to feel like home. My flat is a stone's throw from the metro, which helps enormously.

blocks.text: Do you think you will continue living there for a long time?

Probably, yes — at least for the foreseeable future. My whole family is here and I've built a life around them that would be hard to dismantle. Had a really good offer come along five years ago, I might have gone abroad, but that moment has passed. Now I'd rather settle down properly and stop turning it over in my head.

blocks.text: — No, you want to move away

I doubt it, to be honest. I've been planning my escape quietly since I finished university — I'd like a change of scenery while I'm still young enough to enjoy it. If I'd saved a bit harder in my twenties, I'd have moved already. As it stands I'll probably up sticks the moment I've got enough put aside.

annotations.text: I've been planning my escape quietly since I finished university

blocks.text: Would you like to live in the countryside in the future?

I'd love to, one day. I've been fantasising about a small house with an orchard for years — somewhere I can get away from it all and hear something other than car horns. My wife has never been keen on the idea, mind you; she reckons she'd have cabin fever inside a fortnight. So it's more of a retirement plan than anything concrete.

annotations.text: I've been fantasising about a small house with an orchard for years

blocks.text: — No, you are a city person

Not a chance, I'm afraid — I'm a city person through and through. I spent one summer at my grandmother's farm and I'd had enough after two weeks. Everything is an hour's drive away, the internet is patchy, and you feel completely cut off. If I'd been born fifty years earlier, I'd have adapted, no doubt, but I'm far too used to having a supermarket downstairs.

annotations.text: my grandmother's farm and I'd had enough after two weeks.
If I'd been born fifty years

blocks.text: Have you ever lived in the countryside?
— Yes, when you were a child

Yes, for about two years when I was small. My parents had been teaching in the city until a village school ran short of staff, so we packed up and went. It was fairly basic — we had to rough it with a wood stove and a well — and it was back-breaking for my mother. I've had a soft spot for that valley ever since, all the same.

village school ran short of staff,
a soft spot for that valley ever since,

blocks.text: Never properly, no — I've only ever gone for weekends and the odd summer holiday. My uncle keeps bees outside Parkent and we drop in on him a few times a year, but a long weekend hardly counts as first-hand experience. Had my parents not moved to the capital when I was two, my whole childhood would have been rural.

blocks.text: Do you ever spend time in the countryside?

Fairly often, yes. We've been driving up to Chimgan most weekends since the spring — it's only an hour and a half from the city. We walk, we grill some meat, we recharge our batteries and come back pleasantly exhausted. It's become a bit of a family ritual, actually. Even in winter we head up there to stretch our legs in the snow.

blocks.text: Far less than I'd like. I've barely set foot outside the city since last Navruz, which is a bit shameful given how close the mountains are. Work eats into every weekend, and by Sunday I just want to put my feet up. If I'd learned to drive when my friends did, I'd have got out far more often — as it is, everything depends on someone else's car.

blocks.text: What is the difference between living in the countryside and the city?
— You focus on pace and cost

The obvious one is the pace. In a village nobody hurries, whereas here you're locked into the daily grind from six in the morning — I've spent half my adult life sitting in traffic. Cost is the other big difference: property in the capital costs an arm and a leg, while a whole house out there goes for the price of a garage. Had I stayed put back home, I'd own one outright by now.

annotations.text: I've spent half my adult life sitting in traffic.
costs an arm and a leg,
Had I stayed put back home,

blocks.text: For me it boils down to opportunity. Cities have the universities, the hospitals and the jobs; villages have the fresh air. Young people have been drifting towards Tashkent for decades precisely for that reason. If my parents hadn't moved when they did, I'd have finished school in a class of nine. The trade-off is that you lose the close-knit feel — nobody in my building knows my surname.

annotations.text: Young people have been drifting towards Tashkent for
If my parents hadn't moved when they did, I'd have
finished school in a class of nine.

blocks.text: What do people living in the countryside like to do?

A lot of it revolves around the land and each other. People work the land all day, then sit outside with neighbours until it gets dark. My aunt has been drying apricots on her roof every August for as long as I can remember. Weddings are the big social event — I've never seen a village wedding with fewer than three hundred guests. Otherwise it's tea, gossip and pottering about in the garden.

annotations.text: My aunt has been drying apricots on her roof
every August for as long as I can remember.
seen a village wedding with fewer than three hundred guests.

blocks.text: — You think village life is changing

It's changed more than people think. The older generation still make a living from farming, but the younger ones are glued to their phones like everybody else. Satellite dishes and 4G have reached even the smallest villages, so they watch the same shows as we do. If you'd asked me ten years ago, I'd have described something far more traditional. That still happens, just less often.

annotations.text: dishes and 4G have reached even the smallest villages,
If you'd asked me ten years ago, I'd have described something far more traditional.

blocks.text: What do you like to do in the countryside?

Walking, mostly. I've been hiking the trails above Chimgan since I was at school, and a long climb still blows away the cobwebs better than anything. If there's a river I'll swim, and in the evening we grill kebabs and go stargazing. Had anyone told me at eighteen that I'd enjoy a five-hour walk uphill, I'd have laughed out loud.

annotations.text: I've been hiking the trails above Chimgan since I was at school,

blocks.text: Honestly? As little as possible. I've never been one for organised hikes — I go to my grandmother's, eat far too much plov and sleep. It's the one place where I properly unwind, because nobody expects anything of me. Last time, I'd promised myself I would read three books and I managed nine pages. Pure peace and quiet, basically.

blocks.text: How has your town changed over the last 20 years?

Enormously — the place has changed beyond all recognition. Twenty years ago there was one decent road; now there's a bypass, a shopping centre, and new cafes spring up faster than I can try them. They've been renovating the old bazaar for two years as well. Property prices have gone through the roof, which is lovely if you own a flat and miserable if you don't. On the whole, though, it's a change for the better.

annotations.text: the place has changed beyond all recognition.
They've been renovating the old bazaar for two years

blocks.text: — You think it lost its charm

On paper it's improved, but something has been lost along the way. They pulled down the old teahouse and put a bank there, and most of the little courtyards have gone the same way. If the council had listened to residents, we'd have kept at least half of those buildings. By the time anybody complained, the bulldozers had come and gone. It's cleaner and wealthier, certainly, but it's a far cry from the town I grew up in.

annotations.text: If the council had listened to residents, we'd have kept at least half of those buildings.

blocks.text: 10 questions · two or three model answers each — pick the one that is true for you
What colour would you choose to paint the walls of your room?

Something understated — a soft off-white, or maybe a warm sand colour. I've always found that pale walls make a small room feel twice the size, and they never end up looking dated the way a bold shade does. My old bedroom was dark green and it honestly felt like a cave. If I'd gone for something paler back then, I'd have saved myself two years of gloom. So yes, neutral every time.

annotations.text: If I'd gone for something paler back then, I'd have saved myself two years of gloom.

blocks.text: Honestly, I'd go for something quite dramatic — a deep teal, probably. I've been meaning to repaint that room for about a year now, and I'm sick of magnolia; it's so bland. A strong shade gives a room a bit of personality, and you can always tone it down with pale furniture and a big mirror. Had my landlord not been so fussy about it, I'd have done the whole wall last summer.

annotations.text: to repaint that room for about a year now,
Had my landlord not been so fussy about it,

blocks.text: What colour would you never use in your home?

Black, without question. I've seen it done beautifully in magazines, but in an ordinary flat it just sucks the light out of the room. A friend of mine did her hallway in charcoal and by the time she'd finished, the place had turned into a tunnel. She repainted it within a month. Anything that makes a room feel poky is a definite no from me — our winters are dark enough as it is.

annotations.text: the time she'd finished, the place had turned into a tunnel.

blocks.text: Bright orange, definitely — it's just far too in-your-face. I once stayed in a guesthouse in Bukhara where the whole dining room was tangerine, and I couldn't relax for a second. I've been telling that story for years as a sort of warning. If the owner had asked anyone's opinion first, he'd have picked something calmer. A colour that loud wears thin very fast; you love it on day one and can't stand it by day ten.

annotations.text: I've been telling that story for years

opinion first, he'd have picked something calmer.

blocks.text: Can you describe the place where you live?
— You live in a lively city area

I'm in a fairly built-up part of Tashkent, about ten minutes from the metro. It's noisy, but everything is on your doorstep — bakeries, a decent gym, a little bazaar at the end of the road. I've been living in the same block since I finished university, and I've never seriously thought about moving. The neighbours all know each other, so it feels quite close-knit, which you don't really get in the newer districts.

annotations.text: I've been living in the same block since I finished university,

blocks.text: — You live in a quiet suburb

We're right on the outskirts, about forty minutes out of the centre by bus. It's leafy and quiet — the sort of place where nothing much ever happens, which suits my parents perfectly. We'd been renting in the middle of town for years before we finally moved. If we hadn't found this house when we did, we'd have been priced out completely. The one drawback is the commute; it eats into my evenings.

annotations.text: We'd been renting in the middle of town for years

blocks.text: What kind of housing accommodation do you live in?

A three-room flat on the fifth floor of a Soviet-era block — nothing fancy, but surprisingly roomy by modern standards. We've been there since I was born, so it's really the only home I know. The ceilings are high and the walls are solid, which you simply don't get in these flimsy new-builds. Had my grandparents not been given the place in the eighties, we'd have struggled to get on the property ladder at all.

annotations.text: We've been there since I was born,
Had my grandparents not been given the place in the eighties,

blocks.text: — You live in a family house

We've got a house with a small courtyard, which is pretty typical for Samarkand. There's a grapevine my grandfather planted, and all summer the family eats out under it. My dad knocked through into the veranda about ten years ago, because the family had outgrown the original two rooms. If he hadn't, I'd have ended up sharing with my brother for life, which doesn't bear thinking about.

annotations.text: the original two rooms. If he hadn't, I'd have ended up sharing with my brother for life,

blocks.text: What do you like about your flat?
— You love the light and space

The light, mainly. It faces south-east, so the kitchen is flooded with light from about six in the morning. I've been getting up early for years just to sit in there with a coffee before anyone else is awake. It's also within walking distance of my office, which saves me a fortune. I've rented three flats now, and this one is easily the pick of the bunch.

blocks.text: Honestly, it's the neighbours more than the flat itself. Everyone looks out for each other — if I'm away for a week, somebody waters my plants without being asked. I'd always assumed city people kept themselves to themselves, so it came as a real surprise. Had we ended up in one of those anonymous new towers, I doubt we'd have hit it off with anyone. The building's a bit shabby, but the atmosphere more than makes up for it.

blocks.text: Which room does your family spend most of the time in?
— Your family gathers in the kitchen

The kitchen, hands down. It's the biggest room and it's where everything happens — homework, arguments, guests, all of it. My mother has cooked in that room for thirty years and she still won't let anyone near the stove. If we'd built the house ourselves, we'd have made it even bigger, because six adults round one table gets cramped. The living room, meanwhile, lies empty most of the week.

blocks.text: — Your family gathers in the living room

Definitely the living room — we've got a big low table and everyone sprawls on the floor cushions rather than the sofa. We've been having dinner in there since my grandmother moved in, because the kitchen's too small for seven. In the evening the television goes on and nobody moves for hours. We'd been meaning to buy proper armchairs for ages, but the cushions are cosier and they take up far less space.

blocks.text: What can you see from the windows where you live?

We're on the twelfth floor, so on a clear day you can see all the way to the Chimgan mountains — it's a cracking view. I've never got tired of it, even after all these years; the light on the peaks at sunset is something else. Had the developers put our building fifty metres further back, we'd be staring straight at another block. The skyline is changing fast, though.

topics.title: Family Member That Made You Feel Proud

blocks.text: Describe a family member that did something that made you feel proud.

How to use the one minute

I'd like to talk about my mum, Nodira. She teaches maths in Namangan, and for most of my childhood she was the least adventurous person in our house — the sort of woman who wouldn't dream of driving further than the bazaar. She'd been promising to learn to drive since I was in primary school, but she never seemed to get round to it.

annotations.text: She'd been promising to learn to drive
since I was in primary school,

blocks.text: Then, two winters ago, my dad slipped on the ice outside our gate and broke his ankle, and suddenly nobody could take my grandmother to her hospital appointments. So at forty- seven my mum decided to take the plunge and booked twenty lessons. She'd never once sat behind the wheel before. She failed the test twice, and after the second attempt she came home ready to throw in the towel.

What made me proud wasn't the licence. It was watching her swallow her pride and be a beginner in front of a nineteen-year-old instructor who rolled his eyes every time she stalled. I'd always assumed people stop taking risks once they hit forty, and she has proved every one of us wrong at an age when my uncles are winding down.

Had she given up after that second attempt, she'd have spent the next thirty years waiting for lifts, and I'd have inherited exactly the same fear. I've been quoting her ever since — usually to friends who tell me they're too old to start something new.

annotations.text: Had she given up after that second attempt,
I've been quoting her ever since

blocks.text: — If you prefer a story about quiet integrity

The person I'd choose is my father. He runs a small furniture workshop on the edge of Fergana with six employees — sawdust everywhere, a kettle permanently on, the radio playing to nobody. He's the least dramatic man you could meet; he has never once raised his voice at me.

During the pandemic our orders began to dry up almost overnight. He'd been running that workshop for eighteen years and he had never seen anything like it. Everyone in the family told him to lay half of them off until things picked up. Instead he sold his car — a green Nexia he'd saved four years for — and paid all six men their full wages for five months out of his own pocket. He didn't breathe a word about it at home. I only found out that September, when one of his carpenters stopped me outside the mosque and welled up telling me about it. It was genuinely humbling, because I'd spent that entire spring complaining about being stuck indoors with bad wifi. If he'd put the business first, not one person would have blamed him.

annotations.text: he had never seen anything like it.
business first, not one person would have blamed him.

blocks.text: I've been thinking about that decision ever since, especially now that I'm about to start earning myself. He'd be the last person to call it a sacrifice; he'd just say he was doing the decent thing — and that quiet kind of pride is the sort that stays with you.

annotations.text: I've been thinking about that decision ever since,

blocks.text: The card asks for something the person did, so a portrait of your kind grandmother will not score. Name the action inside the first thirty seconds, then spend the rest of your time on it. Note too that family member is taken literally — a teacher or a best friend answers a different question, however moving the story is.

My perfect job would be an ordinary one — teaching English to teenagers at a small private centre, the kind with four classrooms and a kettle that never works. I'd never taught anybody before that summer after school, when my aunt asked me to help my cousins, and it slowly started growing on me. I've been tutoring them ever since.

blocks.text: Getting in isn't complicated, but it isn't automatic. You need a degree, a C1 certificate and a CELTA — I'd already been putting money aside for that course before I graduated. Then most centres make you teach a trial lesson in front of the director, who really puts you through your paces. Had I not sat in on a friend's class first, I'd have walked in unprepared.

blocks.text: The teaching is only half of it. You'd plan lessons, mark endless writing, and keep tabs on every student in a spreadsheet nobody else opens. I'd run a free speaking club on Saturdays too, to get the quiet ones talking. And then there's the nitty-gritty — placement tests, parents' meetings, arguments about refunds. Two hours in a classroom fly by.

I've always wanted work where you can see the effect of what you do. In an office you produce a report; here, a boy who couldn't order a coffee in September argues about films by May. My uncle talked me out of it — teaching doesn't pay the bills, he said. But if you stick at it, eventually it does.

blocks.text: If I could design my own job, I'd be a restoration architect — somebody who repairs old buildings instead of putting up new ones. Specifically, I'd want to work on the mud-brick houses in the old quarter of Bukhara, the ones with carved wooden doors that are quietly falling apart. I've had that idea in my head since a school trip there.

blocks.text: It's a long road. Five years of architecture, then a conservation specialisation — the serious programmes are in Italy and they cost an arm and a leg. I'd been looking into scholarships for months before I found one in Florence. You also have to build up a portfolio of survey drawings, unpaid. If I hadn't spent last summer measuring a crumbling madrasa for free, I'd have had nothing to show them. Most of the work isn't drawing at all. You pore over archive photographs for weeks, working out what a façade looked like before somebody had ripped out the original windows in the eighties. Then you argue with builders who use cement because it dries faster — they'll cut corners wherever you let them. It's painstaking: two buildings a decade.

The clearest example is the morning of my university entrance exam. We'd been warned that phones were strictly off-limits, so I had to hand in my phone at the gate and watch it vanish into a numbered plastic tray. I'd been revising for it for the best part of a year, and suddenly it was just me, a pen and four hours of silence.

annotations.text: I'd been revising for it for the best part of a year,

blocks.text: It was the first week of August, two years ago — a scorching morning, thirty-two degrees by eight o'clock. I'd never sat a state exam before, so I was on edge anyway, and losing my phone made it worse. For twenty minutes I kept patting an empty pocket out of force of habit.

annotations.text: I'd never sat a state exam before,

blocks.text: It was at the national university, in a hall they normally use for basketball. Four hundred desks were taped to the floor in rows, and invigilators walked up and down the aisles. Watches, bags and phones were confiscated at the door and kept under lock and key until the end.

The reason was obvious — cheating. The year before, photographs of the paper did the rounds on Telegram within an hour, and the ministry has been tightening the rules ever since. Had I been caught with a phone in my sock, like the boy two rows in front of me, I'd have been banned for two years. I've come round to their way of thinking: it puts everyone on a level playing field.

blocks.text: — If you'd rather talk about a job

A completely different one: two summers ago I was a junior counsellor at a children's camp in Chimgan, where staff phones stayed in a drawer in the director's office all day. Instead of scrolling, I spent my days keeping an eye on thirty nine-year-olds round the clock and breaking up arguments about bunk beds. It was a baptism of fire.

That was July and August — three shifts of twelve days, back to back. I'd been working in a café before that, where I could check my messages whenever it went quiet, so the first week was brutal. I'd never gone a whole day without my phone, but by the third morning I'd weaned myself off it.

annotations.text: I'd never gone a whole day without my phone,

blocks.text: The camp sits in a valley ninety minutes above Tashkent — wooden cabins, a football pitch on a slope and one brick building with the office. The signal up there is patchy anyway, but this was a written rule in our contracts, not just bad reception.

The reason was partly the children — a counsellor glued to a screen is not supervising anybody — and partly photographs: nobody wants pictures of other people's kids online. At the time I thought it was overkill. If I'd had my phone that summer, I'd have missed half of what actually happened — the campfire singing, a boy finally learning to swim on the last morning. I've kept my own version of that rule ever since.

annotations.text: If I'd had my phone that summer, I'd have missed half of
I've kept my own version of that rule ever since.

blocks.text: Three of these bullets — when, where, why — take about ten seconds each, so the whole card can collapse into forty seconds. Put your detail into what you did, and read it as what you did instead: the hours without the phone are the story. Then give the reason plainly at the end. Examiners notice when a candidate never actually answers why.

The person I'd choose is Eldor Shomurodov, the striker who plays up front for our national team. For anyone who follows football here he's a household name, and I've been a die- hard fan since he was still at Bunyodkor. I've been following his career for the best part of ten years.

blocks.text: Oddly, I wouldn't want to meet him at a stadium. I'd pick somewhere completely ordinary — a teahouse in Chilanzar, green tea on the table, nobody filming. At a match you get thirty seconds and a blurry selfie; over a long lunch you could get past the small talk and actually talk.

I only know him through a screen, obviously. He worked his way up from a village team, and he'd been playing in half-empty provincial stadiums for years before Genoa signed him. I'd watched most of those matches on a laptop with dreadful internet, so it feels oddly personal. He's never once forgotten where he came from — he still keeps his feet on the ground in every interview.

blocks.text: Mainly I'd want to ask how he survived that first winter in Italy: no language, no friends, no plov. The person I'd most like to meet is Hayao Miyazaki, the Japanese director behind Spirited Away and My Neighbour Totoro. I'd never even heard of Studio Ghibli until I was about fifteen, and I've watched those films more times than I'd like to admit since then.

blocks.text: I'd want to meet him at the Ghibli Museum in Mitaka, which is tucked away in a quiet suburb rather than in central Tokyo — twenty minutes on a little green train, and then a building that looks hand-drawn itself. Better still would be his studio, with sketches pinned to the walls and paper everywhere. I know him through a scratched DVD, basically. My cousin left it at our flat one summer; I'd been avoiding subtitled films because I assumed they were hard work, and I only put it on out of boredom. I was completely hooked within ten minutes. Had my cousin not forgotten that disc, I'd probably never have discovered any of it.

annotations.text: that disc, I'd probably never have discovered any of it.

blocks.text: What I'd really want is to pick his brains about the drawing. Every frame is done by hand — painstaking, slow, a genuine labour of love — and he refuses to cut corners or hand the work to a computer. He builds whole worlds from scratch. I've been arguing about this with friends for years: they say technology moves on, and I say that is exactly why his films stand the test of time.

The bullet candidates skip is where you'd like to meet this person — they drift into the celebrity's biography instead and answer three bullets out of four. Spend twenty seconds putting yourself in a real room: a teahouse, a training ground, a museum. Watch the tense as well. This meeting is imaginary, so it is I'd ask and I'd want to know, never I asked.

It's going to sound very ordinary, but the place I relax is the balcony of our flat in Chilonzor, on the eighth floor of a crumbling Soviet block in Tashkent. It's two metres by one, more corridor than room, and my father glazed it in years ago, so it works even in February.

There's a folding chair that has seen better days, a low table my grandmother used for rolling dough, and fifteen tomato seedlings in yoghurt pots along the ledge. We'd been using it as a junk room for years, and I'd never noticed how much light it got until I finally cleared it out last spring.

annotations.text: using it as a junk room for years,
I'd never noticed how much light it got

blocks.text: What I do out there is nothing much. I've been going out there with green tea almost every evening since March, putting my phone face down and switching off for an hour. Sometimes I read; more often I watch the number nine tram go past. I water the tomatoes too, which is a standing joke in my family.

annotations.text: I've been going out there with green tea almost every

blocks.text: It relaxes me because nobody follows me out there — it's the one square metre of the flat that's off-limits to everybody else. It's where I wind down, and I've come to think of it as a decompression chamber between the outside world and family life. If my father hadn't glazed that balcony in, I'd have grown up without a corner of my own, and I'd be a far more highly strung person.

Mine isn't really a room — it's the far end of our kitchen in Samarkand, tucked away behind the door, with a window onto the courtyard and the apricot tree. There's a long wooden bench under it, piled with kurpachas — our quilted mattresses — and that corner has been my spot since we moved in with my grandparents.

blocks.text: It isn't remotely stylish. The walls are a pale institutional green that went out of fashion decades ago, the shelves are cluttered with jars of quince jam, and the radio hasn't been retuned since 2014. My grandmother had been cooking in there for nearly forty years before she let me touch anything, and she'd worn a shallow groove into the floorboards between the sink and the stove. I've been getting up at six in that kitchen since I was about fifteen, mainly to have the place to myself before the household springs into life. I make coffee, put my feet up and write out the day's plan on the back of an envelope. Occasionally I bake, though I'm hopeless at pastry.

blocks.text: Last October she rang me at about eleven at night, completely at her wits' end. She'd failed her anatomy resit at medical college for the second time and had made a snap decision to drop out. Her parents were up in arms, which of course only made her dig her heels in harder. blocks.text: I deliberately didn't tell her what to do, because that would have backfired completely. What I said was: change how you study, not what you study. Past papers instead of rereading notes, and a proper night's sleep before an exam. And I asked her to stick it out for one more semester, because quitting in the middle of a terrible week isn't a decision, it's a reaction. Sleep on it, I said.

She stayed. She's just started her fourth year and she has never looked back. Had I agreed with her that night, I'm fairly sure she'd have been miserable within a year. And honestly, I've been choosing my words far more carefully ever since.

blocks.text: — If you prefer a work story

The person is Bekzod, an old classmate who runs a phone-repair counter in Malika bazaar. We're not particularly close, but we'd known each other since primary school, so he tends to ring me whenever he wants a second opinion.

blocks.text: Two summers ago he decided to go all in: sell his car, take out a loan from an uncle and open a proper shop on Amir Temur Street with three staff. He'd been reading business books all winter and was absolutely fired up about it. The trouble was, his counter was barely breaking even, and he hadn't worked out the rent. So I said the least welcome thing you can say to an excited man: slow down. I asked him to spend one month writing down every som that came in and went out, and only then decide. I told him not to sell the car, because a loan isn't something you can wriggle out of in a bad month. He accused me of raining on his parade.

He did the month, and the figures were sobering — the new rent alone would have swallowed his whole margin. So he kept the counter, hired one assistant instead of three, and he's been expanding quietly ever since. If I'd simply cheered him on that evening, he'd have lost the car and the shop. He still teases me, but he did take it on board, and I've never regretted saying it.

The app I'd like to talk about is Anki, a flashcard program that drums vocabulary into your head using spaced repetition. It's a bare-bones thing to look at: a white screen, one blue button and a small number telling you how many cards are waiting. But it has quietly changed the way I study.

I'd been fighting with English vocabulary for the best part of a year, and I'd tried everything - notebooks, sticky notes on the fridge, even writing on the back of my hand. Then one afternoon in the university library a girl at my table looked at my list and said, just install this instead. Had she not been sitting opposite me that day, I'd probably still be going round in circles.

blocks.text: Now I use it entirely in dead time. On the metro from Chilonzor into the centre I get through about fifty cards, so the day's session is finished before I even sit down at my desk. Anything I come across during the day goes straight in, and the algorithm takes care of the timing, showing me the word the moment before I'd forget it.

Honestly, I'm a little evangelical about it. I've been using it every single day for three years, and it is easily the least glamorous thing on my phone. But it works, and whenever a friend tells me they're drowning in word lists, it's the first thing I mention.

blocks.text: — If you'd rather talk about photos

The program I'd choose is Snapseed, a photo editor that Google gives away for nothing. On the surface it is just a grid of grey icons, but hidden inside there is a healing tool that can breathe new life into a picture you had written off completely.

I'd never given photo editing a second thought until my cousin's wedding in Samarkand two summers ago. The photographer had been working through his shots on a battered tablet in the corner all evening, and when I finally asked him what he was using, he let me in on it - the app doing half his job cost nothing at all. I installed it in the taxi home. These days I use it almost entirely on my grandmother's photographs. She keeps a shoebox of dog-eared prints from the sixties: cracked, yellow, one of them half eaten by damp. I photograph each one by the window in daylight, then spend an evening touching up the scratches a millimetre at a time. It's painstaking work - a single portrait can swallow an hour.

The country I've set my heart on is Japan — Kyoto specifically, not Tokyo. I wouldn't want to emigrate; I'd go for one autumn, three or four months, long enough to stop feeling like a tourist.

I've known about it since I was eleven, when a documentary about Kyoto's tea houses came on at my grandmother's flat. Since then I've been collecting scraps of it — a phrasebook, a map above my desk. My sister's classmate Dilnoza spent a year there, and her photographs of the whole city grinding to a halt for the cherry blossom still blow me away.

blocks.text: The job itself wouldn't be anything high-flying. Ideally I'd work in a small family guesthouse — a ryokan — carrying luggage and serving breakfast at six in the morning. By the time I started university I'd already spent a summer in a hostel in Samarkand, so I know I can get by, and I'd learn the ropes from people whose families have run these places for generations.

blocks.text: I'd been putting it off for years, waiting for better English and bigger savings. What I actually want is a change of scene severe enough that I can't read a single street sign. If my family had moved around when I was small, I'd have got this out of my system years ago — as it is, I'd pick up more in three months in a Kyoto kitchen than in three years of classes here.

blocks.text: Mine would be Germany — Berlin, to be exact. It isn't a beautiful city, but for the kind of work I want to do, four months there would be worth more to me than another year of lectures.

I'd been following Berlin's start-up scene online long before I met anybody who had actually lived there. By the time I left school I'd taught myself enough German from song lyrics to read job adverts. The rest came by word of mouth — a lecturer of mine did his master's at Humboldt and warned me about the red tape, six weeks of queuing just to register an address. What I'm after is a paid internship as a junior data analyst: cleaning messy spreadsheets, building dashboards, nothing cutting-edge. I've applied to two Berlin companies already and been turned down by both. Still, if I could land a placement even for one summer, I'd cut my teeth on real data and rub shoulders with engineers from a dozen countries.

I'd like to talk about my grandmother's samovar — a heavy brass one, the size of a bucket, that sits on top of the wardrobe in her house in Chirchiq. The base is crooked and the metal has gone dark with age, but it still has pride of place in the main room, and it's the most battered thing we own.

Nobody bought it. It came with the family when they moved from Namangan in the fifties. They had left almost everything else behind, because my great-grandmother had been carrying my grandfather on one arm the whole journey — but she refused to put the samovar down. That first winter they had to make do with one pan and two spoons, so it got passed down as a survival story.

blocks.text: It has sat on that wardrobe for the best part of seventy years, and I've been drinking tea out of it since I was about four. For most of the year it just stands there gathering dust, but it really comes into its own at Navruz, when my uncle lights it with real charcoal in the yard.

blocks.text: It matters because it's the one object linking four generations. Every time we light it, somebody tells the story again.

The thing I'd describe is a photograph album — a fat, dog-eared one bound in dark green cloth, which my grandmother keeps in the bottom drawer of her dresser. The spine is coming apart at the seams and half the black paper pages are loose, so you have to open it flat on the table.

It began as my great-grandfather's. He bought it the year he came home from the army, and by the time he died he had filled about half of it with tiny square photographs. The shop I go to most is actually a sportswear shop on the second floor of a shopping centre near Chilonzor, about twenty minutes on the metro from my flat. It's enormous, and it's the closest thing my part of the city has to a one-stop shop for anything sporty.

It sells absolutely everything: running shoes, football kit, tents, bicycle parts, swimming goggles, protein bars by the till. I'd been running in the same falling-apart trainers since school when my brother finally dragged me there. The clothes are hard-wearing rather than fashionable, which suits me, and almost nothing in there will break the bank. Mainly, though, it's the staff. My brother had recommended it precisely for that reason — they're all genuinely clued up, because they do the sports they sell. If I hadn't asked the assistant about my flat feet, I'd have bought completely the wrong shoes and given up running by March. They let you try on almost anything, and nobody hovers over you.

It was the second week of October, right in the middle of exams, which is probably why we'd been putting it off for days. Nobody had ever asked us to invent something out of nothing — every other assignment had been pure analysis. Two young British soldiers are sent across enemy ground to deliver a message that will stop an attack and save sixteen hundred men, one of them the younger soldier's brother. I saw it in the cinema in a shopping centre in Tashkent, on a Tuesday afternoon with maybe nine people in the room. blocks.text: Bullet three is really two questions, and the second half — why you want to watch it again — is the one candidates quietly drop. Give the plot twenty-five seconds at most; nobody is marking your summary. Then name a concrete reason to rewatch it: a detail you know you missed, or a change in your own life that will make the ending land differently.

— A short story you can read tonight

The one I keep thinking about is O. Henry's short story The Last Leaf. Two artists share a studio in New York, and one of them, Johnsy, catches pneumonia. She lies in bed counting the ivy leaves on the wall outside, decides that when the last one falls she will die, and quietly gives up on getting better. She is at death's door.

I read it a month ago, on the metro, from a dog-eared paperback my sister had left on the kitchen table. I'd been putting off reading in English for months because I associated it with homework, and I polished off the whole thing between two stops.

annotations.text: I'd been putting off reading in English for months

blocks.text: I loved it, and I'm not usually a fiction person. It is barely six pages, but it has a twist in the tail that made me sit up. The old painter downstairs climbs out in the storm and paints a leaf on the wall so Johnsy will not lose hope, and dies of pneumonia himself. I hadn't seen it coming at all, and I finished it with a lump in my throat.

What stayed with me is the idea that the kindest thing anyone does for you might be something you never find out about. If I'd read it at school, I'd have dismissed it as sentimental; at twenty-two it really hit home. I've read it three times since, and I've been recommending it to everyone, because it takes ten minutes.

annotations.text: If I'd read it at school, I'd have dismissed it as
I've read it three times since,

blocks.text: — If you'd rather talk about a novel

The last proper book I finished was Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner. It follows two boys in Kabul in the nineteen-seventies: Amir, the son of a wealthy man, and Hassan, the servant's son who sticks by him through thick and thin. At a kite tournament Amir watches something terrible happen to Hassan and says nothing; the rest of the book grows out of that silence.

I read it in February, mostly at night — it is the kind of book you can't put down, and I finished the last hundred pages in one sitting, at three in the morning. I'd been meaning to read it since school, but the library copy had always been out. Liked is an odd word, because parts of it are harrowing. But yes. It is gut-wrenching and beautifully written, and the second half, where Amir goes back to Kabul to make amends and come to terms with what he did, is one of the few endings I have believed. I'd never cried at a book before.

annotations.text: the library copy had always been out.

blocks.text: What I took from it is how much damage you can do by turning a blind eye. Amir's whole life is shaped by thirty seconds of silence at twelve. Had I read it at fifteen, I'd have taken his side without thinking; now I am not so sure. I've thought about that scene more than once since, usually when I have kept quiet myself. It puts things in perspective.

annotations.text: Had I read it at fifteen, I'd have taken
I've thought about that scene more than

blocks.text: The plot bullet is a trap. Candidates retell the whole story and run out of time before what you learned, which is the bullet that earns the interesting language. Give the plot in about thirty seconds, in the present tense, and stop at the turning point. Note recently as well: a book you last opened at school will not do.

topics.title: Person Who Solved a Problem in a Smart Way

blocks.text: Describe a person who solved a problem in a smart way.
◆why you think it was a clever solution
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on who this person is .
About 30 seconds on what the problem was .
About 45 seconds on what solution they gave .
About 30 seconds on why you think it was a clever solution .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.

The person I'd talk about is my uncle Bahodir, who runs a small non bakery in Yunusabad. He isn't a businessman in any grand sense — he's a baker with flour on his sleeves — but he has kept that bakery going through two currency crises.

annotations.text: has kept that bakery going through two currency crises.

blocks.text: The problem was waste. He bakes about four hundred loaves a day, and he'd been throwing sixty or seventy of them away every night, because nobody buys yesterday's bread — a quarter of his profit going to waste. He'd already tried baking smaller batches, but then he sold out by three and his regulars kicked up a fuss. For a year he genuinely struggled to make ends meet.

annotations.text: sixty or seventy of them away every night,
He'd already tried baking smaller batches,

blocks.text: He racked his brains all winter and then hit on something embarrassingly simple: a Telegram channel called Evening Bread. At seven every evening he posts one photo and one line — how many loaves are left, half price. There's a student dormitory two hundred metres up the road; the lot goes in twenty minutes.

What I admire is that it fixed two things at a stroke. The waste vanished, and those students turned into morning customers, so the bakery's name spread by word of mouth across the district. If he'd taken out a loan instead, he'd have made everything far worse. He's been running that channel for three years now, and it is still the shrewdest thing anyone in our family has done.

annotations.text: If he'd taken out a loan instead, he'd have made everything far worse.
He's been running that channel for three years now,

blocks.text: — If you want a school story

The cleverest solution I've watched anyone find came from my biology teacher, Nodira opa — a small, unhurried woman with dreadful handwriting. She'd been teaching in that same lab for twenty-odd years by the time our class arrived.

annotations.text: She'd been teaching in that same

blocks.text: The problem was equipment. There were twenty-eight of us and exactly one working microscope. A shoestring budget meant nothing would change — the school had promised new equipment three years running and never delivered. So we'd take it in turns, thirty seconds each, and by mid-lesson the boys at the back had stopped even pretending to look. That one microscope was a stumbling block for the whole course.

Rather than complaining upwards, she came at it from a completely different angle. She borrowed her son's phone, taped it over the eyepiece with insulating tape and a bent paperclip, and plugged it into the classroom projector. Suddenly an onion cell was two metres wide on the wall and all twenty-eight of us were looking at it together.

It was clever because she didn't try to get around the shortage with money she didn't have; she improvised with what was in the room. Total cost: one paperclip. Had she waited politely for that budget, we'd still be queueing at the eyepiece today. That is what being resourceful really means, and I've told the story in two job interviews since. Sometimes you just have to make do with what's on the table.

annotations.text: politely for that budget, we'd still be queueing at the eyepiece today.
I've told the story in two job interviews since.

blocks.text: The trap here is proportion. Candidates spend ninety seconds describing the problem and ten rushed seconds on the solution, which is the part the card is really about. Time yourself: problem in twenty seconds, solution in forty. And the last bullet asks why it was clever — that needs a judgement of your own, not a second telling of what the person did.

topics.title: Person Who Likes to Protect the Nature

blocks.text: Describe a person who encouraged you to protect the nature.
◆what this person encouraged you to do
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on who this person is .
About 30 seconds on how this person encouraged you .
About 45 seconds on what this person encouraged you to do .
About 30 seconds on how you feel about this person .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.
— A relative you grew up with

The first person who comes to mind is my grandmother, Zulfiya buvi, who lived in a courtyard house on the edge of Bukhara until her death four years ago. She was no environmentalist — she'd never heard the word — but she was the most frugal person I have ever met.

She never preached at me. She'd been living with real water shortages since the 1970s, so it was simply how she ran the house, and I picked it up by copying her. A zinc bucket under the sink caught washing-up water for her roses, and if she found a tap running she gave you a look that could strip paint.

annotations.text: She'd been living with real water shortages since the 1970s,

blocks.text: What she encouraged was making do with what was already in the house. We mended things instead of replacing them, jars were reused until the labels came off, scraps went to the chickens. Her philosophy boiled down to waste not, want not. She also made me plant a mulberry sapling by the far wall and was adamant that I water it myself.

I feel enormous respect, and some guilt. For her it was a way of life, not a cause, and I've become far less careful since I moved to Tashkent. If she hadn't built those habits into me so early, I'd have carried on without thinking twice — as it is, turning off a tap mid-wash is second nature. That mulberry is taller than the house now.

annotations.text: become far less careful since I moved to Tashkent. If she hadn't built those habits into me
so early, I'd have carried on without thinking twice

blocks.text: — If you'd rather talk about a friend

Mine is a friend rather than a relative — a guy called Sardor, two years above me at university in Tashkent, who ran the student eco-club almost single-handedly. He studied hydrology, he cycled to lectures in a city where nobody cycles, and he'd been organising clean-ups long before any of it became fashionable.

annotations.text: clean-ups long before any of it became fashionable.

blocks.text: He never guilt-tripped anyone. What he did instead was rope you in: a message on Thursday saying a minibus was leaving at seven on Saturday, and somehow you agreed. I'd assumed it would be an hour of tidying and a photo for Instagram — in fact we filled about forty bin bags along the shore of the Charvak reservoir and dragged a fridge door out of the shallows. After that he badgered me into small, dull, permanent things rather than grand gestures: a cloth bag, refusing plastic bottles at the gym, separating rubbish even though collection here is patchy at best. I've been taking my own container to the samsa place by the metro ever since, which my friends find hilarious.

annotations.text: assumed it would be an hour of tidying and a photo for Instagram
I've been taking my own container to the samsa place by the metro

blocks.text: I admire him, though he'd cringe at the word. He's the only person I know who genuinely practises what he preaches. Had I not climbed onto that minibus, I'd probably still think this was somebody else's problem — a job for the government, or for rich countries. So I owe him a fairly serious shift in mindset, and I've never actually told him so.

annotations.text: Had I not climbed onto that minibus,
I've never actually told him so.

blocks.text: Bullets two and three look like the same question, and most candidates answer them once and then dry up. Keep them apart: bullet two is the person's method — the example they set, the trip they dragged you on — while bullet three is the list of concrete things you now actually do. Two separate bullets deserve two separate half-minutes.

topics.title: Item on Which You Spent More Than Expected

blocks.text: Describe an occasion when you paid more than expected.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on what you bought .
About 30 seconds on how much you paid .
About 45 seconds on why you bought it .
About 30 seconds on why you paid more .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.

A year ago I bought a second-hand fridge - a tall white LG - from a man in Yunusobod who had advertised it on OLX. In the photos it looked in mint condition, and at two million four hundred thousand so'm it struck me as a steal.

I ended up handing over just over three million one hundred. That is seven hundred thousand more than the number in the advert, which doesn't sound much until you remember it was a student's entire month. I'd budgeted right down to the taxi fare, and the extras added up far faster than I could follow.

annotations.text: I'd budgeted right down to the taxi fare,

blocks.text: I'd been sharing a flat with two classmates and our old fridge had finally given up - it froze the milk solid and left the meat warm. We were throwing food away every week, so I bit the bullet rather than eat in cafés all winter.

annotations.text: I'd been sharing a flat with two classmates

blocks.text: The extra went on things nobody mentions. The delivery he had promised to throw in suddenly cost more once he heard there was no lift; two porters carried it up four flights; and the door seal was perished and had to be replaced. Had I read the advert to the bottom, I'd have seen the words 'collection only'. The money had already changed hands, so it was too late to back out - seven hundred thousand out of pocket. I've read every listing twice since then, right down to the small print.

annotations.text: Had I read the advert to the bottom,
I'd have seen the words 'collection only'.

blocks.text: — A celebration that got out of hand

Last summer I took eight friends out to dinner to celebrate finishing my degree. It was a Georgian place in the centre of Tashkent, the kind with a courtyard and a man playing live music between the tables, and I had decided in advance that for once I was going to push the boat out.

I had six hundred thousand so'm in my head as the total. The bill came to one million nine hundred - an eye-watering number to be looking at on a small piece of paper at midnight. That single evening set me back nearly a month's money from my part-time job.

I'd been counting every thousand so'm for four years - living on a shoestring, walking instead of taking taxis - and I'd promised myself one proper evening with the people who got me through it. So I don't think of it as a mistake exactly. I wanted to splash out on them, and I did.

annotations.text: I'd been counting every thousand so'm for four years

blocks.text: Three things caught me out. Nobody had mentioned a hefty service charge for the musicians; two friends brought someone with them; and the table quietly racked up four rounds of drinks I never saw arriving. If I'd asked what was included when I booked, none of that would have happened - but I didn't, and the person who does the inviting has to foot the bill. I've learned my lesson, and I've been reading menus properly ever since.

annotations.text: If I'd asked what was included when I booked, none
I've been reading menus properly ever since.

blocks.text: This card is about a gap, not about an expensive thing. Say both numbers out loud - what you expected and what you actually handed over - because an examiner who never hears the difference hears a different answer. Then protect the last bullet: why you paid more is where the language lives, so give two separate reasons rather than one.

Describe a person who often helps others.
◆why you think this person is helpful
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on who this person is .
About 30 seconds on how you know this person .
About 45 seconds on how this person helps you .
About 30 seconds on why you think this person is helpful .

The person I'd like to describe is our next-door neighbour, Gulnora opa. She's around seventy, a retired nurse, and she's the person the whole building turns to whenever something goes wrong — a burst pipe, a sick child, somebody's cat on the roof.

We've lived on the same landing since I was six, so I've known her all my life. She'd been working at the district clinic for thirty years before she retired, and I suspect that's where the habit comes from: she's used to people knocking at strange hours. When both my parents were at work she'd keep an eye on me after school and feed me far too much.

annotations.text: We've lived on the same landing since I was six,
working at the district clinic for thirty years before she retired,

blocks.text: She still goes out of her way for us now. During my exams she'd run errands for my mother so nobody disturbed me, and she had left soup outside our door before we'd even told anyone my sister was ill. She'll do it at the drop of a hat, at eleven at night if necessary.

annotations.text: she had left soup outside our door before we'd even
told anyone my sister was ill.
at the drop of a hat,

blocks.text: What makes her genuinely helpful, though, is that she manages it without making a fuss; she never mentions it afterwards. She's also taken a first-year student from Namangan under her wing simply because the girl looked lost. She is selfless in a way that feels rare now, and I've been meaning to thank her properly for years. If she hadn't smelled the smoke that night in February, our kitchen would have burned straight through.

annotations.text: taken a first-year student from Namangan
I've been meaning to thank her properly for years. If she hadn't smelled the
smoke that night in February, our kitchen would have burned straight through.

blocks.text: I'd rather talk about somebody my own age: Bekzod, a friend from my university group. On paper he studies economics; what he actually does with his weekends is run a volunteer group that delivers coal and firewood to elderly people in the Yangiyul district.

We'd been sharing a desk in lectures for two months before I discovered any of this. He'd never once mentioned it — somebody else told me, and he changed the subject when I asked. That's the sort of person he is: everything happens behind the scenes, and he does the boring legwork himself — the phone calls, the permissions. He's helped me more times than I can count. When I moved flat he dropped everything and arrived with his brother's car before I'd finished packing. Before my first job interview he talked me through every likely question twice, and he'd already found out who would be sitting on the panel. Half our group now pitches in with each other's coursework thanks to a chat he set up.

annotations.text: We'd been sharing a desk in lectures for two months before I discovered any of this.
He's helped me more times than I can count.
he'd already found out who would

blocks.text: Why is he like that? Partly he's level-headed — nothing rattles him. Partly he's a man of his word: if he says Saturday at nine, he is there at nine. Mostly, he's simply there for people, without calculating anything. Had I not ended up next to him in that lecture hall, I'd have been a far more selfish student, and I've been trying to copy him ever since.

annotations.text: Had I not ended up next to him in that lecture hall, I'd have
been a far more selfish student,
I've been trying to copy him ever since.

blocks.text: There are two traps in the wording. First, often: one dramatic rescue story does not answer this card, so describe a habit — what this person does most weeks. Second, the third bullet says helps you, not people in general. Examiners notice when a candidate never appears in their own story, so keep one concrete favour in reserve for that bullet.

topics.title: Piece of Technology You'd Like to Own

blocks.text: Describe a piece of technology (not a phone) that you would like to own.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on what it is .
About 30 seconds on how you knew it .
About 45 seconds on how much it costs .
About 30 seconds on why you'd like to own it .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.

The thing I'd most like to own is an electric bicycle — the neat kind with the battery hidden inside the frame, not the clunky sort with a box strapped to the rack. Nothing fancy: just something that turns a forty-minute ride across Tashkent into fifteen.

I'd never given them a second thought until last summer, when a colleague turned up at the office on one. He'd been commuting from Yunusabad on it for a year and swore he arrived less sweaty than people who came by bus. He let me ride it round the car park, and I was sold in thirty seconds — the way it picks up speed on a slope is addictive.

annotations.text: I'd never given them a second thought
He'd been commuting from Yunusabad on it for a year

blocks.text: The decent ones cost an arm and a leg here — eight or nine hundred dollars once you add import duty, roughly three months of my salary. There are three-hundred-dollar ones behind Chorsu, but people say the batteries give up the ghost after one winter, so that is a false economy.

annotations.text: cost an arm and a leg

blocks.text: I want one because the traffic here drives me up the wall. I've been sitting in the same jam on Amir Temur Street for four years, watching cyclists sail past me. Had the city not built those new bike lanes, I probably wouldn't even consider it — but they exist now, so the only obstacle is money. I've already saved half of it, and by next spring it should be in my hallway.

annotations.text: I've been sitting in the same jam
on Amir Temur Street for four years,
I've already saved half of it,

blocks.text: If I could pick anything, it would be a drone — a DJI Mavic. It's the folding kind that fits in a rucksack and shoots proper cinematic footage rather than shaky holiday video.

I'd come across drone footage on YouTube for years without thinking much about it, but two autumns ago a friend brought one to Nurata. We'd been walking uphill for three hours to reach a ridge, and when he sent it out over the reservoir and handed me the controller, the picture on the screen was the sort that takes your breath away. I was hooked from that moment.

annotations.text: I'd come across drone footage on YouTube for years
We'd been walking uphill for three hours

blocks.text: They don't come cheap. I'd have to shell out roughly two thousand dollars for the model I want, and once you add spare batteries and a memory card you're looking at two and a half. That is a serious chunk of change for something you fly over a lake. I'd love one because I've been making short travel films since my second year at university, and every shot is at eye level. A drone would let me show the actual scale of a place like Aydarkul from a bird's-eye view. I've never owned a proper piece of kit, so it would be a first. And it could pay for itself eventually — wedding videographers here charge well. If I'd taken it up three years ago, when they cost half as much, I'd have paid it off long ago.

annotations.text: I've been making short travel films since my second year at university,
I've never owned a proper piece of kit,
taken it up three years ago, when they cost half as much, I'd have paid it off long ago.

blocks.text: Two traps sit in the wording. It says not a phone, and it says would like to own — describing the laptop you already have answers neither. The cost bullet is the one candidates skip; give an actual figure and compare it to something real, such as a month's rent, because vague price talk sounds evasive and wastes a whole bullet.

Describe a music event that you didn't enjoy.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.

Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.

About 45 seconds on why you went there .
About 30 seconds on why you didn't like it .

— A big outdoor concert that failed

The event I'll describe was an open-air pop festival on the edge of Tashkent last August - three stages in a field behind the hippodrome, seven or eight acts, and easily the biggest concert of the summer.

I went with my two cousins, Aziz and Kamila, and a school friend of theirs I'd never met. The four of us travelled out in one overloaded taxi, packed in like sardines and shouting over the music, which in hindsight was the best part of the whole evening.

I'd wanted to see the headline band since school, and they'd been touring Europe for years without ever coming to Central Asia, so when Aziz sent me a photo of the tickets I said yes before I'd even checked the date. It was also his birthday plan, and you can't very well turn down something like that.

annotations.text: I'd wanted to see the headline band since school,
they'd been touring Europe for years
without ever coming to Central Asia,

blocks.text: It was a washout in every sense. The heavens opened at about eight, the field turned to mud, and the sound was so poor that the bass drowned out the vocals completely - the singer was out of tune, or the speakers were, and you genuinely couldn't tell which. We grinned and bore it for an hour, then called it a night and queued forty minutes for a taxi. If the organisers had spent half the ticket money on the sound system, it would have been a wonderful night.I've been avoiding open-air concerts ever since.
