wonderful night.I've been avoiding open-air concerts ever since.

blocks.text: — A small gig you had to sit through
The evening I have in mind was a free-jazz gig in a basement club off Sayilgoh Street - a trio, no support act, one set, two and a half hours, no interval.

I went with a colleague, Dilnoza, who twisted my arm for about a fortnight. She'd been going to that club since her student days and she talks about the place as if it were a religion. I've never worked out how to say no to her, which is how I ended up underground on a Thursday.

annotations.text: going to that club since her student days
I've never worked out how to say no to her,

blocks.text: I went partly out of politeness and partly because I'd been telling everyone at the office that I wanted to widen my musical taste - a mistake, because she'd remembered every single word of it. Her brother got the tickets free, so I had no excuse either. The music was self-indulgent from the first minute. The drummer took a solo that droned on for a good twenty minutes, the room was airless, and the drinks cost an arm and a leg. Worse, there were no gaps between the pieces, so there was no way to slip out without the whole room turning round. I spent the second half clock-watching and putting a brave face on it. Free jazz is clearly an acquired taste; had I started with something shorter and gentler, I might have got somewhere with it, and I've been meaning to give it one more try ever since.

annotations.text: cost an arm and a leg.
had I started with something shorter and
I've been meaning to give it one more try

Also resist ending after two negative sentences - say what you had expected instead, and the complaint turns into a story.

— A simple story about a family member

The person is my mother. She's forty-seven, she teaches maths at school number twenty- four in our neighbourhood, and she is the calmest woman alive indoors and the most nervous person I know outdoors.

Two winters ago I talked her into taking driving lessons. She'd been catching the same two buses to school for nearly twenty years, and by that autumn my father had had his knee operation, so he couldn't drive her any more. I found an instructor, a patient woman called Nodira, and paid for ten lessons before I told her.

annotations.text: She'd been catching the same two
buses to school for nearly twenty years,
by that autumn my father had had his knee

blocks.text: My mother is the sort of woman who digs her heels in the moment she feels pushed. Learning to drive at forty-seven was out of the question, she said: at her age, with her eyes, in Tashkent traffic. It took her a month to come round, and even then she agreed grudgingly, to one lesson only, purely to prove me wrong.

I kept pushing because I could see what those buses cost her: an hour and a half of every single day. She's been driving herself to work since March, and I've never seen her so pleased with herself. Being behind the wheel has given her a new lease of life. If I hadn't kept on at her that winter, she'd have talked herself out of it for good, and I'm glad she's finally taken the plunge.

annotations.text: She's been driving herself to work since March,

blocks.text: — If you prefer talking about a friend

This is about my closest friend, Bekzod. He works in a bank now, which suits him about as well as a suit suits a cat, and he has always had a knack for writing quiet, funny songs about ordinary Tashkent life.

— A child in your own family

The child I'd like to talk about is my cousin Malika, who's eight, from Fergana. She's the middle of three and by far the quietest, and she clearly takes after my aunt, who paints icons on wood. From an early age, all Malika has wanted is a pencil and paper.

I've known her since the day she was born — our families spend every Navruz together — but I only noticed it when I stayed with them for two summers. She'd been drawing on the corridor walls long before she could write her own name, and by then my aunt had given up trying to stop her and just painted over it twice a year.

blocks.text: Constantly. Not as a hobby — as a default setting. She scribbles on receipts in the car, she's glued to her sketchbook at family dinners, and last summer she covered every inch of an old wardrobe door with an underwater scene. I've watched her fill three sketchbooks this year alone, and she's been taking classes at the art school since September.

The child I'd describe is a boy called Bekzod, who was about seven when I met him. He was one of thirty children at a community centre in my neighbourhood where I volunteered on Saturdays, and easily the most silent child in the room.

I started helping there in my second year, mostly with English games. He'd been coming to the centre for over a month before he said a word to me, and he shied away from every group activity. He has an eye for detail most adults don't have; he'd count the wheels. He's been filling notebooks with buses ever since. I think it's simply how he talks. He can lose himself in one picture for an hour, completely engrossed — I've never seen a child concentrate like that — and he's utterly hooked on it. Drawing is where he comes out of his shell. The place I always think of is the old reading room on the third floor of the Navoi National Library in Tashkent. It's a stone's throw from my faculty, but it feels like another century — green desk lamps, parquet that creaks under your feet, and a librarian called Zulfiya who makes it very clear that phones are frowned upon.

I go twice a week, usually Tuesday and Friday mornings, when the place is nearly empty. I started in my first year because I'd been revising in noisy cafés, paying for coffee I didn't even want, and I had never been able to concentrate at home with the television on. I've been going almost every week since.

Mine is the pine section of the Tashkent Botanical Garden — right at the back, well off the beaten track, where hardly anybody bothers to walk. There's one wooden bench, a stand of pines planted in the sixties, and in April so much birdsong that you can hear it over the traffic outside.

I go two or three mornings a week, at the crack of dawn — about seven, before the gates get busy and before my first class. I started in my second year: I'd been living in a hostel room with three other lads who played music until two in the morning, and I had barely slept for a fortnight. I've been going ever since. Not a great deal, deliberately. I take a thermos of green tea, potter about with my old film camera for twenty minutes, and then just sit and let my mind wander — no headphones. Sometimes I walk one slow lap of the lake first and soak up the light coming through the branches, which honestly helps me unwind.

blocks.text: That hour is worth its weight in gold, because the rest of my day is made of other people's noise — flatmates, minibuses, group chats. What I like is how good-natured it is. Nobody stabs anybody in the back — when one contestant's sauce splits, three others abandon their own dishes to help. — An unusual building in your own country

The building I'd most like to see up close is the Kalta Minor in Khiva — the minaret that was never finished. The khan wanted the tallest tower in the Muslim world, the best part of seventy metres, and when he died the work ground to a halt at twenty-nine. So it simply stops, flat on top, like a pencil with no point.

I'd seen it on a banknote for years without asking what it was. Then last winter I came across a photograph of it under snow — turquoise against a grey sky — and it stopped me in my tracks. I've been reading about the Khiva khanate ever since, late at night, on my phone.

blocks.text: It is squat: much wider than it is tall, more like a giant tiled barrel than a tower. The whole thing is wrapped in glazed tiles in turquoise, white and green, in bands from the base to the flat top. Beside the slim minarets you usually see, it looks wrong, and that is exactly why I like it.

I want to go because I've never actually set foot in Khiva, which is embarrassing for someone who talks about architecture. I also like the idea of a building that failed and became famous for it. Had the khan lived another ten years, we'd have ended up with one more tall minaret. It is a one-off, and I want to tick it off this spring.

A cathedral that is a work in progress after a hundred and forty years strikes me as wonderfully strange.

I'd been studying for an architecture entrance exam when my tutor put a photograph of the interior on the screen, and the whole room went quiet. I hadn't even realised it was still unfinished — I assumed it was medieval. I've watched more documentaries about it than I would like to admit.

Inside is the part that gets me — the columns branch out overhead like a stone forest, and the stained glass turns the floor blue on one side and orange on the other. Photographs really don't do it justice. I want to see it while it is still unfinished, with the cranes up, because they've been promising to complete it for years and after that it becomes one more beautiful church. If I'd accepted my cousin's offer of a cheap flight last April, I'd have seen it by now — that still rankles. It is top of my list for the first free week I get.

The series I'd choose is Brooklyn Nine-Nine, an American comedy set in a police station in New York. It sounds like a crime show and it honestly isn't — nobody ever solves anything serious. It's twenty minutes of colleagues irritating each other in an office that happens to have handcuffs in it.

The main character is Jake Peralta, a detective in his thirties who behaves like a fourteen- year-old and is somehow excellent at his job. Opposite him is Captain Holt, his boss — completely deadpan, never raises an eyebrow, and every single line he says cracks me up. Then there's Amy, who colour-codes her folders and slowly wins you over.

Mostly it's how I wind down. I'd been working twelve-hour shifts at a call centre the autumn I found it, and bite-sized episodes were all my brain could handle. I'd heard friends talk about it for years and ignored them completely. Now I've seen every episode at least twice, and there's a running joke about Halloween bets that still makes me laugh.

The central figure is Valery Legasov, the scientist advising the commission — exhausted, frightened and honest at exactly the wrong moment. Beside him is Boris Shcherbina, a party official who arrives ready to play down the whole thing and gradually changes his mind. There's also Ulana Khomyuk, who keeps asking the questions nobody wants asked. Partly it's my own family. My grandmother had been living outside Kiev that spring, and nobody had told them anything for days; she still remembers the beautiful weather. Watching officials cover up the scale of it while children played outside was chilling, and it kept me on the edge of my seat as no thriller does. blocks.text: We had seats on the six o'clock Afrosiyob, and the station is forty minutes away, so there was no margin for error. I had to shower, load the boot with boxes of sweets and a suit bag, scrape frost off the windscreen and get three people out of the door by five. My mother insisted on making tea first, which nearly scuppered everything. As it was, we cut it fine and ran along the platform.

I was with my mother and younger sister. My sister is famously not a morning person — she came down with her eyes half shut and snapped at everyone for an hour. My mother, by contrast, was as bright as a button, humming in the kitchen at half four as if it were midday.

At the time I felt awful: groggy, cold and slightly sick from tea on an empty stomach. Dragging myself out of bed was the hardest part of the whole trip. Mine was a whole summer of early mornings, but I remember the first one perfectly. It was the June after my first university year, when I took a job at a bakery near Chorsu. The shift started at four, I'd never worked anywhere before, and it was a baptism of fire.

Dough must be handled while it is still warm, and if you are slow the whole morning goes down the drain. By half four I was up to my elbows in flour and completely wide awake, which surprised me.

I worked beside Rustam-aka, a baker in his sixties who had been getting up at three every day for thirty years and treated four o'clock as a civilised hour. He barely spoke — he's the sort who just gets on with it — but by sunrise he'd be telling stories and taking the mickey out of my technique. That first morning I felt like death warmed up. By the second week, though, something odd happened: I'd started waking a minute before the alarm, and it had become second nature. If I hadn't taken that job, I'd have slept until noon all summer and learnt nothing at all. I've been going to bed before eleven ever since, and I'm still an early riser.

So I put the whole thing on the back burner for a year. I weighed up what was left and took a junior analyst job at a logistics firm in Tashkent. At first it felt like failure, and it was daunting; everyone else was posting photographs of their new campuses. It took two months to come to terms with it. But the delay did pay off: I arrived with savings, better English and a supervisor who knew my name. Had everything gone to plan that July, I'd have been the youngest and least prepared person in the room, and I've never regretted that lost year.

The food I'd choose is plov — osh, as we call it. It's rice cooked with lamb, carrots, onions, cumin and whole heads of garlic in a huge cauldron called a kazan, and it's the food of every wedding in Uzbekistan.

Partly it's practical: one kazan feeds four hundred people, so for a wedding it's the only option. But it's also about status — the family pulls out all the stops, and everybody quietly judges the result, because the plov is the star of the show, not the cake. And it's hearty, which matters when guests arrive at six in the morning.

Everything is done from scratch, and it's always men who cook it. My uncle had been up since three the last time I watched — the meat browned first, then onions, then carrots cut into matchsticks by hand, never grated. They'd been soaking the rice in salted water for hours beforehand. Then the rice goes on top, then water, and it simmers away under a cloth for forty minutes.

I've been going to nahor oshi with my father since I was six, and I've eaten it hundreds of times without getting bored. My uncle's is second to none. If I'd tried to cook it myself, it would have been a disaster, so I tuck into it and keep quiet.

Mine is a Napoleon cake — the layered one, with a dozen paper-thin pastry sheets and custard between them, crumbs dusted on top. In our family it appears exactly once a year, on the thirty-first of December.

For Russian-speaking families here it's simply what New Year tastes like: Olivier salad, tangerines and a Napoleon. Nobody buys one; the whole point is that somebody in the family made it. Ours was handed down from my great-grandmother on a card written in pencil, and it takes pride of place on the table at midnight. It's genuinely painstaking. You make the dough, chill it, divide it into twelve balls and roll out each one until you can read through it. Each layer bakes in four minutes. The custard is the fiddly part — it splits if you look at it wrongly. My grandmother had been making it every New Year since the nineteen-seventies, and she'd learned the recipe from her own mother. Then it stands overnight so the layers soften.

Mine wasn't in a stadium at all. It was the Olympic boxing final two summers ago, when our heavyweight fought for gold. I'd been waiting for that fight for a fortnight, and he had come within a point of going out in the semi-final, so the whole country had it circled.

Nine of us, neighbours included, on the tapchan under blankets, tea going cold. Nobody even suggested recording it. In our family the point isn't the boxing; it's being in the same place at the same moment. Besides, by seven every group chat would have given the result away. So we stayed up, all nine of us, glued to a screen the size of a suitcase, and half the street was rooting for him.

The third round was so close that we were all on tenterhooks, my grandfather actually holding his breath. He won by a whisker, three judges to two, and the courtyard erupted — my aunt in tears, a car alarm going off. I had a lump in my throat myself, which never happens. Had that fight been shown at a sensible hour, half those neighbours would have watched it alone. I've watched the replay a dozen times, and I've been telling people about it ever since.

blocks.text: Describe a place you've travelled to that you'd recommend to others.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.

I'd like to talk about the Chimgan mountains, which are only about a two-hour drive from Tashkent. I went there last spring with two university friends, mainly because we'd been working flat out for months and we badly needed to recharge our batteries. I'd never actually been there before, which sounds ridiculous given how close it is.

We didn't plan a thing. We booked a tiny guesthouse and simply played it by ear. On the first day we hiked up to a ridge with absolutely breathtaking views over the valley — had we set off an hour later, we'd have missed the light completely. On the second we took the cable car and then sat by a stream doing precisely nothing for three hours.

annotations.text: we set off an hour later, we'd have missed the light completely.

blocks.text: What made it special was the silence. I've lived in the city my whole life, so being somewhere you can genuinely hear the wind was a breath of fresh air, literally and figuratively. If I hadn't switched my phone off, I don't think I'd have relaxed at all.

annotations.text: I've lived in the city my whole life,
If I hadn't switched my phone off, I don't think I'd have relaxed at all.

blocks.text: I've been recommending it to everyone ever since, because most tourists only see the historical cities and completely miss out on the natural side of the country. It's an hour off the main route, but it is well worth the detour.

annotations.text: I've been recommending it to everyone

blocks.text: The place I'd recommend is Istanbul. I went two years ago; it was my first trip abroad on my own, and I'd been saving up for it for the best part of a year.

I went partly out of curiosity. I'd heard so much about this city straddling two continents that I wanted to see whether it lived up to the hype. Had it disappointed me, I'd probably have given up on travelling altogether — but it absolutely didn't.

annotations.text: Had it disappointed me, I'd probably
have given up on travelling altogether

blocks.text: I did all the obvious things — the Blue Mosque, a ferry along the Bosphorus — but honestly the best part was stumbling across tiny back-street cafés with no plan at all. I also haggled in the Grand Bazaar for a lamp I definitely didn't need. If I'd booked a guided tour, I'd have seen more monuments and far less of the city.

blocks.text: I've been trying to go back ever since. It genuinely broadened my horizons, and it's the kind of place that gets under your skin: I was only there five days, and I've thought about it almost every week since. So yes, I'd recommend it to absolutely anyone.

blocks.text: The card says recommend to others, so a description of a nice holiday is not enough — you must at some point speak to a listener who might go. Save your last twenty seconds for that: who it suits, what to avoid, when to go. Candidates who skip it lose marks on task response.

Describe an important decision you made.
◆what the results of the decision were

How to use the one minute

The biggest decision I've made was turning down a university place. I'd passed the entrance exam in 2022, though not well enough for the faculty I wanted, so they offered me food technology instead. After three days I gave it up and registered to sit the exam again the next summer. On paper I was throwing away a whole year.

I was in two minds for those three days, mostly at two in the morning on the kitchen floor. My father wanted me to take it; my aunt kept saying a diploma is a diploma. What helped was weighing up how I'd feel at twenty-five rather than eighteen. I decided to sleep on it one more night, then stand my ground and tell them at breakfast.

The year itself was grim. I taught English to schoolchildren for pocket money and I'd been working through past papers for eleven months by the time the exam came round. It did pay off — nine points higher, and the faculty I wanted. The odd part is that those lessons decided my career: I've been teaching in some form ever since.

annotations.text: working through past papers for eleven months
I've been teaching in some form ever since.

blocks.text: It mattered because it was the first time I'd disagreed with my whole family and turned out to be right. I've approached every decision since with more confidence and I don't agonise over small things for weeks any more. Had I taken that place, I'd be finishing a food technology degree right now with no intention of using it.

annotations.text: I've approached every decision since with more confidence

blocks.text: — If you'd rather talk about work

Two years ago I handed in my notice at a bank and joined a four-person software company above a pharmacy on Amir Temur Street. The office had one window, the money was a third less, and everybody I knew thought I'd taken leave of my senses. I'd been at that bank for four years by then.

I'm not someone who acts on impulse, so I did it properly — a spreadsheet, two columns, six weeks of rewriting. The real evidence was that I'd been teaching myself to code at weekends for over a year and still looked forward to Saturday mornings. Then a friend there put in a good word for me, and it stopped being a daydream. The first six months were sink or swim. I had to take a pay cut, I made mistakes in front of people eight years younger, and twice I nearly asked for my old desk back. But I've learnt more in two years than in the previous four, and last spring they made me team lead. The company is nineteen people now, not four.

more in two years than in the previous four,

blocks.text: It was important because it broke an assumption — that a steady job is the only sensible kind — and in my family that idea runs deep. If I'd stayed at the bank, I'd have been comfortable and quietly bored for thirty years. I still get cold feet occasionally, and my brother has been threatening to do the same ever since, which is entirely my fault.

blocks.text: Bullets three and four look alike, and candidates often merge them into one vague sentence. Keep them apart: results are facts — what changed, in what order, how long it took — while importance is about you, what the decision proved or altered. If you run short, add one other person's reaction; that is always concrete, and it buys you twenty seconds.

In our third year we were put into fours for a marketing project, and my group was a real mixed bag. Dilnoza ran everything from a spreadsheet, Aziz was the ideas person who never wrote anything down, and Timur was flaky — he turned up to about half our meetings.

I didn't join it, exactly; we were assigned. But I'd been avoiding group work all year, because I'd had a miserable experience in the first semester, when I ended up writing everyone's slides at four in the morning. This time I decided to speak up in week two instead of quietly doing it all myself.

blocks.text: The task was a campaign for a local honey brand. I did the market research and the pricing, and I spent a lot of time ironing out arguments, because Dilnoza and Aziz didn't see eye to eye about anything, least of all the logo. We met the deadline at two in the morning, down to the wire as usual.

At the time I was furious, mostly at Timur, who got away with doing almost nothing. Looking back, we got the highest mark in the year group, and I learned to say what I think in a meeting. blocks.text: — If you'd rather talk about volunteering

Two summers ago I joined a volunteer group that renovated the library of a village school outside Kokand. There were about fifteen of us — students, two retired teachers and a carpenter called Rustam who did the work of three people. Nobody was formally in charge, but everybody pitched in, and we hit it off within a day.

My cousin forwarded the announcement on Telegram. I'd been feeling completely useless that summer — no job, no plans — and the school was the one my grandmother had taught in for thirty years, so it felt personal. I signed up the same evening, before I could talk myself out of it.

annotations.text: the school was the one my grandmother had taught

blocks.text: We took the room back to bare walls, sanded and repainted the shelves, and catalogued about two thousand books from scratch. My own job was the catalogue, which was back- breaking in its own way: four days on a plastic chair with a laptop and no fan. Rustam made light work of the carpentry. Honestly, it was the best fortnight of that year. There was a real sense of camaraderie — we ate together, argued about music and still finished on time, which for fifteen volunteers is close to running like clockwork. Had my cousin not forwarded that message, I'd have spent August scrolling. I've signed up for two more projects since.

annotations.text: Had my cousin not forwarded that message, I'd have
spent August scrolling. I've signed up for two more projects since.

blocks.text: What the team was like means the people, not the project, and most candidates describe the task without saying a word about anyone in the room. Name two or three of them and give each one detail: who kept the spreadsheet, who never turned up. Then how you felt needs two answers — at the time, and now.

The person I'd describe is our neighbour Gulnora opa, a woman in her fifties who lives four gates down from us and now has eleven people working for her. Nobody in our street would call her a businesswoman to her face.

I've known her since I was about six, mainly because her daughter and I walked to school together. So I've been watching this business grow from my own doorstep — I remember when it was one machine in a front room.

blocks.text: She makes school uniforms. It began when her husband lost his job in 2013; she'd been sewing for the neighbours for years anyway, and she simply turned her hand to doing it properly. She'd borrowed the money for that first machine from her brother and repaid him within eight months. She had to take on two assistants by the autumn; now there are eleven machines in a converted garage and a steady stream of orders from four districts.

blocks.text: Two things, I think. She is ferociously meticulous — she'll remake a whole jacket rather than send it out with a crooked pocket, which is how she made a name for herself. I've known the family since primary school and eaten at their table hundreds of times, so I heard it in pieces. He never calls it a success — he talks about the spring the crop froze. The house I'm thinking of is in old Bukhara, a stone's throw from the Lyabi-Hauz pool, down one of those lanes where two people can't pass without turning sideways. It belongs to my friend Aziza's grandparents, and it had been in her family for about a hundred and forty years.

blocks.text: From the lane it's deceptively plain: a blank mud wall and a low wooden door. Then you step into a courtyard with a pomegranate tree, a raised sitting platform, and carved columns propping up the balcony. The ceilings are painted faded red and green; every room smells of cold plaster. The whole place is frozen in time.

I went for a wedding — Aziza's cousin's — in the spring of 2023. I'd been to Bukhara twice as a tourist, but never inside a house like that. The family pulled out all the stops: they'd been getting it ready for nearly a month, whitewashing walls, borrowing quilts, cooking plov for two hundred people.

annotations.text: I'd been to Bukhara twice as
getting it ready for nearly a month,

blocks.text: As a guest I loved it; living there would be another matter. There's no real heating — in winter they huddle round a gas heater in one room — the bathroom is across the yard, and the roof needs work every spring. I've stayed there in February, and the romance wears off at four in the morning. Had it not been for that wedding, I'd never have realised what these houses demand. They are wonderful, and extremely high-maintenance.

annotations.text: Had it not been for that wedding, I'd never have realised what these

blocks.text: This one is the opposite: a flat on the twenty-second floor of a glass tower in Tashkent City, the new business district built where an old mahalla stood. It belongs to my uncle's business partner, and I'd never set foot in anywhere like it.

annotations.text: I'd never set foot in anywhere like it.

blocks.text: One enormous open room, floor-to-ceiling glass on two sides, a window that takes in the city as far as the mountains. Everything was white or grey — a state-of-the-art kitchen nobody appeared to cook in, a sofa the size of my bedroom — and there wasn't a hair out of place.

We went for dinner in December. My uncle dragged me along because his partner wanted to show the place off, and refusing would have been rude. I've been inside plenty of flats in Tashkent, but that was the first time I'd looked down on the traffic. We stayed four hours; I spent half of them at the glass. It's beautiful, but I couldn't last a month there. The glass turns it into a greenhouse by ten in July, the lift takes four minutes, and you never hear a neighbour. It felt sterile. If I'd grown up somewhere like that, I'd have missed the whole point of a mahalla — people shouting across the yard, a grandmother watching the street. I've been thinking about that evening ever since: it had everything except a sense of belonging, and that's the one thing a home can't do without.

I'll talk about Charvak, technically a reservoir rather than a lake, seventy kilometres north- east of Tashkent. It sits in a bowl of snow-capped mountains, the water is that crystal- clear turquoise you only see in photographs, and by our standards it is a stone's throw from the capital - ninety minutes in the car.

The main thing to know is that it is man-made. In the early seventies a dam was thrown across the Chirchiq river, and they'd flooded an entire valley to fill it - several villages went under, and people had been farming those slopes for centuries. The dam holds back the meltwater off the Tien Shan and turns much of it into electricity.

annotations.text: people had been farming those slopes for centuries.

blocks.text: It matters for two different reasons. Practically, much of the city's water and power starts there, which in a country this dry is no small thing. Socially, it is where everybody goes: by July the shoreline is teeming with families and the resorts up there draw in thousands of people every weekend.

For me it is personal as well. We've been driving up there every May since I was about six, always to the same picnic spot behind the rocks, and I've swum in that water more times than I can count. Had the valley never been flooded, half of Tashkent would have grown up without a single memory of open water - so whatever it cost, the lake comes into its own every summer.

than I can count. Had the valley never been flooded, half of Tashkent would have grown up
without a single memory of open water

blocks.text: If a lake counts, I'd choose the Aral Sea, in the far north-west on the border with Kazakhstan. Calling it a sea now is generous: it is a shadow of its former self.

annotations.text: a shadow of its former self.

blocks.text: It was once the fourth largest lake on earth. From the sixties onwards the two rivers that fed it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya - the lifeblood of the whole region - were siphoned off into cotton canals, and the water had been draining away for thirty years before anyone admitted the problem. By the nineties the shoreline had retreated more than a hundred kilometres from the town of Muynak. All of it happened within living memory: my grandfather remembers the fish factory working. It is important precisely because of what happened to it. Both rivers now run dry long before they reach what is left of it; salt blown off the old seabed has taken its toll on people's health, and the farmers there bear the brunt of it. Scientists have been warning about this for decades, and it is now a cautionary tale in every geography class.

annotations.text: the water had been draining away for thirty years

blocks.text: I've seen the photographs of the rusting boats at Muynak more times than I'd like. If those two rivers had been shared more sensibly, the sea would have survived in some form, and a hundred thousand people would still have work. That is why I'd choose it: an important lake is not always a beautiful one.

annotations.text: I've seen the photographs of the rusting boats at Muynak
two rivers had been shared more sensibly, the sea would have survived

blocks.text: This card has three bullets, not four, so most candidates dry up at ninety seconds. Treat what you know about it generously - how it was formed, who lives on it, what it looked like when your grandparents were young. And note the words in your country: the Volga or the Nile will cost you marks, however much you know about them.

blocks.text: Describe a thing you did to learn a language.

How to use the one minute

— A quiet habit you did alone

The language is English. I'd been studying it at school since the fifth form, so I could read almost anything, but the second anyone asked me a question out loud I went tongue-tied. By my second year I had clearly hit a plateau.

annotations.text: I'd been studying it at school since the fifth form,

blocks.text: So I started a voice diary. Every night at eleven I recorded three minutes of myself on my phone, talking about whatever had happened that day — the canteen queue, an argument with my brother, nothing clever. Then, the painful part, I listened back to it. I kept a list of my repeated mistakes and tried to iron out one a week, and I made myself stick at it for a hundred days.

I've paid for two speaking courses, and neither did as much. The earliest recordings still make me cringe — enormous silences, 'how to say', four adjectives. By day sixty I could think on my feet, because I'd rehearsed unprepared speech two thousand times. In the mock exam I could feel it paying off: the examiner asked about my weekends and I just talked.

annotations.text: I've paid for two speaking courses,
I'd rehearsed unprepared speech two thousand times.

blocks.text: At first I hated the sound of my own voice so much I nearly stopped in week one. Now speaking English is close to second nature, and the diary is the reason. If I hadn't kept those files, I would have missed how much had changed.I've been recommending the same trick to every student I know ever since.

blocks.text: — If you learned it outside a classroom

I'd like to talk about Russian, which I learned by accident, nowhere near a classroom. My uncle keeps a stall selling car parts just off Chorsu bazaar, and the summer I turned sixteen he needed somebody behind the counter on Saturdays.

So for two summers I stood there from seven in the morning. Nearly every customer spoke Russian — drivers, mechanics, older women wanting a bulb changed — and I was thrown in at the deep end within the first hour. I'd never spoken a full sentence to a stranger in Russian before that day. I learned to strike up a conversation while I hunted for a part, and I picked up more slang in one summer than in six years of lessons. It has helped me more than any textbook ever did. My Russian came on in leaps and bounds, because there was no escape: you can't say 'repeat, please' to a queue of eight men. I got the hang of the polite forms by copying the customers, and I stopped worrying about making a fool of myself by week three.

It has helped me more than any textbook ever did.

blocks.text: I'd been dreading those Saturdays for the whole first month — I'd go home with a headache. Looking back, I'm grateful, and my uncle's patience rubbed off on me too. Had he not needed cheap help that summer, I'd still be too shy to open my mouth in Russian.I've been using it at work every week since.

Describe a law on environmental protection.

How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on what the law is .
About 30 seconds on how you first learned about it .
About 45 seconds on who benefits from this law .
About 30 seconds on how you feel about it .

— A local law you have seen working

The law I'd choose is the ban on burning leaves and dry grass, tightened a few years ago. Before that, every October the whole mahalla vanished under a blanket of smoke: people raked their gardens into a pile and set fire to it, and the authorities turned a blind eye. Now there is a hefty fine.

I'd been complaining about that smoke for years without knowing anything had changed. Then our neighbour Anvar-aka was fined a million som, and the story spread like wildfire through the courtyard. I've never seen a man look so astonished as he did holding that paperwork. I'd never thought of a bonfire as a crime until that afternoon.

annotations.text: I'd been complaining about that smoke for years
I've never seen a man look so astonished
I'd never thought of a bonfire as a crime

blocks.text: The obvious winners are children and anyone with weak lungs — my nephew spends every autumn wheezing into an inhaler. But the city gains too: Tashkent is already plagued by bad air all winter, and leaf smoke is one of the few sources we can control. It's the low- hanging fruit of air pollution.

I'm broadly in favour, though the law doesn't go far enough. If you fine people for burning leaves, you must give them somewhere to put them, and many neighbourhoods still have no green-waste collection. Had the city introduced bins alongside the fines, people would have accepted it far more readily. As it is, some still burn after dark, which defeats the object — although the air has been getting cleaner every autumn since.

annotations.text: Had the city introduced bins alongside the fines,
the air has been getting cleaner every autumn since.

blocks.text: The law I'd describe isn't ours — it's the German bottle deposit, the Pfand. Every plastic bottle and can carries a twenty-five-cent deposit, which you get back when you feed it into a machine at the supermarket. Bin it and you are literally throwing money away.

I'd been following my cousin's studies in Leipzig through voice messages, and one night he sent a video of a machine that gobbled up his empties and printed a coupon. He'd collected them from his flatmates all week and got nine euros back — enough for dinner. It's the sort of thing that sticks in your mind. Everybody benefits. Recycling plants get clean, sorted plastic, not rubbish. Shoppers get their money back, so nobody is out of pocket. And there's an informal economy of students and pensioners collecting bottles in parks, which kills two birds with one stone: the parks stay clean and someone earns a little. The rivers benefit most.

annotations.text: I'd been following my cousin's studies in Leipzig
collected them from his flatmates all week
kills two birds with one stone:

blocks.text: I think it's brilliant, because it doesn't rely on people being good — it relies on them being careful with money, which is far more reliable. I've often wondered why we don't copy it, and I've been saving bottles in a sack ever since — admittedly a drop in the ocean. If we'd brought in something similar ten years ago, the Chirchiq would have far less plastic in it today. It wouldn't be cheap, but in the long run it would pay dividends.

annotations.text: I've often wondered why we don't copy it,
I've been saving bottles in a sack ever since
brought in something similar ten years ago, the Chirchiq would have far less plastic in it

blocks.text: You are not being tested on law, so don't stall trying to recall an official title — a rule with a fine attached is enough. The real danger is drifting into a Part 3 essay about pollution in general. Stay with one law, one story of how you heard about it, and one honest opinion, including what the law still fails to do.

topics.title: Special Day Out That Didn't Cost a Lot

blocks.text: Describe a special day out that didn't cost a lot.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on what you did .
About 30 seconds on when it was .

It was nothing more than a bike ride and a picnic. We decided to throw together a meal from whatever was in the fridge - non, tomatoes, boiled eggs, a thermos of tea - and rode out along the Bo'zsuv canal until the city stopped. The day cost us next to nothing: forty thousand som.

It was the second Sunday in May, with not a cloud in the sky and scorching by two, which is how we ended up in the water fully dressed. We'd been planning something far grander - Charvak, a hired car - but the driver had let us down the night before.

annotations.text: not a cloud in the sky
We'd been planning something far grander
the driver had let us down the night before.

blocks.text: I went with my younger brother Sardor and two friends from my faculty. Sardor is fifteen and normally impossible to prise off his computer, so getting him out of the flat before nine felt like a victory.

What made it special was that nothing was planned. We ate under a willow, slept for an hour, then drank tea while the light went orange - the perfect way to wind down. Later we decided to make a day of it and stayed until dark: a change of scene for the price of a bus ticket. If that car hadn't fallen through, we'd have spent five times as much and remembered half as much.I've been back to that bridge twice since, because the best days out are the ones done on a shoestring.

remembered half as much.I've been back to that bridge twice since,

blocks.text: — A quiet day with an older relative

I spent an entire Saturday pottering around the old town in Bukhara on foot: the pool at Lyabi-Hauz, the covered bazaars, and the history museum, which happened to be free of charge that weekend for the city's anniversary. Lunch was two samsas each from a bakery behind the mosque.

It was early October, two years ago, and it happened on the spur of the moment: my grandmother rang on the Friday evening to say the museum was free next day. I'd been putting that visit off for three years - I'd promised twice and cancelled twice - so this time I took the night train.

annotations.text: on the spur of the moment:
putting that visit off for three years
I'd promised twice and cancelled twice

blocks.text: It was just the two of us, which had never happened before. She is seventy-eight, walks about as fast as the queue moves, and knows everything. Crossing the bustling bazaar, she filled me in on who had lived in which street before the war, and which door used to be a bakery. Halfway through the afternoon it dawned on me that I had never spent a full day alone with her. Then she stopped outside a low blue door and said, that is the house I was born in - and I had a lump in my throat for the rest of the street. I've never told her that, but I treasure that Saturday, and the whole thing cost two train fares. Had I cancelled on her one more time, I'd never have had that day at all.

The examiner is listening for didn't cost a lot, so put a real number in - the bus fare, what lunch cost - rather than saying it was cheap. And why it was special is the bullet candidates rush at the end. Decide before you start speaking what the special part was, then spend your last thirty seconds on it.

Describe a time when you ogranized a happy event successfully.
◆say whether it was easy or difficult

How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on what the event was .
About 30 seconds on when and where it was .
About 45 seconds on say whether it was easy or difficult .
About 30 seconds on how you prepared .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.

The event was a surprise sixtieth birthday party for my grandmother — about forty people, mostly relatives, plus three colleagues from the school where she taught. The surprise part was mine, which meant keeping the whole thing under wraps for six weeks.

It happened in September, two years ago, in the courtyard of our family house in Yunusobod — the grapevine gives shade there until October. We'd been planning it since June, in a group chat that my grandmother, who owns a smartphone, was very deliberately not added to.

Honestly? Difficult, but not for the reasons you'd expect. The cooking was fine — my aunts offered to lend a hand and the plov was ready by two. The hard part was the secrecy. By the final week two of my cousins had already let something slip, and my mother invented a dentist appointment to get her out of the house. I've never seen my grandmother speechless before.

annotations.text: final week two of my cousins had already let something slip,

blocks.text: We did it on a shoestring, about a million so'm. I borrowed lights from a neighbour, pegged old photographs along a string, and spent a hectic final afternoon setting up tables and putting the finishing touches to the courtyard. If my cousins hadn't kept her talking at the gate, none of it would have worked — but we pulled it off, and I've been telling the story ever since. I never expected it to go off without a hitch.

annotations.text: If my cousins hadn't kept her talking at
the gate, none of it would have worked

blocks.text: Two summers ago I organised the end-of-year concert for the small language centre where I was teaching. Around a hundred and twenty people came — students, parents, a few teachers from other schools — and eleven groups performed sketches and songs in English.

It was the last Saturday in May, in a hired hall belonging to a music college near Mustaqillik. Finding the venue took the longest: I'd been ringing round halls for three weeks, and two of them had already cancelled on us before I found that one. It was far harder than I had imagined. I had a nasty feeling early on that I was about to bite off more than I could chew, because I was handling the logistics, the rehearsal timetable and the sound system single-handed. Two whole evenings went on ironing out the running order, since every teacher wanted their group to perform last.

annotations.text: I'd been ringing round halls for three
two of them had already cancelled on us
off more than I could chew,

blocks.text: We had run through the entire programme twice that week, and I kept a meticulous list on my phone: microphones, water, a spare laptop, printed certificates. My director doubted a school concert would draw a crowd; in the end we ran out of chairs. I've organised three more since then and I've been using the same checklist every time. Had that first hall not cancelled on us, we'd never have found a room with proper acoustics. Watching it all come together that evening was the best hour of my year.

annotations.text: I've been using the same checklist every time. Had
that first hall not cancelled on us, we'd never have found a room with proper acoustics.

blocks.text: The third bullet is an instruction rather than a topic: say whether it was easy or difficult. Answer it in one clear sentence and then justify it, or the examiner hears description where a judgement was asked for. Remember the word successfully as well — offer one piece of evidence that it worked, such as guests staying until midnight or running out of chairs.

Describe an occasion when you got stuck in a traffic jam.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.

About 30 seconds on how often you do this .

About 30 seconds on why you dislike it .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.

The occasion that sticks in my mind was a drive out to Tashkent airport to meet my aunt, who was flying in from Istanbul. It's twenty-five kilometres from our flat in Yunusobod, and normally takes forty minutes. We set off at half past five on a Sunday evening in November, in heavy rain.

I only make that trip three or four times a year, whenever somebody in the family travels. But I drive across the city daily, so I know which junctions grind to a halt at rush hour and which are fine. I have been driving here for six years, and the traffic has got noticeably worse.

annotations.text: I have been driving here for six years,

blocks.text: We had been crawling along for about twenty minutes when everything stopped dead: a lorry had shed its load near the ring-road junction. Nobody could tell us what the hold-up was, and we sat bumper to bumper for over an hour. By the time we reached the terminal, my aunt had already collected her suitcase and was waiting outside in the rain. To make matters worse, my phone had died.

annotations.text: We had been crawling along for about twenty minutes
By the time we reached the terminal,
my aunt had already collected her suitcase

blocks.text: What I dislike is not the waiting so much as the helplessness. You can't reverse, you can't walk, and you sit watching the clock knowing somebody is waiting for you. We had cut it fine, as usual. I rarely lose my temper in a car, but I came close — if we had left an hour earlier, none of it would have happened.

annotations.text: if we had left an hour
earlier, none of it would have happened.

blocks.text: The time I always think of was the morning of my first job interview, at an office just off Amir Temur Square. I was living in Sergeli, at the opposite end of Tashkent, roughly fifty minutes by taxi on a normal day.

I did that journey every weekday for two years, so I know the route far too well. Traffic builds up from about seven, and by half past eight the whole of Chilonzor is gridlocked. I have never once managed it in under an hour midweek. This was in December, on the first morning of proper snow. It had been snowing since about four, and the city had not gritted a single road. The taxi moved at a snail's pace for forty minutes and then stopped altogether. I sat there on edge, gritting my teeth, watching the meter and the clock. In the end I gave up on the taxi, paid the driver, walked six blocks through the slush and hopped on the metro.

annotations.text: have never once managed it in under an hour

blocks.text: Oddly, it turned out to be a blessing in disguise. I arrived nine minutes late and soaked, but the interviewer had been stuck too, so we started by laughing about it. Had I stayed in that taxi, I would have missed the interview altogether.I have been taking the metro ever since, and I always leave plenty of time now. What I hate about jams is the powerlessness: you can do nothing but sit.

annotations.text: that taxi, I would have missed the interview altogether.I have been taking the metro ever

blocks.text: Bullet two quietly changes the tense on you: how often you do this means the journey, not the jam, so you need present-simple habit language in the middle of a past story. And why you dislike it asks for a feeling — helplessness, wasted hours, the person waiting at the other end — not simply that it is boring.

Describe a long-term goal you would like to achieve.

My long-term goal isn't glamorous at all: I want to own a flat of my own in Tashkent before I turn thirty — two rooms, a balcony, anywhere on the metro line. I'm dead set on it, because getting a foot on the property ladder here is harder every single year.

annotations.text: a foot on the property ladder

blocks.text: I've had the idea in my head since my second year at university, so roughly five years. It started the winter our landlord raised the rent twice and my mother had to borrow money from her sister. Back then it felt like a pipe dream — I'd never even opened a savings account.

annotations.text: I've had the idea in my head since my second year at university,
I'd never even opened a savings

blocks.text: Slowly, is the honest answer. I've been putting about a third of my salary into a separate account for two years, squirrelling it away where I can't see it, and I translate documents at weekends. My brother and I will scrape together a deposit between us. It means tightening our belts — no holidays, no new phone — but you chip away at it.

annotations.text: I've been putting about a third of my salary into a separate

blocks.text: Why? Because renting means somebody else decides how long you stay in your own home. If my parents had bought their flat in the nineties instead of renting, our whole family life would have been calmer. I want that kind of stability for my own children, and for the first time it feels genuinely within reach.

annotations.text: If my parents had bought their flat in the nineties instead of renting, our whole family life

blocks.text: Mine is a long one. I want to qualify as a clinical psychologist and open a proper counselling centre in Namangan, my home city, where there is essentially nothing of the kind. Not a private clinic for wealthy families — something ordinary, that a teacher or a taxi driver could actually afford.

I've wanted this since I was seventeen, so about seven years. A friend of mine had a terrible year at school and there was simply nobody for him to talk to; the word itself carried such a stigma that his family pretended nothing was wrong. I'd been planning to study economics right up until that autumn.

annotations.text: I've wanted this since I was seventeen,

blocks.text: Realistically it's another six or seven years. I've been shadowing a psychologist at a clinic in Chilanzar since January, I finish my master's next summer, and then I have to rack up two thousand supervised hours, which nobody warns you about. After that I'd build the practice from scratch — a rented room, two chairs and word of mouth. You simply have to stick at it. I set my sights on this because of that friend. One counsellor in a city of six hundred thousand won't fix anything on its own, but it would make a dent in the problem. Had I not watched how quickly he recovered once he finally got help, I'd probably have drifted into banking like everyone else. I'm in it for the long haul.

watched how quickly he recovered once he finally got help,

The friend I want to talk about is Sardor, who I sat next to from the second year of school to the eleventh. I've known him since we were about seven. He's the calmest person I know, which matters, because the year I'm describing was anything but calm.

blocks.text: In our final year he won a state-funded place at the University of World Economy and Diplomacy — a grant, not a paid place, which here means about one applicant in twenty. He did it against all odds: his father had been seriously ill since the previous autumn, and the family were struggling to make ends meet.

blocks.text: He got a job at a bakery near Qo'yliq — the night shift, ten until six — then went straight to school. He'd been doing that for four months before any of us found out. He'd sleep two hours in the afternoon, then knuckle down with past papers until midnight. It was relentless, and it was starting to take its toll: he lost about eight kilos that winter.

The person I'd describe is Kamila, a friend from my old neighbourhood. We're not especially close now, but our mothers are, so I've followed her story from a distance. She's a judoka — she started at eleven, at a small club above a shop on Amir Temur Street.

Two years ago she took bronze at the national championships in her weight category, which sounds modest until you know that a year earlier the surgeon had told her she would probably never compete again. She'd torn a ligament at a training camp, the recovery was excruciating, and nobody expected her to bounce back.

annotations.text: the surgeon had told her she would

blocks.text: Everyone around her was quietly waiting for her to throw in the towel. She'd been training six days a week since she was eleven, and suddenly she was doing forty minutes of leg exercises while the others sparred. She did that for a year. She set her sights on one specific tournament, changed coaches, and taught herself to attack on the other side entirely. It was sheer grit, nothing else.

annotations.text: six days a week since she was eleven,

blocks.text: I was proud because people who should have known better were quick to write her off, and she never argued — she just trained. I've never seen anyone work that hard. If she'd taken that advice, she'd have stopped at nineteen and always wondered. She's gone from strength to strength since, and she's been coaching a girls' group at weekends. I'm honestly not sure I'd have what it takes.

The one that still makes me feel ill is the night my laptop refused to start. No warning at all — I closed the lid, opened it twenty minutes later and got a black screen with one line of white text. It had crashed completely out of the blue, and I'm terrible at backing up anything.

It was a Sunday evening in May, in my hostel room, fourteen hours before a coursework deadline. I'd been working on that essay for three solid weeks, and I had saved every version to the desktop and nowhere else. Panic set in almost immediately.

blocks.text: It was well beyond me. I know how to restart a machine and clear some space, but that's it. I spent four hours on trial and error — safe mode, a recovery disc, three YouTube tutorials in Russian — and by two in the morning I was at my wits' end. The hostel wifi kept dropping, which made it impossible to get to the bottom of anything.

In the end my flatmate Jasur remembered his brother's USB caddy — you take the hard drive out and read it like a memory stick. That little plastic box was a lifesaver: every file was intact and I submitted at nine. Had I spent forty cents on a memory stick in September, I'd have slept that night. I've been backing everything up to two clouds since, and I've never trusted that laptop again.

Mine is a small-business one. My mother had been taking cake orders through a Telegram bot for about a year, and on the busiest morning of her year — the day before Navruz — the thing chose to go down. Customers kept messaging, but not one order reached her list, so she was swamped with enquiries she couldn't even see.

I had set the whole system up myself the previous autumn, so it was very much my mess to clear up. Harder than anything in my degree, honestly. It wasn't a glitch you could see: the bot was online, it simply wasn't passing anything on. I spent two hours troubleshooting blindly — restarting the server, checking the token, racking my brains — before I managed to narrow it down to an expired webhook.

If I hadn't kept a copy of the customer list in that spreadsheet, we'd have lost about forty orders and a fair bit of my mother's reputation. I've built two more bots since, and I've been checking that webhook every Monday morning ever since.

The problem was, in hindsight, gloriously stupid. Two days before a coursework deadline my laptop refused to turn on — no light, no fan, nothing. I'd been writing that essay straight onto the desktop for four weeks, and I'd never backed a single file up in my life. A month of work sitting on a drive I couldn't reach.

blocks.text: It happened last November, in my room, at eleven at night. I tried the obvious things — a different cable, holding the power button down, some shouting — and by midnight I was frantic. By one I was at my wits' end, so as a last resort I messaged my flatmate's cousin Bek, who repairs computers at the market near Malika.

He told me to bring it in at nine. He listened for four seconds, said 'power board' off the top of his head, and had the case open before I'd sat down. He clearly knows his way around a motherboard — the drive came out, went into a caddy, and my files were on a memory stick inside twenty minutes. Then he waved away the extra money I offered.

He was an absolute lifesaver; I submitted with two hours to spare. I've never trusted a hard drive since, so now I back up everything to the cloud twice a week, and I've been taking everything to him ever since. I still owe him one. Had my flatmate not mentioned his name that night, I'd have handed in half an essay.

blocks.text: — If you'd rather describe a teacher

My problem was paperwork, which sounds dull but very nearly cost me a place at university. I was applying abroad, and my school certificate spelled my surname one way while my passport spelled it another — a single letter. The admissions system rejected the file automatically, and the deadline was eleven days away.

This was in the spring of my final year, outside the staff room. I read the email on my phone and decided it was the end of the road. Nobody in my family had dealt with notarised translations, so I was at a loss — and I'd been putting the whole thing off for a fortnight out of embarrassment.

annotations.text: I'd been putting the whole thing off for a

blocks.text: My English teacher, Nodira opa, offered to take it upon herself to fix it. She rang the registry office and discovered, as luck would have it, that a correction certificate exists for this. She gave up a Saturday — bus, queue, notary, second queue — and wrote a covering letter in a tone I could never manage: polite, firm, faintly threatening. She cut through weeks of red tape in a day.

I felt relief and, underneath it, shame, because I'd assumed adults were too busy to be bothered with me. If I hadn't finally messaged her, I'd have missed that deadline by a week. What I took from it is simple: swallow your pride and ask, because the person you're afraid of troubling usually doesn't bat an eyelid. She's been asking about my results ever since.

Bullet three needs real steps — what they said, where they took you, how long it took — and save twenty seconds for how you felt, which should be something more interesting than grateful.

Describe a time when you changed your opinion.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on what the original opinion was .
About 30 seconds on why you changed it .
About 45 seconds on when it was .
About 30 seconds on how you felt about it .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.
— A simple, everyday change of mind

For years I was adamant that learning to cook was a waste of time. My mother offered to teach me and I turned my nose up at it. I genuinely thought it was something you absorbed automatically, like walking, or something you paid other people to do. I could manage tea and fried eggs, and that was that.

Then I moved into a rented flat with two friends and had to fend for myself. For about six weeks I chose to live on somsa, instant noodles and shop bread. I felt awful — no energy, permanently tired — and I was constantly out of pocket, because I'd been telling myself that takeaway food was cheaper. It isn't.

That was in my second year, the winter of 2022. The turning point was a Sunday in December when my grandmother talked me through plov on the phone, step by step, for forty minutes. I'd never cooked anything with more than three ingredients before. It came out slightly grey, and I was still absurdly proud of it.

annotations.text: I'd never cooked anything with more than three ingredients before.

blocks.text: At first I felt stupid, because I'd been dismissing something my whole family does well, and I had to eat my words in front of my mother. Now it is second nature: I've made plov almost every Sunday since, and it was a genuine change of heart, not just a new habit. If I hadn't been forced to feed myself, I'd have learned nothing at all.

annotations.text: I'd been dismissing something my whole family does well,
hadn't been forced to feed myself, I'd have learned nothing at all.

blocks.text: I used to believe, quite firmly, that people are born either good or bad at languages. It is easy to write yourself off at fourteen, and that is exactly what I did after a teacher told me my accent was hopeless. From then on I treated effort as beside the point.

What changed my mind was watching a classmate, Sardor, go from a 4.5 to a 7.5 in eight months. He was not gifted; he was relentless — an hour of listening before school every morning, and a notebook of his own mistakes that he actually reread. I'd been blaming my genes for something that came down to putting in the hours.

It was two years ago, in March, and I can date it exactly because of one conversation on the bus home. He showed me that notebook and told me he had rewritten the same twelve mistakes for a month. That was the moment the penny dropped. I'd assumed all along that he was simply lucky. I felt cheated at first, and then embarrassed, because I had spent four years treating my own ability as set in stone. Had I understood that at fourteen, I'd have started properly years earlier. In the end it was a wake-up call: I've been keeping the same kind of notebook ever since, my speaking has improved more in two years than in the previous ten, and I am finally making real headway.

annotations.text: Had I understood that at fourteen, I'd have started properly
I've been keeping the same kind of notebook
ever since, my speaking has improved more in two years than in the previous ten,

blocks.text: The card is really about two beliefs, and most candidates describe only one. Spend your first twenty seconds arguing the old opinion as though you still held it — that is what makes the change worth hearing. And when it was wants one dated moment, not a vague period: a single conversation, a single evening. It also keeps your tenses steady.

Describe a time when you sent a message or an email to someone but received no reply for a long time.

How to use the one minute

About 30 seconds on what it was about .

About 30 seconds on how you felt about the experience .

— A story about an old friend

I sent it to Aziz, who was my closest friend all through school. His family moved to Kazan when we were seventeen, and we'd been messaging almost every day until then. Afterwards it thinned out to birthdays, then nothing, and we drifted apart completely. I've never been good at keeping in touch.

annotations.text: we'd been messaging almost every day
never been good at keeping in touch.

blocks.text: Then last March I saw on Instagram that his grandfather had died — the same grandfather who used to drive us to football. So I dropped him a line on Telegram. Nothing clever: condolences, one memory about that car, and a line asking how he was. It took me forty minutes to write four sentences.

He read it within the hour — two blue ticks — and then nothing. I was left on read for five months, and eventually stopped checking. Then, completely out of the blue, at two in the morning, a voice message arrived: eleven minutes long, his voice sheepish and older, explaining that he had spent most of that spring in hospital.

annotations.text: he had spent most of that spring in hospital.

blocks.text: For those five months I did take it personally, and spent weeks overthinking every sentence — wrong tone, too late, too familiar. Had he never replied at all, I'd have gone on assuming I'd said something wrong. Instead we picked up where we left off, which was a weight off my mind. I've been answering people much faster ever since: silence usually says more about someone's life than about you.

picked up where we left off,

blocks.text: — If you prefer a work story

Mine was an email rather than a message. It went to the founder of a small design studio in Almaty whose work I'd been following on Behance for a year. I had no contact there — I just used the address on their website.

It was two paragraphs asking for a summer internship, unpaid if necessary, with eleven pieces of work attached. I'd been putting that portfolio together all winter, and I reread it eight or nine times before pressing send, because it felt like putting myself out there for the first time. Nothing came back for three months. I chased it up twice, politely, and both reminders fell on deaf ears — not even a stock reply about the volume of applications. Being left in limbo was worse than a straight no, and by May I'd given up on it and taken a job in a call centre. Then in June the founder did finally get back to me.

blocks.text: Two lines, an apology, and an offer to meet in September. His explanation was that he had disappeared onto a film project for two months and was completely snowed under, which I believe, though a single line would have taken nine seconds. If I hadn't sent that second reminder, I'd have heard nothing at all.I've applied for a lot of things since, and I've been telling younger students the same thing: silence is not a verdict on your work.

Answer it explicitly — yes or no, and how long the wait was — because that is the turn the whole story needs. Note also that how you felt covers two moments: during the silence and after the answer arrived. Contrast them and the ending writes itself.

blocks.text: Describe an ad with a famous person in it.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.

About 45 seconds on where you can see it .

The ad I always come back to actually has two people in it: Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. They're the footballers my whole generation grew up arguing about — I'd spent years defending Messi in the school playground — and they have been household names here since I was about eight.

annotations.text: years defending Messi in the school playground

blocks.text: It's a Louis Vuitton campaign, shot by Annie Leibovitz just before the 2022 World Cup. The two of them are bent over a chessboard balanced on one of those brown monogrammed trunks, mid-game, completely absorbed. The board is a nod to the rivalry. Nobody holds anything up to the camera: it's the opposite of the in-your-face advertising we usually get, and understated almost to the point of arrogance.

A photograph like that is built to go viral, and it did: I saw it on Instagram two days before I saw it anywhere physical. I've since spotted it as a full page in an in-flight magazine and on a lightbox at the airport, and people have been recreating it with their own photos ever since.

I like it a lot, and I'm mildly annoyed with myself, because I couldn't afford a single thing in that picture. If the two of them had been grinning at the camera holding handbags, I'd have scrolled straight past. Instead it lets you cotton on by yourself, which is what makes it stick in your mind. It gives the viewer some credit.

annotations.text: If the two of them had been grinning at the camera holding handbags, I'd have

blocks.text: — A local ad you cannot escape

Mine is a local one. The face in it is Bakhodir Jalolov, our Olympic heavyweight champion, an enormous man from Sariosiyo who won gold in Tokyo and again in Paris. He'd been fairly unknown outside boxing until that first medal; now he is plastered across half the billboards in the country.

annotations.text: fairly unknown outside boxing until that first medal;

blocks.text: It's for one of our banks, a payment app essentially. Thirty seconds: he wraps his hands, hits the bag, stops, taps his phone once, and the transfer goes through. The camera cuts between the gym and an ordinary kitchen where somebody's mother receives the money. The final line is about strength being simple. It isn't subtle, but it is well put together. Everywhere is the honest answer — the thing is inescapable. I've been seeing it before every YouTube video I open for about six months, there are two versions on television, and a billboard the size of a house on the ring road near Yunusabad. My eight-year-old brother can recite it word for word.

annotations.text: every YouTube video I open for about six months,

blocks.text: Mixed feelings. The first few times I thought it was rather good; by the fiftieth I was sick to death of it. And yet I've had to admit that it works — my father had never used a payment app in his life, and he signed up for that one in March. Had they picked a singer rather than a boxer, I don't think he'd have bothered. So, grudgingly, it does the job.

blocks.text: The commonest failure here is a biography: ninety seconds on the celebrity's career and ten on the advertisement itself. Bullet two wants the content — say what actually happens, shot by shot, in the present tense. Bullet three deserves ten seconds at most, so spend what you save explaining why the ad works on you personally.

The most boring place I know is the waiting hall of a public services office in Tashkent - a ticket machine at the door, forty grey plastic chairs bolted to the floor, one screen on the wall that changes number every four minutes. No windows, soul-destroying lighting.

I went with my mother, in March, to sort out a document for her pension. She'd taken the whole morning off work, and we had both assumed an hour would be plenty. We pulled ticket B-114 out of the machine while the screen showed B-61.

Nothing. That is the point. We killed time on our phones for half an hour, and then the signal died. My mother will strike up a conversation with anybody, so she spent an hour comparing vegetable prices with the woman beside her; I stared into space and counted ceiling tiles. We'd been sitting on those chairs for nearly three hours before our number came up.

annotations.text: We'd been sitting on those chairs for nearly three hours

blocks.text: It was boring because there was nothing to look at and nothing you were allowed to do: you can't go for a coffee in case you miss your turn, so time drags on as it does nowhere else. It was like watching paint dry, except with the queue crawling at a snail's pace and the fear of losing your place. Had I known it would take four hours, I'd have brought a book. They've been promising to put the whole system online for years.

annotations.text: Had I known it would take four hours, I'd have brought a book.
They've been promising to put the whole system online for years.

blocks.text: — A whole week with nothing to do

A different kind of boring: a small town in the Jizzakh steppe where my father's relatives live. Two shops, one café that shut at seven, a main street, a bus stop, and flat brown land in every direction. It is the middle of nowhere - a one-horse town in the literal sense.

I went with my younger sister for ten days one August, while our parents were working. We'd imagined swimming in the canal and long walks at sunset; that lasted a day and a half. Our cousins are lovely, but they'd been living that rhythm their whole lives and couldn't see what we were waiting for. We wandered around the same three streets. We ate. We watched a Turkish series dubbed into Russian with our aunt every afternoon at four. I twiddled my thumbs through the hottest hours, which was stifling - forty-two degrees and no air conditioning - and I counted down the days on the kitchen calendar, which is a shameful thing to admit.

they'd been living that rhythm their whole lives

blocks.text: It was boring because nothing was ever chosen. At home, if I'm at a loose end, I can go somewhere; there, the day decided itself, and by the fourth morning I had proper cabin fever. I've thought about it a lot since, though: I slept nine hours a night and finished two books. If I'd packed a few more of those, I'd have called that week a holiday rather than a sentence.

annotations.text: I've thought about it a lot since, though:
If I'd packed a few more of those, I'd have called that week a holiday rather than a

Specifics are never dull. And don't let who you went there with shrink to one word; that person is your only source of a story, and candidates almost always skip past them.

The video I'd like to describe is a twenty-five-minute restoration film on YouTube. A man in Seoul — you never see his face, only his hands — takes a rusted, seized-up 1970s sewing machine and, with no commentary at all, brings it back to life: he strips it into two hundred pieces, cleans every screw and repaints the body.

I watched it at one in the morning, in my bedroom, the night before a chemistry exam. I'd been sitting at that desk since eight, putting off two chapters, and I promised myself one video. Twenty minutes later I was down a rabbit hole of restoration films and surfaced at half two.

The work is painstaking — he spends four minutes on one screw — and there's no music, just metal and brushes. I'd never thought of a sewing machine as beautiful before that night.

Mine isn't from the internet at all: it's forty minutes of my parents' wedding in 1994, filmed on a borrowed camcorder. My grandmother's courtyard in Andijan, my father with an alarming moustache, and about a hundred relatives, half of whom I've never met.

My uncle had unearthed the tape in a box in the garage, and he had already paid a shop near the market to digitise it before he told anybody. We watched it because nobody knew it existed. He'd been clearing out that garage for a week before the box turned up. There was another reason: my grandfather died in 2019, and he's in the film, arguing cheerfully about the plov. The picture is grainy and the sound comes and goes, but it works as a time capsule — the wallpaper, the cars, the way people spoke.

My grandmother says it takes her straight back. If my uncle hadn't emptied that garage, the tape would have rotted quietly in a box, and for us it's priceless — I've been meaning to make copies for everyone ever since.
