topics.title: Story or Book with Animals in It

blocks.text: Describe a story or book with animals in it.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute
Write one short note per bullet — nouns and verbs only, never full sentences. You will not have time to read them properly anyway.
About 25 seconds on what it is about .
About 30 seconds on what animals are in it .
About 45 seconds on why you read it .
About 30 seconds on what you think of it .
Never stop early. If you run out of story, add a comparison or a piece of advice until the examiner stops you.
— A childhood book you still love

The book I'd talk about is a battered collection of Krylov's fables that lived on my grandmother's shelf. I've read it twenty times. Each fable is a page long, each pokes fun at some human weakness — vanity, laziness, greed — and each ends with a line that hits the nail on the head.

It's full of animals. There's a crow with a piece of cheese and a fox who flatters her into opening her beak; a monkey who buys spectacles and can't work out how to use them; a dragonfly who sings all summer, then knocks on the ant's door in December. The animals aren't cuddly, they're recognisable — everybody knows a fox, and everybody has been the dragonfly.

I read it because my grandmother had been reading it aloud to me long before I could read myself. Years later I picked it up alone, partly out of nostalgia, partly because I'd forgotten how sharp it was. It helped that the fables are short, which matters when you're eleven and easily put off by fat books.

annotations.text: my grandmother had been reading it aloud to me long before I could read

blocks.text: Books like that stand the test of time. The language is old-fashioned and some lines go over your head at first, but the observations are spot on. Had my grandmother handed me a serious novel instead, I doubt I'd have become a reader, and I've been buying copies for my nieces ever since. It's the one book I never think twice about giving.
— A modern novel for a higher band

The book is Life of Pi by Yann Martel. A boy from an Indian zoo-keeping family is shipwrecked on his way to Canada and spends two hundred and twenty-seven days in a lifeboat. The twist — I won't give away too much — is that at the end you're offered a second, far darker version.

The lifeboat starts with a zebra, a hyena, an orangutan and a Bengal tiger called Richard Parker. Within days only Pi and the tiger are left. What makes it work is that Richard Parker is never sentimentalised: he isn't a friend, he's two hundred kilos of muscle Pi must feed to stay alive. What they have is an uneasy truce, not a friendship. I'd seen the film first, which is usually the kiss of death, and I'd been avoiding the novel for years, assuming I knew the ending. A teacher talked me into it. She was right: the film gives you the ocean, the book gives you Pi's mind, and it's far more gripping.

annotations.text: I'd been avoiding the novel for

blocks.text: It's one of the few books that left me genuinely in two minds. I still don't know which version I believe, and that's the point: would you rather have the truth or the better story? If I'd stopped after fifty pages, which I nearly did, I'd have missed the whole argument. It isn't an easy read, but it stays with you, and I've recommended it to half my class since.

annotations.text: If I'd stopped after fifty pages, which I nearly did, I'd have missed the whole argument.
I've recommended it to half my class since.

blocks.text: With animals in it is not the same as about animals, so a fable or an allegory counts and you are not limited to children's books. Watch bullet three: why you read it asks about you, not the plot, and one honest sentence — a teacher pushed me, I saw the film first — is worth more than another minute of summary.

topics.title: Person Who Works in a Successful Company

blocks.text: Describe a person who works in a successful company.
◆what this person does in this company
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
How to use the one minute

— A relative with a practical job

The person I want to talk about is my cousin Sardor. He's twenty-eight, he studied transport engineering, and he works for Uzum, the Uzbek online marketplace whose delivery vans now seem to be parked on every street in Tashkent.

He runs dispatch at a warehouse out past the ring road: deciding which orders go on which van, and sorting out the mess when a driver breaks down at midnight. He started on the shop floor, packing boxes, and worked his way up the old-fashioned way — he'd been packing on the night shift for barely a year when they moved him upstairs, and by twenty- six he had already become a shift supervisor.

blocks.text: The business is easy to describe and clearly not easy to run: an online marketplace, its own delivery fleet, and a payments app alongside it. Ten years ago almost nobody here shopped online; now it is a household name, and my aunt, who is sixty-one, orders her flour through it.

It works because they built the dull part first — warehouses, vans, support running round the clock — and they were ready before online shopping began to take off here. Sardor says the pace is relentless, and he's been working six-day weeks since spring, though I've watched three competitors appear and disappear since. Had the founders waited another two years, somebody else would have owned this market, and I see no reason why it shouldn't go from strength to strength.

I'll describe a former classmate of mine, Kamila. We finished school together in Namangan, and she now works in Tashkent as a product designer for one of those payment apps everybody here has on their phone.

She designs the screens people actually touch: the transfer flow, the receipts, the animation when a payment goes through. It sounds trivial until you watch her test it on her grandmother. She has an eye for the moment a user hesitates, and last year her team rolled out a redesign that cut failed transfers by a fifth. She'd been designing posters for a print shop before all this, which taught her more about deadlines than university did.

blocks.text: The company handles payments — utility bills, mobile top-ups, card transfers, and now accounts for small businesses. They wrote the whole system from the ground up instead of licensing a foreign platform. Everybody had told them that was madness, but it means they can change anything in a fortnight.

blocks.text: Why is it successful? Because they never cut corners on the dull things: security, support, an interface that stays intuitive on an old phone. That is what sets them apart from the prettier apps that came and went. Their market share is close to a third, and they've been growing through recommendations, not advertising. Two rivals have already tried to poach her. If she hadn't taken that unpaid internship, she'd have ended up in a print shop for good — she's told me that story ten times.

Describe local news that people were interested in.
You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.

— A neighbourhood argument with the council

The story I'll describe was about a tree — an enormous old chinor at the end of our street in Namangan, maybe a hundred and fifty years old. In March the city announced that the road was being widened and the tree would go. A tree doesn't usually make the headlines, but that one was the talk of the town for a month.

I didn't read it anywhere official. My neighbour's daughter photographed the survey marks and put them in the mahalla Telegram group, and after that it spread like wildfire — Telegram, then a local news site, then somebody's cousin on city television. By that evening my mother had already had three phone calls about it.

blocks.text: Almost everybody. The residents were up in arms, because they had been living under that tree their whole lives and used its shade at weddings. A retired teacher, Sobirjon aka, kicked up a fuss at the district office and got four hundred people to sign a petition. The contractors said it was a done deal.

annotations.text: they had been living under that

blocks.text: People cared because it was never about a tree, but about who decides how a neighbourhood looks. Everyone here has watched old buildings disappear over the past decade, and we have been grumbling about it for years without being asked. In the end the council backed down and the road now curves around it. If nobody had posted that photograph, the tree would have gone within a fortnight.

blocks.text: — If you prefer a good-news story

The item I remember best was about Rustam aka, an eighty-eight-year-old former football coach who still trains children in the courtyard of a block in Chilonzor. A schoolgirl filmed him on her phone one morning, and completely out of the blue the clip took off.

I'd come across it late one night on Telegram, before it really began to go viral. I had not been following local news at all that month, but by the weekend it was on the city radio station and even in one national newspaper, and my grandmother rang me about it twice. Rustam aka himself, obviously — he has been coaching in that yard since the seventies. Then the girl who filmed him, the neighbours who rallied round with paint and new nets, and a shop owner two streets away who paid for the goalposts. About two hundred families chipped in, and they had raised enough for a proper pitch before the district administration even replied.

blocks.text: I think it strikes a chord because everybody remembers one adult who gave them their time for nothing. It was heartwarming in a way local news usually isn't: no scandal, no politics, just an old man with a whistle. He is a household name in that district now, and the yard has been full of children every evening since. Had that girl not stopped to film him, he would have carried on unnoticed for another decade.

blocks.text: The word local is doing real work here: an election result or a world event answers a different card, so anchor your story to one street, one mahalla, one district. And why people were interested is not answered by saying it was interesting — name the nerve it touched, whose life it changed, what people argued about afterwards.

The person I'd choose is my cousin Kamola. She's two years older than me, and we've been running in and out of each other's houses since we were toddlers — our mothers are sisters and live on the same street in Chirchik. She works as a tour guide in Samarkand now.

I take my hat off to her, honestly. I've had private English lessons since primary school, and she overtook me in two years flat. Mine is Bakhtiyor-aka, who sells carpets in a shop just behind the Kalon minaret in Bukhara. I met him three summers ago, when I was driving for a travel agency: I'd bring tourists there twice a week and end up drinking tea for an hour. He'll strike up a conversation with anybody, get half the endings wrong, and simply not care. He can hold his own in Spanish too, because he claims it is just Italian pronounced badly — nonsense, but it works for him. He is completely self-taught.

He puts me to shame, frankly. I've spent nine years in classrooms and I still hesitate before I open my mouth; he has never been frightened of a single sentence. Had I not spent that summer watching him, I would still believe you need a certificate before you are allowed to speak. He throws himself into every conversation, and that is the entire secret.

— A practical present for a friend who cooks

The gift I've got in mind is a proper chef's knife — a Japanese-style one, about twenty centimetres long — for my friend Sardor. I've been saving up for it since the spring, because a decent one costs far more than I'd normally spend, and I want it ready for his birthday in November.

blocks.text: Sardor and I have been friends since university. He lives in Yunusobod with his parents and is a dab hand in the kitchen. But he does everything with an ancient blunt knife that was probably his grandmother's. I'd never noticed it until last Navruz, when I watched him hacking away at a carrot for ten minutes, and it dawned on me that he had never owned a sharp knife in his life.

annotations.text: I'd never noticed it until last Navruz,

blocks.text: The reason I want to buy it now is that he's going through a rough patch: he's been out of work since June, and cooking for other people is the one thing that keeps him going. He'd been talking about opening a little café for years before that, and lately the plan has gone quiet. I want a present that says, without a speech, that I still believe in the café.

blocks.text: As for why a knife, I did consider a cookbook, but it felt run-of-the-mill — something you unwrap and forget. A knife he'd use every single day, and my uncle, who cooks for a living, says a sharp blade is worth its weight in gold. One catch: in Uzbekistan you're not supposed to give knives, because supposedly they cut the friendship, so Sardor will pay me a coin for it, just to be on the safe side.

Had I not sat in that kitchen at Navruz, I'd probably have bought him a shirt, but I've already found the right stall in Chorsu. It's the kind of gift that outlasts the birthday — which, to me, is the whole point.

blocks.text: — A second-hand camera as a leaving present

I'd like to talk about a camera — not a new one, but an old Soviet film camera, a Zenit, which I want to buy for my closest friend Malika. She's leaving for Germany in October to do a master's degree, and I've known about it since May, so I've spent four months racking my brains for a present.

annotations.text: I've known about it since May,

blocks.text: Malika and I grew up on the same landing in Chilonzor. She photographs everything — she's taken thousands of pictures on her phone — but never looks at them. She often mentions her grandfather's old Zenit; the family had sold it long before she understood what it was, and she still talks about it with a certain sadness.

annotations.text: she's taken thousands of pictures on her phone
the family had sold it long before she understood

blocks.text: Why this present? Partly because she'll be far away and I want her to have something with sentimental value, not another scarf. But mainly because film is unforgiving: thirty-six frames instead of a thousand, so you think before you press the button. If she'd had one in Bukhara, we'd have come home with fifty photographs worth keeping instead of nine hundred nobody has opened.

annotations.text: Bukhara, we'd have come home with fifty photographs worth keeping instead of nine

blocks.text: As for why a Zenit, I spent two Sundays at the Yangiobod flea market and finally hunted down one in mint condition — the light meter still works. It was dirt cheap, so the money goes into film instead. It's a fiddly thing to use, and it'll take her a few rolls to get the hang of it, but I'll shoot the first roll myself and slip a print inside the case.

I'd been planning to buy her a digital camera before I saw the Zenit. But the old one strikes a chord with her whole story, and I'm fairly sure she'll cry. I've been carrying it around in my bag for a week now. Finding it has been a labour of love, and that, honestly, is what a present should be.

blocks.text: The two final bullets look identical, and most candidates answer them with the same sentence twice. Treat why you'd like to buy this gift as the person and the occasion — what is happening in your friend's life that makes a present necessary now — and why you've chosen that gift as the object itself, ideally set against one or two alternatives you rejected. Notice also that the card says you'd like to buy: the gift is still in the future, so a story about something you gave last year, however good, does not answer the question. Keep at least one sentence about what you have already done to get it.

— A retired archaeologist on the Samarkand train

The person I want to talk about is a woman called Malika-opa, a retired archaeologist who spent thirty years digging at Afrasiyab, the ruined old city on the edge of Samarkand. I know her first name and her profession, nothing else, and I've been thinking about her far more than a two-hour conversation deserves.

blocks.text: We met last March on the afternoon train from Tashkent to Samarkand. I was going down for a cousin's wedding and was rather at a loose end — my phone had died before we'd even left the station — so when she asked whether the seat opposite was taken, I was glad of the company. Within ten minutes we'd hit it off completely. She'd been going to the same site every spring since the Soviet days, and she talked about broken pottery the way other people talk about football.

I sat there hanging on her every word while she explained how you can date a wall by the colour of its bricks. I'd walked past those ruins a dozen times without giving them a second look, and here was somebody who'd spent her whole life underneath them. Two hours barely scratched the surface.

I've been kicking myself ever since for not asking for her number. Had I been a little less shy, I'd have a proper friend in Samarkand now instead of a half-remembered surname. He was riding from Amsterdam to Beijing, alone, on a bike that looked older than he was, and I think about him every time I complain about the metro.

It was the end of August last year. A few of us had gone up on a whim — my friend Sardor had borrowed his father's car and there was nothing to do in the city heat. We crossed paths at a little chaikhana near the chairlift: he was ordering in German and the owner was answering in Uzbek, so I translated, and he ended up eating with us for three hours.

He was a man of few words at first, but once he'd got through a plate of shashlik he opened up. He'd been on the road for four months by then, sleeping in a tent, crossing Turkey, Iran and the Caspian. It took me a while to pluck up the courage to ask the obvious question — why? — and his answer was that he'd simply grown bored of being comfortable. I recognised that instantly; he felt like a kindred spirit.

blocks.text: The trap is only once: candidates describe the person as if they were an old friend, and the examiner hears a contradiction. Keep it honest — a train, a queue, a wedding table — and let how you met this person carry the detail, because that is where the story lives. When you met this person wants a season and a reason, not just a year. And why you want to know more is the bullet with the marks in it: name the one unanswered question, and say what you have already tried to do about it.

An older man you know well — an uncle or a neighbour — who started with nothing and built a small furniture workshop into a real business, makes things by hand, grows vegetables and grapes in his yard, and is known across the whole mahalla.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The person I want to talk about is Rustam-aka, a neighbour of ours who is somewhere in his sixties. I've known him for as long as I can remember — our families have lived on the same street for decades. He started out with next to nothing: one second-hand machine in a shed and a stubborn belief that he could make furniture better than the factories could. By the time I started school he had already turned that shed into a proper workshop with eight or nine people on the payroll. What I admire most is that he has never rested on his laurels — he has been getting up at five every morning for thirty years. He keeps an immaculate garden as well: tomatoes, grape vines, and he gives half the harvest away. Had he not been so patient in those first lean years, the business would have gone under. Everyone in our mahalla knows his name.
What stays the same every time
The man himself: his name, his age, how you know him, his workshop, his garden, his character — patient, generous, organised.
How the story moves between cards
Only the opening sentence and the last “why” move. Each card asks you to spotlight one side of him: the business, the hard years, the hands, the garden, the reputation.
What to change, card by card
Describe a person you know who loves to grow plants (vegetables, fruits, flowers).
Open on his garden — the tomatoes, the grape vines, the neighbours he gives the harvest to. The business becomes one line of background.
Describe a successful business person you know.
Open on the business — how he started with one used machine, what he sells now, how many people he employs.
Describe a person who met difficulties but succeeded.
Lead with the hard years: no money, a first shop that failed, borrowing from relatives. Then the success as the payoff.
Describe a person who works in a successful company.
Reframe his workshop as “a successful company” and describe HIS role in it — owner, still on the floor every day.
Describe an important old thing that your family has kept for a long time.
Switch the subject to an object: a hand-carved chest he made for your family, or a tool passed down. He stays in the background.
Describe a person who encouraged you to protect the nature.
Lead with what he taught you about not wasting water, composting, planting a tree each spring — and what he actually said to you.
Describe a person who often helps others.
Lead with three quick examples of people in the mahalla he has helped. Breadth beats depth here.
Describe a person who makes plans a lot and is good at planning.
Lead with his notebook and the way he plans the season, the week, every delivery. Add one example of a plan that paid off.
Describe an older person you admire.
This is the base version of the story — tell it straight, with admiration as the frame.
Describe a person who is good at making things by hand.
Lead with the workshop: the tools, what he makes, how long a piece takes, how he learned.
Describe a person famous in your local area.
Lead with the fact that everyone in the district knows his name, and why — his work, his help, his reputation.
MASTER STORY 2 OF 19 · COVERS 8 CUE CARDS · 148 WORDS

Your friend since primary school who taught himself English — and coding — from YouTube and free apps, fixes problems in clever ways, taught you a skill when you were children, and now plans to study medicine.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The person I'd like to describe is Javlon, who I've been friends with since primary school. What makes him unusual is that almost everything he knows, he taught himself. He had never taken a single English lesson before the age of fourteen, and yet by sixteen he was speaking more fluently than anyone in our class — just films, free apps and a great deal of shadowing. He picked up coding in exactly the same way. He has a real knack for thinking outside the box: the night before a deadline my laptop died, and he cobbled together a fix with an old hard drive in twenty minutes flat. He taught me chess when we were nine. He has been talking about medicine for the last two years now, and he's dead set on becoming a doctor. Had he grown up with proper resources, he would have been unstoppable.

annotations.text: knack for thinking outside the box:

blocks.text: What stays the same every time
Who he is, how you met, what he is like, his self- teaching method, one concrete problem he solved for you.
How the story moves between cards
Change which of his qualities you open with, and change the tense for the medical-career card — future plans instead of past.
What to change, card by card
Describe a friend from your childhood.
Lead with how you met in primary school and what you did together as kids. Keep the self-teaching for the last point.
Describe a person who did something to help you solve a problem.
Lead with YOUR problem — the laptop that died the night before a deadline, or being stuck on a piece of writing — then what he did about it.
Describe a person you know who would like to work in the medical field.
Future tense: his plan to become a doctor, why he chose it, what he is doing now to get there.
Describe a person who is good at learning and speaking new languages.
Lead with the languages — English, Russian, some Arabic — and his exact method: films, shadowing, apps.
Describe a person who solved a problem in a smart way.
The same problem as card 25, retold from the angle of how clever the solution was, not how grateful you were.
Describe one of your friends who learned something new (not from a teacher).
Stress “not from a teacher”: YouTube, free apps, trial and error — no course, no tutor.
Describe a person who taught you a skill when you were a child.
Shift the time frame to childhood — the skill he taught you as a kid: chess, cycling, swimming.
Describe a person who taught you a skill.
The same skill as card 73 with no time restriction — you can use the childhood version word for word.
MASTER STORY 3 OF 19 · COVERS 8 CUE CARDS · 149 WORDS
A surprise birthday that you and three friends organised for a close friend: the planning, the cake, the plov, the gift, and the moment he walked in and every face in the room was smiling.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I'd like to talk about a surprise birthday party that three friends and I organised for Aziz last spring. We had been planning it for the best part of a month before the day itself. One of us took charge of the cake, another rounded up the guests, and my job was to keep him away from the house with some far-fetched story about a football match. The cake was enormous and homemade, with his nickname piped across it, and there was a vast dish of plov, which is what we cook for anything worth celebrating. The moment the door opened, the whole room lit up — I don't think I have ever seen so many people smiling at once. I've helped organise a few events since, but none of them has come close. Had we let the secret slip even a day earlier, that moment would have been lost.
What stays the same every time
The friend, the four organisers, the venue, the cake, the food, the evening.
How the story moves between cards
Zoom in or out: on the cake, on the food, on the teamwork, on the smiling faces, or on the evening as a whole. Card 67 flips the whole thing into the future — the gift you WOULD buy.
What to change, card by card
Describe a special cake you received.
Zoom into the cake: what it looked like, who made it, the writing on it, his face when he saw it.
Describe a type of food that people eat at special events.
Zoom out to food at celebrations generally — plov at weddings and birthdays, why people cook it — and use this party as your example.
Describe a time when you worked in a group.
Foreground the four of you: who took the cake, who took the guests, who kept him away from the house.
Describe a time when you organised a happy event successfully.
Base version — tell the whole organisation story from start to finish.
Describe an occasion when you saw a lot of people smiling.
One moment only: the door opening and every face in the room smiling. Slow it right down.
Describe a time you needed to use your imagination.
The cover story you invented to get him there, and the decorations you improvised. Imagination is the angle.
Describe a gift you'd like to buy for your friend.
Future tense: the gift you'd buy that same friend next time, and why it suits him.
Describe an enjoyable evening you had with your friends.
Drop the surprise — just the evening: the food, the music, what you all talked about, when it ended.

topics.title: The Gadget I Can't Live Without

blocks.text: MASTER STORY 4 OF 19 · COVERS 6 CUE CARDS · 148 WORDS

The one device you use every single day — noise-cancelling headphones or an e-reader — plus the app that goes with it: how you found it, how it saves you an hour a day, the week it broke, and the newer model you are saving up for.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The one object I genuinely couldn't manage without is my pair of noise-cancelling headphones. I've had them for a little over two years; I bought them second-hand after I had been saving for months and giving up taxis to do it. They are nothing special to look at, but the moment I put them on, the bus, the traffic and my brother's music all fade into the background. I use them for about three hours a day, mostly for podcasts and studying, and they have paid for themselves many times over. There was one dreadful week when the left side gave out and I realised quite how much I depend on them — I was at a loose end on every journey. Had I not tracked down a repair shop near the bazaar, I would have had to replace them outright. There's a newer model I'm slowly saving for.
What stays the same every time
The device, how you found it, your daily routine with it, the day it failed, the upgrade you want.
How the story moves between cards
Card 42 bans a computer and a phone, so the hero object must NOT be your phone. Card 24 needs the failure, not the love.
What to change, card by card
Describe a challenging technological problem you faced.
Negative: the week it stopped working, what you tried, who fixed it, what you learned.
Describe something you can't live without (not a computer or phone).
WARNING — the card bans a computer and a phone. Make the hero the headphones, the e-reader or the bicycle, never the phone.
Describe an app or program in your computer or phone.
The app version — the one on your phone you open most, how you found it, what it does for you.
Describe a piece of technology (not a phone) that you would like to own.
Future: the newer model or a different device you'd like to own, and what you'd do with it.
Describe something that you saved money to buy.
The saving-up angle: what it cost, how long you saved, what you gave up to get it.
Describe something you do that helps you save your time.
The time-saving angle: the routine it replaced, and roughly how much time it gives you back.
MASTER STORY 5 OF 19 · COVERS 6 CUE CARDS · 145 WORDS
The morning you set off for another city at four a.m., sat two hours in a traffic jam, had to change the whole plan, lost your wallet, and ended up paying far more than you had expected.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I want to describe a journey to Bukhara that went pear-shaped from the very beginning. We set off at four in the morning, which meant getting up at three — and I had barely slept, because I'd been packing until midnight. Twenty minutes outside the city we ground to a halt in a jam caused by roadworks, and we sat there for two solid hours watching the sun come up. By the time the traffic inched forward, our original plan was useless, so we scrapped it and rebooked everything from the car. Then, at the first petrol station, I discovered my wallet was gone. I've never felt so foolish in my life. We ended up paying nearly double what we had budgeted — new tickets, a taxi and a hotel we hadn't planned on. Had we simply travelled the night before, none of it would have happened.
What stays the same every time
The date, the destination, who you were with, the four a.m. start, the jam, the lost wallet, the extra cost.
How the story moves between cards
Pull one link out of the chain per card. Card 77 shifts from that one day to the journey you make every week and dislike — the same traffic vocabulary, in the present.
What to change, card by card
Describe an occasion when you got up extremely early.
Open at four a.m.: the alarm, the dark, why you had to leave so early.
Describe a plan you had to change.
Open on the original plan and what forced you to scrap it. The jam becomes the cause.
Describe an occasion when you got stuck in a traffic jam.
The jam itself: how long, how far, what you did while you waited, how you felt.
Describe an occasion when you paid more than expected.
The money: what you had budgeted, what it actually cost, and why — new tickets, a taxi, a hotel.
Describe a short journey that you often take but dislike.
Shift from that one day to the journey you make every week and dislike — same traffic and crowding language, present tense, “every time”.
Describe an occasion when you lost something.
The wallet: what was in it, the exact moment you realised, what you did next.

topics.title: The City I'd Go Back To

blocks.text: MASTER STORY 6 OF 19 · COVERS 5 CUE CARDS · 144 WORDS
A trip to a city you loved: the old town, the packed bazaar, a stranger you talked to for an hour, and a day that cost you almost nothing.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The city I'd go back to tomorrow is Samarkand. I'd only ever seen it in photographs before I finally went two summers ago with my cousin. We spent three days wandering the old town, and the scale of the tilework there is jaw-dropping — photographs simply don't do it justice. The bazaar was heaving by seven every morning, and we haggled badly and cheerfully over dried apricots. One afternoon we got chatting to a retired teacher in the square, and he gave us an hour of local history for nothing. That whole day — walking, street food, a museum that happened to be free — cost us less than a cinema ticket at home, and we still felt we had barely scratched the surface. I've recommended the place to every visitor I've met since. Had we booked an organised tour instead, we would never have met him.
What stays the same every time
The city, when you went, who with, what you saw, the food, the bazaar, the stranger.
How the story moves between cards
Cards 36 and 66 are the same question in two different exam lists — one answer. Card 19 narrows to the cheap day; card 68 narrows to the stranger.
What to change, card by card
Describe a place you've travelled to that you'd recommend to others.
Recommendation frame: who you'd recommend it to, and what they should not miss.
Describe a special day out that didn't cost a lot.
Narrow to one day there that cost almost nothing: walking the old town, street food, a free museum day.
Describe a city you've been to and want to visit again.
Base version — and note that card 66 is the identical question in the newer list.
Describe a city you've been to and want to visit again.
The same question as card 36. One answer, no changes.
Describe a person you met only once and you want to know more about.
Narrow to the stranger: how you started talking, what you learned, what you still wonder about him.

topics.title: The Course That Set My Direction

blocks.text: MASTER STORY 7 OF 19 · COVERS 5 CUE CARDS · 144 WORDS
The course you took that changed your plans: the decision to enrol, the way you drilled the language, the long-term goal it gave you, and the job you are aiming at.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The decision I want to describe is enrolling on an intensive English course two years ago. I had been drifting a little — I'd left school with no real plan, and the alternatives were a job I didn't want or another year of doing very little. I asked my cousin, who had done the same course, and then I took the plunge. The teacher was demanding in the best possible way: daily vocabulary drills, an app for shadowing, and a speaking club every Friday that I dreaded and then came to love. I've made more progress in those six months than in six years of school. It also gave me a long-term goal: I've had my sights set on studying abroad ever since, and I'm two exams away from it. Had I not signed up that September, I'd almost certainly still be putting it off.
What stays the same every time
The course, the teacher, the decision moment, your study routine, where you want it to take you.
How the story moves between cards
Cards 12 and 69 look backwards; cards 22 and 38 look forwards. It is the same story told forwards, then backwards.
What to change, card by card
Describe an important decision you made.
The decision to enrol: what the alternatives were, who you asked, why you chose this.
Describe a thing you did to learn a language.
Narrow to ONE thing you did — the daily drill, the app, the speaking club — and its effect.
Describe a long-term goal you would like to achieve.
Future: the goal the course pointed you at, how long you've had it, the steps left.
Future: the job at the end of that road, what it involves, why it would suit you.
Describe a course that impressed you.
Base version — the course, the teacher, what made it impressive.
MASTER STORY 8 OF 19 · COVERS 4 CUE CARDS · 142 WORDS

The time you persuaded a friend to do something he was refusing to do — apply to university, start training, see a doctor: the message he ignored, the advice you gave, and the fact that you changed your own mind about him in the process.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I'd like to talk about the time I talked my friend Sardor into applying to university. He had decided not to bother — he was convinced he wasn't clever enough — and, to be honest, at first I thought he was simply being lazy. I had sent him a long message about the deadlines and he left it sitting there unanswered for the best part of a fortnight, which irritated me no end. When we finally met, though, it dawned on me that money was the real obstacle, not laziness, and that I had misjudged him completely. So we sat down and went through the scholarship options together. He said no three or four times before he came round. He applied on the very last day and got a place. Had I kept pushing without listening, he would never have told me the truth.
What stays the same every time
The friend, what he was refusing to do, what you said, what happened afterwards.
How the story moves between cards
Card 26 is the trap — it is about YOUR opinion changing, so tell it as “at first I thought he was lazy, then I understood”. Card 27 zooms in on the message that got no reply.
What to change, card by card
Describe a time when you changed your opinion.
TRAP — this card is about YOUR opinion changing. Tell it as: at first you thought he was lazy, then you understood the real reason and changed your mind.
Describe a time when you sent a message or an email to someone but received no reply for a
long time. Narrow to the message you sent that sat unanswered for days: what it said, how you felt, what happened in the end.
Describe a time when you gave advice to others.
Base version — the advice you gave, in your own words, and whether he took it.
Describe a time when you encouraged someone to do something that they didn't want to do.
Foreground the resistance: how many times he said no, and what finally moved him.
MASTER STORY 9 OF 19 · COVERS 4 CUE CARDS · 142 WORDS
The local river or lake everyone in your area knows, the news story about it being polluted, the rule that came in afterwards, and the law you would introduce yourself.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I'd like to describe the river that runs along the edge of our district. Everyone here grew up beside it — people swim in it, fish in it, and it irrigates most of the gardens nearby. Two years ago a local news story reported that a factory upstream had been dumping waste into it for months, and for a fortnight it was all anyone talked about. The council brought in fines for fly-tipping and a clean-up scheme every spring, which has made a real dent in the problem, though the banks are still far from spotless. If it were up to me, I'd introduce a small deposit on plastic bottles — a refund does more good than a slogan ever will. I've been picking up litter on my morning walk ever since. Had that story never been published, nothing would have changed at all.

annotations.text: does more good than a slogan ever will.

blocks.text: What stays the same every time
The river, its importance to the area, the pollution, the news coverage, your proposed law.
How the story moves between cards
Cards 16 and 34 are factual and in the past; cards 5 and 18 are opinion and future. Keep the same river throughout so the details stay concrete.
What to change, card by card
Describe a new law you would like to introduce in your country.
Your own law, conditional tense: what it would change, and whether people would accept it.
Describe an important river or lake in your country.
The river itself: where it runs, what it's used for, what you know about its history.
Describe a law on environmental protection.
The rule that followed — fines for dumping, a clean-up scheme — and how well it actually works.
Describe local news that people were interested in.
The news story: where you saw it, what it reported, why everyone was talking about it.
MASTER STORY 10 OF 19 · COVERS 4 CUE CARDS · 142 WORDS
How you watch things: the film that stayed with you, the series you follow, the short video you couldn't stop thinking about — and the film you walked out of.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I'd like to talk about how I watch things, and one film in particular. Most evenings I watch something on my laptop at home, usually on my own, and I choose by word of mouth rather than by trailers. The film that has stayed with me is one a friend raved about — a quiet story about a father and son driving across the country. I'd never heard of the director, and I nearly switched it off in the first ten minutes, which would have been a grave mistake. The plot is simple enough: a journey, an argument, a reconciliation. What lifts it is the acting — one scene near the end had me on the verge of tears. I've watched it three times now and noticed something different each time. Had I not trusted my friend's taste, I'd have scrolled straight past it.
What stays the same every time
Where and when you watch, who with, how you choose what to watch.
How the story moves between cards
Card 76 needs the opposite verdict — keep the same setting and the same way of choosing, but a different, disappointing film.
What to change, card by card
A short video: where you saw it, what was in it, why you sent it on to someone.
Describe a film you watched and enjoyed.
The film you loved: how you chose it, the plot in three sentences, why it stayed with you.
Describe a program you like to watch.
The series or programme you follow: when you watch it, why you keep going back.
Negative — keep the same setting and the same way you chose it, but a different film that disappointed you.
MASTER STORY 11 OF 19 · COVERS 4 CUE CARDS · 147 WORDS
The concert you had looked forward to that turned out flat: a dull hall, phones not allowed, and three hours gone — the same three hours you lose to scrolling every night.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I want to describe a concert I'd been looking forward to for weeks, which turned out to be a complete let- down. It was held in a dull municipal hall with plastic chairs, strip lighting and no atmosphere whatsoever. I had bought the tickets months in advance and dragged two friends along with me. On top of that, phones were collected at the door — which I understand in principle, but it meant three hours with nothing to fall back on when the band started late and played badly. Time dragged, and the interval seemed to last longer than the music itself. We slipped out before the encore, faintly embarrassed. The irritating part is that those three hours are precisely the three hours I've been throwing away on my phone every night anyway. Had I bothered to read a single review, I'd have stayed at home and lost nothing.
What stays the same every time
The event, who you went with, why it disappointed you, the no-phone rule, how you felt about the wasted time.
How the story moves between cards
All four are negative cards, so the complaint vocabulary is shared. Card 75 moves from that one evening to your daily habit.
What to change, card by card
The venue as a boring place: what it was like, who you were with, why there was nothing to do.
Describe an experience when you were not allowed to use a mobile phone.
The no-phone rule — at the hall, the cinema or an exam: when it was, why phones were banned, how you coped.
Describe a music event that you didn't enjoy.
Base version — the concert you'd looked forward to, and why it fell flat.
Describe an activity you usually do that wastes your time.
Move from that one evening to the daily habit: scrolling, how long it eats, how you feel afterwards.
MASTER STORY 12 OF 19 · COVERS 4 CUE CARDS · 153 WORDS
The country you have wanted to see for years — say Japan: the trip you'd take, the months you'd work there, the road trip across it, and the strange building you want to stand in front of.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The country I have wanted to see for as long as I can remember is Japan. I've been reading about it since I was a teenager — the food, the trains, the way the very old and the very new sit side by side. If I ever get the chance, I'd go in spring, ideally for a month, and I'd travel the length of the country by rail rather than hopping between cities by plane. I'd love to work there for a short spell as well, teaching English, just long enough to stop being a tourist. The one building I'm dying to stand in front of is the great wooden temple at Nara — I've seen it a hundred times on a screen and I suspect photographs flatten it completely. It isn't pie in the sky, either: I've already started putting money aside. Had I been braver at eighteen, I would have gone years ago.
What stays the same every time
The country, why you're drawn to it, what you'd do there, who you'd go with.
How the story moves between cards
All four are imaginary, so one set of conditional grammar carries them: I'd love to, I'm planning to, if I ever get the chance. Only the object changes — place, job, road trip, building.
What to change, card by card
Describe a place you'd like to visit in your free time.
Short, free-time framing — the place itself and what you'd do there.
Describe a country in which you would like to work or live for a short period of time.
Work framing: what job you'd do there, how long for, what you'd gain from it.
Describe a long bike, motorbike, or car trip that you would like to take.
The road-trip version: the route, the vehicle, who with, how long.
Describe an unusual building you'd like to visit.
One building in that country: what it looks like, how you know about it, why you want to stand in front of it.
MASTER STORY 13 OF 19 · COVERS 3 CUE CARDS · 142 WORDS
The live football match you went to: the packed stadium, the noise, the queues, and the goal in the last minutes.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I'd like to describe a football match I went to at the national stadium two seasons ago. I went with my brother and two cousins; we'd been trying to get hold of tickets all year. The queues outside were enormous — we shuffled forward for forty minutes and were packed in like sardines at the turnstiles — and inside there wasn't a spare seat to be had. The noise when the teams came out was extraordinary; you feel it in your chest rather than hear it. It was goalless and frankly dull until the eighty-ninth minute, when our striker scored and the entire stand went berserk. Complete strangers were hugging one another. I've watched hundreds of matches on television and not one of them has felt like that. Had we given up on those tickets, we'd have missed the best minute of the season.
What stays the same every time
The match, who you went with, the crowd, the atmosphere, the result.
How the story moves between cards
Cards 70 and 74 are the SAME question printed twice in the list — one answer covers both.
What to change, card by card
Describe a time when you watched a live sports event and liked it.
The match: where, when, who with, the atmosphere, the result.
Describe a time you went to a crowded place.
The crowd angle — queues, noise, no space. NOTE: identical to card 74.
Describe a time you went to a crowded place.
Identical question to card 70. One answer, no changes.
MASTER STORY 14 OF 19 · COVERS 3 CUE CARDS · 142 WORDS
A world-famous sportsperson or founder you admire, whose career you know well and whose advert you have seen on television and online.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The person I most admire from a distance is a footballer whose career I have followed since I was about ten. What I admire isn't really the talent — it's the work. He has been training at that intensity for the best part of twenty years, long after he stopped needing to, and that kind of staying power is rare at the top of any sport. I've watched almost every season he has played. Away from the pitch he gives a great deal away quietly, which to my mind says more than the trophies do. I've also seen the watch advert he appears in — it is everywhere, on television and online — and I'd say it works, because the product borrows his reputation rather than just his face. Had he been satisfied after his first title, none of us would have heard of him.
What stays the same every time
Who he is, what he achieved, why you admire him, the advert he appears in.
How the story moves between cards
Cards 40 and 82 are past and present admiration; card 28 asks you to describe the advert itself — what it shows, whether it works — rather than the person.
What to change, card by card
Describe an ad with a famous person in it.
Describe the advert, not the man: what it shows, where you saw it, what it is selling, whether his face makes it work.
Describe a famous person you'd like to meet.
Conditional tense: where you'd meet him, what you'd ask him, why him and not someone else.
Describe a sports person you admire.
Past and present: what he has achieved, how you followed his career, what you admire about him off the pitch too.
MASTER STORY 15 OF 19 · COVERS 2 CUE CARDS · 143 WORDS
The balcony or reading corner at home where you go to be alone — quiet, morning light, tea, no phone.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The place I want to describe is the balcony at the back of our flat, which I have slowly turned into a reading corner. There's one old armchair, a small table, a lamp and a shelf of books — nothing else, quite deliberately. I've been going out there first thing in the morning for about three years, with tea, before anyone else in the house is awake. The light at that hour is lovely and you can hear the street stirring into life below. The one rule I keep is no phone, which sounds trivial but is precisely why it works: it is the single place where my mind stops racing. Twenty minutes out there and I feel like a new person. Had we been given a flat without a balcony, I'd have had to find somewhere else entirely — a park bench, most likely.
What stays the same every time
Where it is, what's in it, when you go there, how it makes you feel.
How the story moves between cards
Card 63 lets the place be outside the home as well, but the same description works either way.
What to change, card by card
Describe a place in your home where you like to relax.
Inside the home — the balcony or corner, and why it is the one place you relax.
Describe a quiet place that you like to go to.
The same place with quiet as the angle — or move it to a park bench if you'd rather vary it.

topics.title: The Tower I Wouldn't Live In

blocks.text: MASTER STORY 16 OF 19 · COVERS 2 CUE CARDS · 140 WORDS
The new glass tower in your city — impressive from the street, beautiful at night, and the last place on earth you would want to live.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I'd like to describe the glass tower that went up in the centre of our city three years ago. It is about forty storeys, easily the tallest thing on the skyline, with offices on the lower floors and flats above them. I hadn't paid it much attention until a friend took me up to the café on the top floor, and I have to admit the view is breathtaking, particularly at night when the whole building is lit up like a lantern. So I admire it — from the street. Living in it is another matter entirely. It's sealed, the windows don't open, and you're twenty floors up with no garden and no neighbours who would notice if you vanished. It's not my cup of tea at all. Had they built even a courtyard into it, I might have felt differently.
What stays the same every time
Where it is, what it looks like, what's inside, why you admire it, why you wouldn't live there.
How the story moves between cards
Card 3 lets you choose like OR dislike; card 15 forces the split verdict. Tell it with the split verdict both times and it fits.
What to change, card by card
Describe a tall building in your town that you like or dislike.
The building: where it is, its height, what it's used for, and your split verdict.
Describe a home that you like but don't want to live in.
The same building with the verdict foregrounded: beautiful to look at, wrong to live in, and why.
MASTER STORY 17 OF 19 · COVERS 2 CUE CARDS · 140 WORDS
A book you read recently which happens to have animals in it — a fable, or a novel where animals carry the meaning.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

The book I'd like to talk about is Animal Farm, which I finally read properly last winter. I'd been meaning to read it for years — it's short, which is why I eventually picked it up. On the surface it is a simple story about farm animals driving out the farmer and running the place themselves; underneath, of course, the animals stand for something a great deal larger. What struck me was how quickly the new rules bend out of shape once one group decides it is more equal than the others. I finished it in two evenings, and then I had to go back and read the last chapter again because I couldn't quite believe the ending. I've recommended it to half my friends since. Had it been three hundred pages longer, it wouldn't have hit anything like as hard.
What stays the same every time
The book, when and why you read it, the plot, the message.
How the story moves between cards
Pick the book so that it covers both cards at once — an animal story that you genuinely did read recently.
What to change, card by card
Describe a story or book with animals in it.
The same book, as long as it has animals in it — foreground them and what they stand for.
Describe a story you read recently.
The book as a recent read: when, why, what happens, what you took from it.
MASTER STORY 18 OF 19 · COVERS 2 CUE CARDS · 145 WORDS
The shop you go to every week, and the day one assistant there went well out of her way for you.
The universal answer & how to adapt it

I'd like to describe the little shop on the corner of our street, which I have been going to every week for as long as we've lived here. It's barely bigger than a room: bread, dairy, fruit, and a fridge of cold drinks by the door. I pop in two or three times a week, usually for non and eggs. What makes it worth mentioning, though, is the woman who works there. A few months ago I arrived ten minutes after closing time, soaked through, having left my wallet at home — and she went out of her way to open up again, gave me what I needed and told me to settle up next time. I've never had service like that from a supermarket. Had she simply pointed at the sign on the door, I'd have gone home empty-handed. A small kindness, but it stuck.
What stays the same every time
Where it is, how often you go, what it sells, the assistant, what she did.
How the story moves between cards
Card 49 is the routine; card 71 is the one good-service moment inside that routine.
What to change, card by card
Describe a shop you often visit.
The routine: where it is, what it sells, how often you go, what you always buy.

What is the difference between living in the countryside and the city?

The obvious difference is pace and choice. In a city, whatever you need is more or less on your doorstep — hospitals, universities, work — whereas in a village services are thin on the ground and you plan your whole week around one bus. That gap has been widening for years as everything gets centralised. The countryside gives you space, clean air and neighbours who know your name; the city gives you options. I've lived in both, and honestly the deeper difference is psychological: in a city nobody notices you, which is either liberating or lonely depending on the day.

For me the real contrast is social rather than material. Village life runs on mutual obligation — you turn up at weddings, funerals, everything, and people notice if you don't. Cities let you keep yourself to yourself, which suits some people and quietly damages others. Until I moved to Tashkent I had never had to make friends deliberately; at home they simply came with the street. If I'd stayed in my grandparents' village, I'd have had a much smaller life but probably a warmer one. It's a trade-off, not a ranking.

blocks.text: Do you prefer to live in the city or in the countryside?

The city, without much hesitation. I'm at the stage of life where opportunity matters more than peace and quiet, and cities are where the work, the courses and the interesting people are. I've never once regretted moving, even with the noise and the rent. The hustle and bustle genuinely energises me; when I stay with my parents for a week I start getting cabin fever by about day four. Had I been asked this at fifty rather than twenty-five, I imagine the answer would be the opposite — people drift back towards greenery eventually.

blocks.text: Given the choice now, I'd take the countryside, and that's a complete reversal for me. City life has been wearing me down in ways I didn't notice at the time: the commute, the noise, never seeing the sky properly. Out of town the cost of living is a fraction of what I was paying, and I actually sleep. If remote work hadn't become normal, I'd never have been able to make that choice, so I'm well aware it's a privilege. The honest downside is that decent schools and hospitals are few and far between.

blocks.text: Is it good for elderly people to live in large cities?

On balance yes, largely because of healthcare. A specialist appointment that takes twenty minutes in a city can mean a full day's travelling from a village, and at eighty that difference is enormous. Pharmacies, transport and community centres are within easy reach too. My grandmother has become far more independent since she moved in with my aunt; before that she had relied on a neighbour for every single errand. Loneliness is the obvious counter-argument, and it's a fair one, but arguments about isolation cut both ways — the villages are emptying as well.

blocks.text: I'd argue that cities are becoming quietly hostile to older people. Everything now assumes a smartphone, a bank card and a certain walking speed — buses that pull away too quickly, appointments you can only book online. Councils have been cutting exactly the services older residents depend on: day centres, subsidised fares, community nurses, all of which are a genuine lifeline. In a village somebody notices if you don't appear for two days; in a city people fall through the cracks. If my grandfather had moved to the capital, he'd have lost his entire social world overnight.

blocks.text: Is it possible that all of the population move to cities?

Total urbanisation is hard to picture, simply because somebody has to grow the food. Even highly automated farming needs people on the ground, and the same goes for mining, forestry and tourism. Urbanisation has actually slowed in the richest countries, where those who can afford to leave the city often do. So I'd expect us to hit a ceiling rather than a hundred per cent. If agriculture had gone fully robotic, the picture would have looked different, but we're a far cry from that. More likely, villages simply become commuter belt suburbs.

blocks.text: In practical terms we're closer to it than people imagine. Villages across the region have been emptying for thirty years — the young leave for work, the old stay, and when the school closes that's usually the final nail in the coffin. A century ago most of humanity had lived on the land; now the majority is urban and the curve is still climbing. I doubt the last farmhouse will ever be abandoned, but a country where ninety per cent live in five cities is entirely plausible. Putting all your eggs in one basket rarely ends well, mind you.

blocks.text: Will people live in the countryside in the future?

I think so, though for completely different reasons than in the past. Nobody will be farming by hand; they'll be living rurally and working online, which is a new category of villager altogether. Remote work has changed the arithmetic — if your salary doesn't depend on your postcode, why hand half of it to a landlord? Had the pandemic not forced companies to try it, that shift would have taken another twenty years. The limiting factors are broadband and schools: where they exist, villages are bouncing back; where they don't, the place is on its last legs.

blocks.text: Some will, but I suspect the countryside becomes somewhere people visit rather than inhabit. Services have been disappearing steadily — the post office, the bank, the bus — and once they've gone, families with children stop moving in. What's left is second homes and retired couples, which hollows the place out further. If governments had funded rural infrastructure the way they fund motorways, the decline would have been far slower. Villages will survive as beauty spots and weekend escapes; as working communities, plenty of them are already on borrowed time.

blocks.text: Do you think people in the countryside are friendlier than in cities?

There's something in it, though I'd explain it structurally rather than morally. In a village you'll see the same forty people for the rest of your life, so being difficult is expensive — reputation is the only currency there is. That's what makes it a close-knit community. In a city you'll never meet that person again. I've noticed it most when something goes wrong: half my grandmother's street had turned up before we'd even asked for help. City neighbours can be just as kind, but you have to break the ice yourself.

blocks.text: I'd challenge that, actually. What people call rural friendliness is often plain curiosity, and it's a double-edged sword — everyone knows your business, and an outsider can feel like one for twenty years. Cities aren't unfriendly so much as reserved: you choose your people instead of inheriting them. Anyone who has been living in a big city for a while will tell you their friendships are deeper, if fewer. If I'd judged Moscow by my first month there, I'd have written the whole place off — it just takes longer to get past the front door.

blocks.text: What should the government do to improve citizens' safety?

Most of the evidence I've seen suggests that visibility matters far more than severity. People feel safe when there are officers on foot, lighting that works and cameras somebody actually watches, not when sentences get longer. Cities that have invested in well-lit, well-used public space have seen street crime fall without a single extra prison place. Had my own city not pedestrianised the centre, I doubt the evening streets would feel as safe as they do. Long sentences sound like a deterrent, but for the victim they're too little, too late.

If councils had kept those spaces open, a good deal of that trouble would never have started. At the end of the day, a city that works for children is safe for everybody.

blocks.text: What changes usually take place in cities and towns?

Physically the pattern is fairly predictable everywhere: the centre densifies, the edges sprawl, and old industrial land eventually becomes flats. Cities have been building upwards for twenty years because land near the middle has simply run out. Transport drives the rest — a metro line arrives and within five years cafés and estate agents spring up around every station. I've watched three neighbourhoods in my own city go from workshops to coffee shops. The other constant is that old buildings are either done up or knocked down, depending entirely on who owns them.

blocks.text: The changes that matter most aren't architectural, they're social. A district gets a reputation, rents climb, the people who gave it that character can't afford to stay, and within ten years it's unrecognisable — the familiar story of gentrification. Before the developers arrived, that neighbourhood had been home to the same families for generations. Shops shift too: the butcher and the cobbler give way to chains and nail bars. If planning rules had protected small businesses, our high streets would have aged far more gracefully. It isn't all loss, though — safer streets come with the territory.

blocks.text: Are there any changes in your city?

Enormously — Tashkent barely resembles the city I first arrived in. They've been laying new metro lines and pedestrianising whole streets, and the difference to daily life is real: I can cross the centre in twenty minutes without a car. Cafés and co-working spaces have appeared on streets that were completely dead five years ago. There's noticeably more green space as well. The flip side is that a lot of low-rise, characterful housing was cleared to make room, and once that's gone you can't turn back the clock.

blocks.text: For those who live in cities, is it because they want to or have to?

For the majority I'd say necessity, though people rarely describe it that way. If the only jobs, universities and hospitals within three hundred kilometres are in one city, you have little say in the matter. Families have been moving for work rather than for nightlife for as long as cities have existed.My own parents had never wanted to leave their town; they left because the factory closed. People then put down roots, raise children and come to love the place, which makes the whole thing look voluntary in hindsight. Necessity first, affection afterwards.

blocks.text: Do you prefer to visit well-developed cities or cities with a long history?

Historic cities, every time. Modern developed ones are comfortable but interchangeable — the same glass towers, the same shops, and you could be in four different countries without noticing. Somewhere steeped in history gives you a reason to walk. I've spent whole days in Samarkand doing nothing but wandering, and it never felt like wasted time. If those old quarters had been demolished in the sixties, the way plenty of European centres were, we'd have lost something irreplaceable. Convenience is easy to build; four hundred years of layers can't be produced out of thin air.

blocks.text: What are the disadvantages of living in a very famous city?

The headline problem is cost. Fame attracts money, money attracts investors, and ordinary flats end up as short-term rentals, so locals get pushed further and further out. Rents in cities like Barcelona and Paris have been climbing far faster than wages. Then there's the crowding — you queue for everything and the centre stops belonging to the people who live in it. If tourism hadn't grown quite so fast, those cities would have kept more of their character. A famous city can end up a victim of its own success.

Until I stayed with a friend in Rome, I had assumed fame made daily life easier; in fact she spent forty minutes crossing three streets. The grass is always greener, of course.

blocks.text: Before you travel to a city, what factors would you consider?

Safety and season come first for me, then transport. I'll happily accept a plain hotel if the city has a metro I can use without a word of the language. Cost matters too, but timing matters more — the same city in August and October can be two entirely different experiences. I've been caught out by the weather more than once.Had I checked that Beijing would be fifteen degrees hotter than I expected, I'd have packed very differently. After that I look at whether things are within walking distance, and whether anything off the beaten track is reachable.

blocks.text: Do you think modern cities are suitable for young people or old people?

Modern cities are designed, deliberately or not, around a healthy twenty-five-year-old. Everything rewards speed and independence: apps, stairs, night buses, jobs that assume you can move at short notice. Developers have been building studio flats and co-working space far faster than anything suited to families or pensioners. Older residents have simply been left to adapt to a city that stopped consulting them. Having said that, young people pay for it in rent — the city hands them opportunity and takes most of the salary back. It's swings and roundabouts.

blocks.text: Honestly, I'd say modern cities suit neither group especially well — they suit employers. The young can't afford to live near their work and the old can't cross the road in the time the lights allow. Children and pensioners are an afterthought, while the middle-aged with a car take the lion's share of the space. If planners had started from what a seven-year-old and a seventy-year-old need, we'd have ended up with very different cities: slower streets, benches, shade, shops you can walk to. blocks.text: What kinds of facilities do big cities have?

The obvious ones are transport networks, hospitals, universities and shopping centres, but the facilities that actually shape daily life are smaller — libraries, swimming pools, parks and clinics you can reach on foot. Cities have been investing heavily in whatever can be photographed: state-of-the-art stadiums, opera houses, airport terminals. Those projects have brought a great deal of prestige, certainly, but a family with three children needs a playground more than an opera house. Bread-and-butter facilities never get a ribbon cut, which is precisely why they get neglected.

On what occasions would adults feel proud of themselves?

Most adults feel proudest when something they have worked at for years finally pays off — finishing a degree, getting promoted, buying a first flat. I've been watching friends go through exactly that, and the satisfaction clearly comes from the struggle rather than the prize itself. Nobody I know has ever felt much pride in something that was handed to them on a plate. There is a quieter version too — raising decent children, or keeping a promise nobody was checking on. Having said that, pride is a double-edged sword; had I chased other people's approval that hard in my twenties, I'd have made some very poor choices.

blocks.text: I'd argue the occasions that matter most are almost invisible from the outside. Nobody claps when you admit a mistake to your boss, or keep your temper with an elderly parent for the third time that week, but that is where adults quietly take pride in themselves. I've noticed that people who had been through something genuinely difficult talk far less about trophies. Public milestones are easy to photograph, which is why they dominate the conversation. If our culture had ever learnt to celebrate ordinary decency, I think a lot of people would have felt better about their lives. Recognition tends to go to whatever happens to catch the eye.

blocks.text: Is it a good idea to reward children for doing homework or housework?

Broadly speaking yes, but only as a stepping stone. Small children have no real grasp of long-term benefit, so a modest reward gives them a reason to start, and after a few weeks the habit takes on a life of its own. I've been using a simple chart with my nephew since the spring and the difference is obvious. Where it gets complicated is the scale of the reward — cash for ordinary chores sets a precedent that is very hard to undo. If my parents had paid me for every bed I made, I'd have negotiated over absolutely everything.

Plenty of children who had been reading happily for pleasure lost interest the moment a sticker chart appeared. Housework is a separate case again, because it is not a favour to the household, it is membership of it. Had my mother offered me money for washing up, I'd have missed that lesson completely. Noticing the effort out loud costs nothing and can go a long way.

blocks.text: What would children do to make their parents proud?

The conventional answer is academic success, and there is some truth in it — in most families the whole household tends to rally around exam results. Children pick that up extremely early; they learn which achievements get discussed at the dinner table and aim accordingly. Attitudes have been shifting a little, though, particularly among younger parents who have seen the cost of that pressure. I know two families where the eldest child had burned out completely before university even started. So children chase grades, but largely because adults have told them that is the name of the game.

blocks.text: Is it good to reward children too often?

No, and I'd go further: constant rewards defeat the object. If praise arrives whatever the child does, it stops carrying any information, so they cannot tell a genuine achievement from an ordinary morning. Standards have been drifting in that direction for a while, particularly with participation medals, and children are not fooled by it — automatic praise sounds hollow to them long before adults notice. Had we been rather more sparing with it, the praise that did arrive would have meant something. Flooding them with it simply waters it down.

What kind of jobs do children like?

Every job has a tedious component; the real question is whether you can live with that particular kind of tedium. I've met very few people who genuinely love every part of their work, and the happiest ones simply found something they didn't dread that also pays the bills. If I had spent my twenties holding out for the perfect role, I'd have wasted a decade. Look for work that is good enough and leaves you some energy, rather than a job that has to tick every box.

Your immediate manager affects your daily mood far more than your salary does, and I've never met anybody who resigned purely over money. Location sounds trivial until you're spending two hours a day on a bus. Industry matters enormously too: if I had gone into printing rather than software fifteen years ago, my career would have stalled completely. Job security and genuine prospects are worth more than an extra ten percent in the long run.

Do young and old people use phones in the same way?

Not remotely, in my experience. For anyone under twenty-five a phone isn't really a telephone — it's a camera, a bank, a social life and a shop all at once, and ringing somebody unannounced feels almost rude. My mother treats hers as an emergency device and nothing more: she's been using the same handset for seven years and still asks me to book her taxis. Before smartphones arrived, she had never needed a screen for anything except television. Older users also read every notification as urgent, whereas younger ones tune out most of them. Ordinary life used to go completely unrecorded: only weddings got a photographer, so whole decades of family history survive as four stiff portraits. My grandmother had never been photographed laughing until somebody pointed a phone at her, and that picture is now worth its weight in gold. Every generation from here on will hand down thousands of images instead. Most are rubbish, admittedly, but storage costs nothing. Where I'd draw the line is private behaviour, because the state has no business telling adults how long to look at a screen. What are the advantages and disadvantages of being a famous child?

The advantages are real, but they are almost entirely financial. A child who is famous at ten can earn more in a year than her parents will in a lifetime, and she is offered opportunities most adults spend decades chasing. I've read interviews with former child actors who had already bought a house before they left school. The trouble is that early fame is a poisoned chalice: you are in the public eye while you are still working out who you are. Had those children been left alone until eighteen, I suspect most of them would have coped far better.

blocks.text: What are the benefits of doing exercise?

The physical side is obvious — heart, weight, sleep — so I'd rather talk about what people underestimate, which is mood. People have been ordering everything from groceries to furniture online for well over a decade, and the pandemic simply accelerated a shift that had already begun long before anyone had heard of it. Going to the bazaar was a social event, a chance to haggle and catch up with half your neighbours; now a parcel arrives at the door and nobody speaks. What problems can people face if they ask many different people for advice?

The obvious danger is ending up more confused than when you started. Ask five people and you'll get five perfectly reasonable answers, and suddenly you're spoilt for choice to the point of paralysis. I've been watching a friend do exactly that for months: he has gathered so many opinions that he's permanently second-guessing himself. Advice also arrives with somebody else's priorities quietly attached to it, which people forget. If he had simply trusted his first instinct, he'd have made the decision back in spring. Too many cooks really does spoil the broth, and a decision delayed is very often a decision lost.

blocks.text: In general, what kind of person is most suitable for giving advice to others?

Somebody who has been through the same thing themselves, first and foremost. Theory is cheap; the useful advice nearly always comes from a person who has already paid for the lesson. I'd been struggling with the same problem for months before an older colleague explained, in about two minutes, what she had got wrong at my age. Beyond experience I'd want somebody level-headed, who can give it to you straight without appearing to enjoy it. Advice has been dressed up as concern for centuries and you can always tell. The best advisers are blunt but visibly on your side.

Seasonal work is the obvious answer — hotels, ski resorts, fruit picking, summer camps. What are the differences between the things that people keep today and the things that people kept in the past?

The biggest difference is durability. Things used to be built to last and repaired when they broke, so a copper pot or a woollen coat could stand the test of time and end up with the grandchildren. Today almost everything we own is disposable by design, and manufacturers have been shortening the life of their products for years. The other change is that our keepsakes have gone digital: before smartphones arrived, nobody had ever kept ten thousand photographs they would never once print. So we hold on to far more and treasure far less.

blocks.text: I'd draw the distinction differently. In the past people kept things because they might be needed one day — tools, cloth, jars put aside for a rainy day — and sentiment came second. Now we keep almost nothing for use and everything for feeling: concert tickets, a first phone, a child's drawing. My grandmother had kept every button she ever removed from a shirt, not out of nostalgia but because buttons were genuinely scarce. If she had grown up surrounded by cheap goods, she would never have bothered. So the motive has changed more than the objects, which says a lot about how comfortable life has become.

blocks.text: As well as family photographs, what are some other things that people keep in their family for a long time?
