Jewellery is the classic heirloom — a ring that goes to whichever daughter marries first. Then there are papers: letters, land documents, military records. Those have been sitting in the same wooden box since my great-grandfather's day, and nobody had ever thought to sort them until my cousin started a family tree. In Uzbek families the obvious answers are textiles and land. Houses matter even more: the youngest son traditionally stays in the family home, so a single courtyard can hold four generations. Craft skills travel the same way — ceramics in Rishtan, knives in Chust — although a good many of those trades had almost disappeared before tourism revived them. blocks.text: What kinds of things are kept in museums?

The classics are what everybody pictures — pottery, coins, weapons, manuscripts and paintings — objects that survived because they were made of something hard. That in itself gives a distorted picture, since almost everything made of wood or cloth had rotted away long before archaeologists reached it. So collections lean heavily towards the wealthy, whose possessions were built to last. What has changed is that curators have been collecting far humbler material for a couple of decades: bus tickets, factory uniforms, protest banners. What kind of jobs require imagination?

The obvious ones are the creative industries, where the ability to come up with a fresh idea is literally the product. But I'd widen it well beyond design and advertising. Teaching has quietly been demanding imagination for years: a good teacher has to picture the lesson from a child's head rather than an adult's. Engineering is the same, because before anyone had built a bridge of that shape, somebody had to see it in their mind first. Broadly speaking, any job where the answer isn't cut and dried needs imagination. Genuinely routine work is the exception now, not the rule.

A nurse has to imagine what a frightened patient is feeling; a lawyer has to picture how a case will play out in front of a jury. If firms had hired purely on technical scores over the last decade, they'd have missed most of their best staff. Having said that, imagination on its own is a recipe for disaster; the discipline of testing is what stops a promising idea going off the rails. The two really have to work hand in hand.

What is the right age for a child to learn drawing?

Honestly, as soon as they can hold a crayon — three or four. At that age drawing isn't a subject at all, it's thinking out loud, and children who are given free rein early rarely develop the fear of the blank page that most adults carry around. I've been watching my niece fill notebooks since she was two, and nobody has taught her a single technique. Formal lessons are a separate question; I'd leave those until seven or eight, because corrections too early put a child off for good. If anyone had criticised her proportions at three, she'd have abandoned it on the spot. Confidence first, technique afterwards.

Is it hard to find quiet places in cities?

Increasingly, yes — genuinely quiet corners are few and far between in any large city. Land is expensive, so the small squares and gardens get built on first, and traffic noise now reaches places it never used to reach. Cities in this region have been growing outwards and upwards at the same time, which squeezes out exactly the sort of space where you could once sit and think. I've noticed it most in the older districts, where the courtyards have quietly become car parks. Quiet is at a premium these days: you either pay for it or travel for it.

There's usually a well-kept secret ten minutes from your flat — a courtyard, a rooftop, a garden behind a mosque. I've walked past ours for years without noticing it. I've watched parents manage that beautifully in our local library, and by the age of five my niece had already learned to whisper without being told twice. Do people in your country usually obey the law?

By and large, yes — serious crime is rare and most people are genuinely law-abiding. Where it gets complicated is the small stuff: parking on the pavement, crossing on a red light, the occasional unofficial payment. Those things are treated almost as normal. Enforcement has been tightening for several years now, with cameras on every major road, and behaviour has changed noticeably as a result. That tells you something important, I think. The single most useful thing is consistency. A rule that applies on Monday and evaporates on Friday teaches a child only that rules depend on your mood. There's a fairness argument as well, in that rules create a level playing field, so the person who waits patiently isn't punished for waiting. Do old people often change plans?

Generally speaking no, and I'd say that's a matter of principle rather than habit. For my grandparents' generation, saying you'll be somewhere at four o'clock is very close to a promise, so cancelling is out of the question unless somebody is genuinely ill. They grew up in a world where you had committed yourself the moment you agreed, with no way of messaging an hour beforehand. Attitudes have been loosening among the younger retired, mind you. Most of it is thoroughly mundane. Work runs over, children get ill, trains are cancelled, and bad weather can put paid to a picnic in about ten minutes. I've been let down at the last minute often enough to know exactly how it feels. I'd give the real reason too, because a vague excuse raises more questions than it answers, and then I'd suggest a specific new date on the spot. What food do you eat on special occasions?

In Uzbekistan it is plov, almost without exception — a wedding, a birth, a memorial, and the kazan comes out. Families pull out all the stops: it's cooked by the men, outdoors, in quantities that look absurd until three hundred guests arrive. Beyond that there is samsa, non and a spread of dried fruit nobody ever finishes. We've been eating the same dishes at celebrations for centuries, and I rather like that continuity. Had the menu changed with every generation, those gatherings would have lost much of their meaning. Honestly, the food is almost beside the point — it is the gathering that matters.

Every culture keeps a dish that takes far too long to cook on an ordinary Tuesday — a whole roast, a slow stew, something that needs three people and half a day. The effort is the message; the labour is the gift. Restaurants have been taking that job over in the cities, and I think something quiet has been lost. A delivered feast does not say the same thing. In my family we still make the dumplings from scratch, which is a labour of love, and nobody has ever complained about the hours, because the hours are precisely the point.

blocks.text: Is food now better than in the past?

In terms of choice and safety, unquestionably. You can buy mangoes in Tashkent in February, refrigeration means far less food poisoning, and my grandmother's winter diet of potatoes and preserves would strike anyone today as monotonous. Diets have been getting steadily more varied for thirty years. Where I'd push back is on flavour: a supermarket tomato, bred to survive a lorry journey, is a far cry from the ones she grew behind the house. If we had selected varieties for taste rather than shelf life, we would have kept the best of both. So better in range, not always better on the plate.

blocks.text: Are there any differences between the food people eat today and the food people ate in the past?

The biggest change is that the seasons have more or less disappeared from the plate. My mother's cooking followed the year — apricots in June, pumpkin in autumn, pickles all winter — whereas now you can buy almost anything out of season. Global supply chains have been flattening those differences out for decades. We have gained enormously in convenience and lost the pleasure of waiting for something. If cherries had been available all year when I was small, that first bowl in May would never have felt like an event. When everything is permanently available, you begin to take it for granted.

A lot of people are put off by everything that surrounds the Games rather than the sport itself. blocks.text: What preparations should people make before going on holiday?

The preparation people skip is the unglamorous kind: insurance, vaccinations and a realistic budget. Travel insurance feels like money down the drain right up until the day you need it, and a medical bill abroad can leave you seriously out of pocket. I've been telling my friends this for years — one of them broke an ankle in Turkey and hadn't bought a policy because forty dollars seemed like a waste. Had he paid it, he'd have saved himself about three thousand. I'd also leave your route with somebody at home. It sounds fussy, but it costs nothing and it puts your mind at rest.

Yes, and adults underestimate them because from outside the stakes look tiny. A ten-year- old deciding whether to tell a teacher about bullying is making a judgement call that plenty of adults would struggle with, and children have been carrying that kind of pressure for as long as schools have existed. At fourteen they choose subjects that quietly close doors ten years later. Had nobody nudged me towards science at that age, I'd have ended up somewhere completely different. blocks.text: I'd separate decisions children genuinely make from decisions that are made for them and dressed up as choice. Schools, moving abroad, which language they're educated in — the life-changing ones are settled by parents. What children really decide is smaller: who to be friends with, whether to own up when they break something. Those matter, but they're low-stakes by comparison. I've often thought the biggest choice I made before eighteen was which friends to keep, and even that had largely been decided by where we happened to live. blocks.text: What important decisions do young people need to make after the completion of high school?

Three big ones, really: what to study, where to study, and whether to study at all. The subject is what everybody agonises over, although in practice your first job shapes you more. Where is arguably the bigger question — moving abroad at eighteen is a leap in the dark, and it changes who you become, not just what you know. Increasing numbers have been choosing vocational routes instead, which I think is healthy. If I'd been told at seventeen that a degree wasn't compulsory, I'd have saved two fairly wasted years. Underneath everything sits money, because for most families the cost is make or break.

Eighteen-year-olds pick a profession before they've had a single adult experience, which strikes me as putting the cart before the horse. I've watched friends who had chosen medicine at seventeen walk away from it at twenty-five, exhausted and resentful. People have been agonising over whether to stay near their families since young men first left villages for cities. Next to those two questions, which university you attend is neither here nor there.

blocks.text: Who can children turn to for help when making a decision?

Parents first, obviously, and for most children that works — families have your best interests at heart in a way nobody else quite does. The catch is that parents are rarely neutral: they carry their own regrets and steer children down the road they never took themselves. My father had wanted to study engineering and never managed it, and I've been hearing about that, one way or another, ever since. So the ideal is a wider circle — an aunt, an older cousin, a teacher who can offer an outside perspective and act as a sounding board rather than a judge.

Before counselling became normal, most children had simply kept quiet and hoped the problem would solve itself. Friends help too, though peer advice is frequently the blind leading the blind, and nowadays they go online, which is a mixed blessing — excellent guidance sitting next to complete nonsense.

blocks.text: What are the advantages of advertising?

The obvious advantage is information: without it a new business has no way of telling anyone it exists, and shoppers would be stuck with whatever is nearest. It also levels the playing field a little, because a small company with a clever campaign can take on a household name. And it pays for things we take for granted — free journalism, free search and free social media have all depended on advertising money for decades. If advertising had disappeared ten years ago, most of the internet would have vanished behind paywalls by now. Calling it a public good, mind you, would be stretching a point.

Public attitudes to those things had barely moved until the campaigns started. The flip side, obviously, is that identical techniques sell sugar to seven-year-olds, so the whole tool is a double-edged sword.

blocks.text: Do you think the influence of advertising is good?

On balance, no. The business model depends on making people feel that what they already own is inadequate, and advertisers have been doing that more intensely every year since smartphones arrived. blocks.text: Are rivers and lakes good for transport?

For bulk goods they are excellent, which is why the Rhine and the Mississippi still carry enormous volumes. A single barge shifts what would otherwise take dozens of lorries, the fuel cost per tonne is tiny, and the carbon footprint is a fraction of road freight. Shipping companies have been rediscovering inland waterways for precisely that reason. Before the motorway boom, most European cargo had travelled by canal, so in a sense we are going back to something that already worked. It is slow, admittedly, but when you are moving grain or gravel, speed isn't the be-all and end-all — cost calls the shots.

Follows Part 2 cue card 48 · Thing You Did to Learn a Language
What are the difficulties of learning a new language?

The hardest part is almost always pronunciation, because you're asking your mouth to make sounds it has never produced before. Grammar you can study on paper; sounds you have to rewire. I've been working on my English intonation for years and it still catches me out. Then there's the sheer volume of vocabulary — nobody warns you that you need thousands of words before a newspaper stops looking like a wall. Having said that, a bit of ignorance helps: if I'd known how long it would take, I'd have lost heart immediately, so it was a blessing in disguise.

blocks.text: For me the real difficulty isn't the beginning — it's the middle. Beginners make headway quickly because everything is new, and then you hit a wall where months of study produce almost no visible progress. Most of the learners I've taught had already reached that plateau before they came to me, and that is precisely when people quit. Had someone explained to me that the plateau is completely normal, I'd have been far less discouraged by it. The other difficulty is finding anyone to speak to; genuine conversation partners are few and far between.

blocks.text: What difficulties do people face when learning a language?

I'd say the biggest obstacle is psychological rather than linguistic. Adults hate looking foolish, and speaking badly in front of other people makes you feel about six years old, so learners clam up exactly when they should be talking. Children don't care, which is half the reason they progress faster. I've been teaching teenagers long enough to see the difference — the shy ones fall behind, however good their grammar is. If I hadn't been thrown in at the deep end in my first job, I'd have stayed silent for years. Getting over that fear is half the battle.

blocks.text: Beyond the language itself, the real difficulties are usually practical. Adults are juggling jobs and families, so study tends to fall by the wayside the moment life gets busy — I've been promising myself I'd restart Turkish since 2019. There's also the problem of exposure: if the language isn't spoken around you, you're learning in a vacuum, and what you cover on Monday can go in one ear and out the other by Friday. Had I stayed in Istanbul another year instead of coming home, I'd have reached fluency without really trying. Circumstances matter enormously.

blocks.text: Why do people learn foreign languages?

For the majority, it comes down to work. English has become the price of entry for anything international — banking, IT, aviation — and in my country, decent jobs that don't ask for a foreign language are now few and far between. Salaries for bilingual staff have been climbing steadily for a decade, which is why parents start their children at five. If my own parents hadn't pushed me into English classes, I'd have ended up in a completely different job. That said, I'd hate to reduce it all to money — plenty of people learn Korean purely out of love for the culture.

blocks.text: There's a whole set of reasons that have nothing to do with employment. Migration, obviously — my cousin had been living in Poland for two years before he seriously started learning Polish, and he insists it was the only way to genuinely fit in. Then there's identity: a lot of young people go back to a heritage language because of family history. And some simply enjoy it — for them a language is a puzzle rather than a means to an end. Had the internet not made every culture so accessible, I doubt half of these learners would exist.

blocks.text: Do you think learning a foreign language is important?

Yes, though I'd put it more carefully than most people do. A second language can open doors — study, work, travel — and it changes how you think about your own, which is harder to measure but probably more valuable. I've never met anyone who regretted learning one. Where it gets complicated is the word 'important': for a farmer in a mountain village, English is a luxury rather than a necessity, and pretending otherwise is pure snobbery. If I'd been born somewhere with no tourists and no internet, I'd have spent those thousands of hours elsewhere.

blocks.text: I'll push back slightly here. It's obviously useful, but we've turned it into a kind of moral duty, and that isn't fair on people who genuinely struggle. Aptitude varies enormously — I've been teaching long enough to watch two students work identically hard for completely different results. Meanwhile a brilliant engineer with no English is treated as uneducated, which is nonsense. If we'd valued other skills as highly as we value languages, that engineer would have had a very different career. So yes, important — but not the be-all and end-all.

blocks.text: What can people do to learn a foreign language?

The single most effective thing is to build the language into your daily routine rather than treating it as homework. Change your phone's language, listen to podcasts on the bus, keep a notebook — none of it is glamorous, but I've been picking up German that way for eighteen months and it works. Beyond that, find someone to talk to; apps can only take you so far. Had I relied purely on textbooks, I'd still be translating in my head before every sentence. Consistency matters far more than method — there's no substitute for turning up every single day.

blocks.text: I'd give slightly unconventional advice: stop studying and start using the language badly. Most learners spend years preparing to speak and never actually speak. If I'd started conversation classes in my first month rather than my third year, I'd have saved myself an enormous amount of time. Watch films you already know by heart, read children's books, talk to yourself in the shower — anything that makes the language ordinary rather than sacred. Teaching methods have been moving in that direction for a while, thankfully. Grammar has its place, but most people put off the actual talking indefinitely.

blocks.text: What's the best way to learn a language?

Immersion, hands down — living where the language is spoken beats every course ever designed. You learn out of necessity rather than duty, and necessity is a far better teacher. A friend of mine had studied Russian for six years at school and still couldn't order a coffee; three months in Moscow and he was arguing about football. The reason is simply hours. Obviously not everyone can up sticks and move abroad, so the realistic version is a small immersion bubble at home. If that option had existed when I was at school, I'd have taken it in a heartbeat.

But plenty of people I've met have picked up fluent street language and never learned to write a formal email, which limits them badly at work. The version I'd defend is a hybrid: structured grammar in the morning, real conversation in the evening. If I hadn't put two dull years into grammar at the start, I'd never have written a decent report in English. Without that framework, bad habits set in and become second nature.

blocks.text: Which is better, to study a language alone or to study it in a group?

A group, for most people, and the reason is accountability rather than teaching. Left to your own devices, most of us simply never open the book — I've been meaning to finish an online Turkish course since 2019 — whereas a class you've paid for on a Tuesday evening actually happens. You also need other humans to practise on; you can't hold a conversation with a textbook. Had my university not made speaking clubs compulsory, I'd have graduated with excellent grammar and no ability to talk. The obvious drawback is pace: in any group you're either bored or out of your depth.

blocks.text: I'd defend solo study more than most teachers would. In a class of fifteen you might speak for four minutes an hour; alone, you control every minute and you work on precisely your own weaknesses. Resources have been improving so fast over the last decade that the old argument — no materials, no feedback — barely holds. If I'd waited for a class that matched my level, I'd have wasted another year. That said, it can cut both ways: alone you can go at your own pace, but nobody notices you've been mispronouncing a word for six months.

blocks.text: What are the advantages and disadvantages of learning a language?

The advantages are fairly obvious: more work, more travel, and access to a whole culture from the inside rather than through subtitles — in business that access is worth its weight in gold. What people underestimate is the cognitive side; most of the research I've seen suggests that juggling two systems keeps the mind flexible. But it comes at a price: time, money, and years of feeling stupid. I've been studying German since university and I still sound like a tourist. If I'd put those hours into coding instead, I'd have earned considerably more — though I'd have a much smaller world.

blocks.text: Honestly, the advantages are so well rehearsed that I'd rather talk about the costs. The big one is opportunity cost — a language takes a thousand hours, and nobody ever asks what else those hours could have bought. There's also a quieter disadvantage: half-learning three languages makes you a jack of all trades and master of none, and I've watched friends drift from Spanish to Japanese to Arabic without ever finishing one. On the other side, the gains do snowball — once you've cracked one language, the second is far easier. Had I not struggled through English first, Turkish would have felt impossible.

blocks.text: Some people think that technology has made it unnecessary to learn languages. What do you think?

I disagree, though I understand why people say it. Translation apps have got remarkably good, and they've been improving faster than anyone predicted — for reading a menu or a road sign they'll do the job perfectly well. But language isn't information transfer; it's a relationship. Nobody has ever built real trust with a business partner through a phone screen, and humour, warmth and politeness are exactly what gets lost in translation. If translation software had existed when I was fifteen, I'd probably have skipped English altogether — and I'd be a far narrower person for it.

Where the argument falls apart is at the top end: diplomacy, literature, negotiation, anything where nuance decides the outcome. Machines are still hit and miss there. Had I trusted an app during my last negotiation, I'd have missed the sarcasm completely. Technology has raised the floor without touching the ceiling.

What can teachers do to make students obey rules?

Consistency matters far more than severity. A rule that is enforced on Monday and quietly let slide on Friday stops being a rule at all, because children work out the real limits within about a week. I've been teaching part-time for several years now, and the colleagues with the calmest classrooms are almost never the ones who shout; they simply apply the same standard across the board, including to themselves. Had my own school been half that consistent, most of the arguments we had would have disappeared. Explaining the reason behind a rule helps enormously too — teenagers will accept almost anything except an instruction that looks arbitrary.

blocks.text: Beyond enforcement, the teachers who get genuine cooperation tend to bring the class into the process. If students are allowed to have a hand in drawing up their own code — phones in the box, nobody talks over anybody — they end up policing it themselves, and peer pressure does the difficult part. Attitudes have been moving that way for a while, at least in the schools I know well. The older model, where a teacher could simply lay down the law, worked when children had no other authority to appeal to. If it had really worked, though, we wouldn't have spent a century arguing about discipline.

blocks.text: What are some rules that exist in schools or workplaces in your country?

In schools it's mostly the familiar list: a uniform, no phones in lessons, registers taken every morning and a fairly strict line on lateness. Respect for teachers is taken seriously here — standing up when an adult comes into the room is still normal, which visitors sometimes find quaint. Several of those conventions have been loosening over the past decade, particularly around phones, once staff realised that a blanket ban was a losing battle. I'd have said the uniform rule was untouchable if you had asked me ten years ago, and yet a number of private schools have quietly dropped it.

blocks.text: Workplaces are more interesting, because the written rules are the least important part of it. I've worked in two companies where nobody had ever written a word of that down, and yet everyone absorbed it within a fortnight. People who break those conventions are seldom punished formally; they simply find themselves out in the cold. Had somebody handed me a list on day one, I'd have adapted far faster.

blocks.text: What should parents do to educate children about laws?

Children learn far more from what their parents do than from anything they say, so the honest answer is to obey the law yourself, visibly. If a child watches you cross on a red light, or talk your way out of a fine, no lecture afterwards is going to cut any ice. I've seen adults complain bitterly about corruption and then quietly hand something to a traffic officer — children notice that instantly. Had we all been more consistent about the small rules, I suspect the big ones would have looked after themselves. Everyday moments teach this better than any formal conversation: queueing, paying the fare, returning what you find.

blocks.text: I'd add that rules only stick when the reason behind them is clear. Telling a ten-year-old that something is illegal means very little; explaining who gets hurt when people do it means a great deal. There is a limit worth being honest about, though: laws are not automatically fair, and a child trained in blind obedience is easy prey for the wrong kind of authority. If my parents had only ever said because I say so, I'd have stopped listening. Teaching judgement does cut both ways.

blocks.text: When people break rules, how are they punished in your country?

It depends enormously on the seriousness of the offence. Minor things — speeding, parking, littering — are handled with on-the-spot fines, and cameras have made the whole process far more automatic than it used to be. Enforcement has been tightening steadily for several years; drivers who had grown used to talking their way out of a ticket now just get a text message. Serious crime goes through the courts, and sentences strike many people as heavy. Inside schools and workplaces it is much gentler: a warning, a conversation with the family, and only rarely anything worse than a slap on the wrist.

blocks.text: Formally it still leans on deterrence — fines, licence points, prison in serious cases. Whether any of that changes behaviour is a separate question. Almost everyone I know who had been fined for speeding carried on speeding, just more carefully near cameras. Punishment works when people genuinely expect to be caught, so certainty matters far more than severity. Had the emphasis gone on catching offenders rather than on longer sentences, I think we'd have seen much better results. There is also a grey area around small offences where enforcement is selective, and that quietly erodes respect for the whole system.

blocks.text: Do you think school rules are important?

Absolutely, though not all of them for the same reason. Rules about safety and basic respect are non-negotiable — thirty teenagers in one room need a shared framework or nobody learns anything. Rules about the colour of your socks are a different matter; they mostly exist to establish who is in charge. Schools have been dropping that second category quietly for years, which seems sensible to me. The real value is that children rehearse living under rules they didn't choose, which is the way of the world once you start working. Had nobody made me arrive on time at fourteen, I'd have struggled badly later.

I've met graduates who had followed every instruction for eighteen years and were completely lost the moment nobody gave them one. The systems that do best on creativity tend to run fairly relaxed classrooms. If rules alone had guaranteed a good education, the strictest schools would have produced the best thinkers, and plainly they don't. Rules are a means to an end.

blocks.text: Are children unhappy with the school rules?

Some are, certainly, but they are far more discriminating than adults give them credit for. In my experience children rarely object to a rule that obviously protects somebody; what they resent is arbitrariness — a rule nobody can justify, or one that applies to them and not to the staff. I've been tutoring teenagers for a few years now, and the complaints are almost always about fairness rather than freedom. Had schools explained their reasoning more often, a good deal of that resentment would never have appeared. The grumbling about uniform is half for show anyway.

blocks.text: Less unhappy than my generation was, I'd say. Schools have become noticeably more negotiable: pupils get consulted, uniforms have relaxed, and physical punishment is history almost everywhere. Rules have been softening for decades, so today's complaints are far milder than ours were. Where children genuinely push back now is technology, because a phone ban feels to them like losing a limb. Having said that, grumbling about authority is part and parcel of growing up and I wouldn't read too much into it. blocks.text: What are the rules people should obey at work?

The formal ones are obvious — turn up, meet deadlines, follow the safety procedures, don't touch company money. But the rules that actually decide whether somebody succeeds are reliability and discretion. Colleagues will forgive an honest mistake; they will not forgive people who cut corners or repeat a private conversation. I've watched two promising careers come apart over exactly that, and neither person had broken a single written rule. Had either of them treated a promise as binding, they would still be in those jobs today. Punctuality belongs on the list as well, because chronic lateness announces that your time matters more than everyone else's.

Norms have been shifting quickly since remote work arrived, which makes them harder to read than they used to be. My advice is to watch for a month before deciding anything. blocks.text: 5 questions · two contrasting answers each — a position and a counter-position
Follows Part 2 cue card 50 · Special Day Out That Didn't Cost a Lot
What leisure activities do old and young people prefer?

Broadly speaking, the young go outwards and the old go inwards. Teenagers want noise and company — football, gaming, endless scrolling with friends in the same room. Older people gravitate towards things they can do at their own pace: gardening, chess in the park, long walks, reading. That pattern has been holding steady for as long as I can remember, although much of it must boil down to energy and money rather than taste. Had my grandfather been handed a smartphone at fifteen, he would have been every bit as glued to it as his grandchildren are. So I'd be careful with the phrase generation gap.

Plenty of sixty-year-olds cycle, travel and use exactly the same apps their grandchildren do, and retired people have been signing up for language courses and gym memberships in enormous numbers. Meanwhile a lot of young people take up hobbies we would once have called elderly: baking, birdwatching, growing tomatoes on a balcony. If you had shown my parents that at twenty-five, they would have laughed out loud. What really predicts how somebody relaxes is income and health, so age is largely a red herring.

blocks.text: How do people spend their leisure time in your country?

Almost all of it is social, and most of it revolves around food. A typical Sunday means a courtyard full of relatives, a cauldron of plov and four hours of conversation, and that conversation is the leisure. Weddings work the same way; people will happily set aside an entire Saturday for somebody they barely know. Younger city dwellers have added cafés, cinemas and shopping centres, and those have been opening at a remarkable rate in Tashkent. Even so, going out alone simply isn't the done thing. Before the malls arrived, families had always gathered at home instead, so the venue has changed rather than the habit.

In rural areas the line between work and rest barely exists: people keep livestock and gardens, and relaxing means sitting outside once the work is finished. In the cities there is a proper leisure industry now — fitness clubs, karaoke, pitches you rent by the hour — and disposable income has been rising steadily for a decade. The uncomfortable part is that a great many people had never had genuine free time until quite recently, and plenty still work six days. For them leisure is a luxury, and telling them to switch off is easier said than done.

blocks.text: How does technology affect the way people spend leisure time?

Mostly by making leisure passive and solitary. Watching a series alone counts as rest on paper, yet you finish it feeling flat, whereas an evening of football leaves you tired and cheerful. Streaming services have been designing that stickiness deliberately for years; autoplay exists for a reason. The deeper issue is that a phone blurs the line between work and rest, so people stay quietly available around the clock. Had smartphones arrived without notifications, I doubt any of this would have happened. Real rest needs a boundary, and technology has quietly removed most of them.

Technology has democratised hobbies in a way nothing else ever has: people have been learning instruments, languages and chess from free videos for a decade now, and none of that had ever been available to my parents. A retired man in a village can follow a lecture from Cambridge. Games are far more sociable than critics admit, too — half the teenagers I know spend the evening talking to friends while they play. It does cut both ways, obviously; the same device that teaches you guitar will swallow three hours. But blaming the tool is missing the point.

Companies have been discovering that for years, usually the hard way, which is why the better ones now police annual leave instead of praising overtime. If my old firm had accepted any of this, it would have kept half the staff it lost. Rest isn't a reward for finishing the work; it is part of doing the work properly.

blocks.text: Do you think only old people have time for leisure?

Not at all — if anything it is the reverse. Retirement brings hours but frequently not the health or the money to enjoy them, so a great many pensioners sit at home bored. Young people, meanwhile, have huge amounts of leisure and take it for granted; students complain of being rushed while they've been watching six hours of video a day. The group genuinely pressed for time is the one in the middle — thirties and forties, small children, demanding jobs. Teachers have been sorting children quietly into clever and slow for as long as schools have existed, and those verdicts follow people for decades. blocks.text: Why are some children more intelligent than others?

Almost everything comes back to what happens before school even starts. Children who are read to, argued with and taken places arrive at five with a vocabulary several times larger than children who spent those years in front of a screen. The odds are stacked from the beginning. Sleep, food and stress matter enormously as well — nobody thinks clearly in a chaotic house. Specialists have been making that point for decades, and yet policy barely moves. If governments had spent on nurseries what they spend on universities, the gap would have closed a generation ago.

Age plays a part too: teachers quietly write off the youngest in a year group when they are simply eleven months younger. I've seen exactly that happen to a cousin of mine — a boy who had been top of his class before the family moved. blocks.text: How do children become smart at school?

Expectations matter enormously too: children work up or down to whatever the adult in the room assumes about them. I've had exactly two teachers who changed the way I think, and neither was especially friendly. Class sizes and equipment are the tip of the iceberg by comparison. Had my chemistry teacher not pushed me so hard, I'd have dropped the subject at fifteen.

blocks.text: Do you think society needs people with different types of intelligence?

Obviously it does — a society made up entirely of theorists would collapse inside a week. Somebody has to wire the building, set the broken bone and calm the frightened passenger, and none of that shows up on an intelligence test. We've built a one-size-fits-all education system that rewards one narrow kind of cleverness and then acts astonished when nobody can find a plumber. Attitudes have been shifting a little recently, largely because skilled trades now pay better than plenty of degrees. Practical and academic ability go hand in hand anyway. Had we funded technical schools properly thirty years ago, we wouldn't be importing engineers today.

Most of the genuinely original work I've come across sits where two fields overlap, and teams that had never included an outsider went on repeating the same error for years. blocks.text: Does modern society need talents of all kinds?

Anything rule-based is being automated, so what remains is judgement, persuasion, physical skill and imagination — the very things schools treat as extras. The labour market has been rewarding those abilities for a decade now, quietly. Nursing, teaching, negotiation: none of it can be outsourced to software. Where it gets complicated is that pay hasn't followed the same curve at all, so the talents society praises and the talents it actually rewards are poles apart.

blocks.text: Do you think smart people are happy?

Not automatically, no, and I'd argue intelligence can cut both ways here. Being able to analyse everything means you also analyse the things that are better left alone: your relationships, your career, whether any of it means anything. Overthinking is the classic trap. I've known several people who breezed through university and then found ordinary life oddly disappointing, because by their late twenties they had lost any sense of what they were aiming at — nothing outside an exam hall gives you a mark out of a hundred. Having said that, misery isn't compulsory. The happiest clever people I know found something absorbing to point all that analysis at.

Somebody with a demanding, absorbing job may be exhausted every Tuesday and still feel their life is going somewhere. On the daily measure I'd say clever people do slightly worse, because expectations are higher and so is the pressure that comes with the territory — ever since school they've been told they'll do something remarkable, which is heavy to carry. blocks.text: What ways do people use to judge someone's intelligence?

Mostly by surface signals, and mostly badly. Vocabulary comes first — use a long word confidently and people assume depth behind it. Then accent, speed of speech, eye contact and how quickly you answer, all of which reward the confident rather than the correct. Qualifications do the rest: a famous university name opens doors that a better mind without one never gets near. blocks.text: Do you think there is anything that intelligent people find difficult to do?

Starting anything from scratch, I'd say — being visibly incompetent in front of other people. If you've built an identity on understanding things quickly, a first violin lesson at forty is humiliating, so most people simply avoid the situation. Asking for help is the same problem wearing a different coat. I'd been putting off learning to swim for about fifteen years, purely out of embarrassment. Pride comes before a fall, as my mother used to say. If I'd been thrown into a beginners' class at twenty, I'd have got over myself far sooner. When do children begin to have their own ideas and opinions?

Far earlier than most adults assume, I'd say. By four or five, children already argue fiercely about what's fair, although most of what comes out of their mouths is second-hand. The real turning point, when you genuinely have a mind of your own, tends to arrive in early adolescence. Psychologists have been telling us for decades that the formative years shape almost everything that follows. By the time I left school, I had worked out which of my opinions were actually mine and which I had simply absorbed at the dinner table. Before that, I was quoting my father almost word for word.

Children voice opinions almost as soon as they can talk, but owning an opinion, being able to defend it when somebody pushes back, is a far later skill. I've watched ten-year-olds abandon a position the moment a louder child objects, which tells you how fragile it really is. Critical thinking has to be taught; until somebody teaches it, children take almost everything at face value. blocks.text: Who do children listen to more, their parents or their teachers?

It flips somewhere around eleven or twelve, in my experience. Small children treat their parents as the last word on absolutely everything, whereas teenagers will happily quote a teacher at the dinner table to win an argument. Part of that is novelty: a teacher's authority hasn't been eroded by years of ordinary domestic friction. Had my mother said precisely what my physics teacher said, I would have dismissed it instantly at fifteen. I've watched that pattern repeat in almost every family I know. So it's less about respect than about who still sounds like an outsider.

Honestly, I don't think it's a straight competition, because children compartmentalise far more than we give them credit for. They take academic guidance from teachers and moral guidance from home, and the two rarely collide. Where it gets complicated is when the messages genuinely contradict each other, and then blood is thicker than water almost every time. Attitudes have been forming at home since birth, so a teacher is arriving very late to that argument. If a teacher had told me my family were wrong about something fundamental, I'd have defended them without even thinking.

The obvious risk is that a charismatic voice can lead someone astray just as easily, because being clever and being sceptical aren't the same thing.

blocks.text: How can teachers help children develop their ideas and opinions?

The most useful thing a teacher can do is stop supplying the answer. Set a genuinely open question, make the class defend both sides, and mark the reasoning rather than the conclusion. I've seen that transform a classroom, with pupils who had never once spoken up suddenly arguing hard. Debate works because it forces children to play devil's advocate, and you can't hold a position honestly until you have argued against it. If my school had taught us that way from the beginning, half of us would have left far more confident. A teacher who rewards only agreement does more harm than good.

blocks.text: Atmosphere matters more than technique, I'd argue. Children only risk an opinion when they're confident it won't be laughed at, so the teacher's real job is to set the tone and make disagreement feel safe. That means admitting in front of the class when you're wrong, which a great many teachers find almost impossible. Schools have been rewarding the correct answer for so long that saying 'I'm not sure' feels like failure. Had my chemistry teacher never admitted that he'd misread something, I doubt I would ever have questioned a textbook. Model honest doubt, and children take it on board remarkably fast.

Where they still win is emotional weight, so I'd call the letter a poor medium but a wonderful gesture. If my bank had written to me by post about that deadline, I'd have missed it completely.

What are the advantages of advertising?

The main advantage is that advertising makes competition visible. Without it, a new company would have no way of telling anybody it exists, and the market would belong permanently to whoever got there first. I've watched tiny businesses take off on the strength of one clever campaign, which is no mean feat in a crowded field. It also pays for things we take for granted: if advertising had never funded television and newspapers, we'd have been buying every article separately for decades. The catch is that the playing field isn't level, because the biggest brands can simply drown out anyone smaller.

I'd never heard of half the products in my kitchen before an advert put them in front of me, and one or two of them genuinely made life easier. It also keeps companies honest, because a brand that lets you down publicly pays for it very quickly, and standards have been rising partly for that reason. Where I'd qualify all this is that the information is never neutral. You are being told the flattering half of the story, so the sensible response is to take it with a pinch of salt.

blocks.text: Do you think the influence of advertising is good?

blocks.text: Do you think that children adapt to new things more easily than adults?

Generally yes, and with language the gap is obvious — small children absorb it like a sponge while adults grind away at it. But the reason is less biological than people assume. Children have no dignity to protect: a seven-year-old says something absurd, gets laughed at and carries on, whereas adults freeze. Adults are also set in their ways, with jobs and mortgages competing for their attention. I've been watching my niece pick up English from cartoons with no visible effort at all. Had I been that shameless at twenty-five, I'd have learned Turkish in half the time.

Researchers have been making that point for a while now, as far as I've read. What adults lack is time and tolerance of embarrassment, not capacity. blocks.text: How can people learn new things?

The method that works for almost anything is doing the thing badly until you do it well — trial and error, essentially. Reading about swimming teaches you nothing. What makes the difference is quick feedback, before a mistake hardens into a habit. I had been teaching myself the guitar for two years before anybody corrected my hand position, and undoing that took months. If someone had said something in the first week, I'd have saved myself a year. Adults want to understand first and act second, which is back to front. Start, fail, adjust, and keep sessions short enough that you'll turn up again tomorrow.

Why is it sometimes difficult to buy or choose a gift for someone?

The hardest gifts are for people you don't actually know that well — a colleague, a distant uncle, your fiancé's mother. You're second-guessing their taste with almost no information, so you end up playing it safe with a box of chocolates. I've watched friends spend entire afternoons at the Mega Planet mall and leave with nothing. Even with close people it's tricky, because adults tend to buy whatever they want the moment they want it, which leaves you nothing to give. Had my cousin Nodira not mentioned, in passing, that her old kettle had died, I'd have bought her yet another scarf. Good gifts require doing your homework months before the occasion, and most of us simply don't.

blocks.text: — The fear of getting it wrong

A gift says something about how well you know the person, so the wrong one feels like a small insult — and people read into presents far more than they admit. blocks.text: Is the price of a gift important?

A cheap second-hand book with a note inside outweighs a generic perfume bought at the airport, because one shows thought and the other shows a credit card. I've kept a hand-drawn card from a student for six years, and I couldn't tell you where the expensive watch from that same year is. Had price been the deciding factor, my grandmother's knitted socks would have been worthless, and they were the gift everyone fought over. That said, there is a floor: a present that was obviously thrown together at the last minute tells its own story. Price matters only when it signals indifference.

blocks.text: What gifts are popular in your country?

The traditional ones still dominate. For weddings it's cash in an envelope, or household goods — a carpet, a set of Rishtan ceramic plates, an enormous cooking pot for plov. Sweets and dried fruit arrive with every guest, and a good chapan or a length of atlas silk is the go-to present for older relatives. Those habits have been passed down for generations and they haven't changed much. What has changed is the younger end: I've noticed friends giving gadgets, gym memberships and restaurant vouchers where their parents would have given a tea set. If the shopping centres hadn't arrived, we'd all still be giving crockery. Even so, when in doubt, people fall back on the classics, and nobody has ever been offended by a box of halva.

blocks.text: What factors do parents consider when choosing a gift for children?

The sensible parents I know think about three things: age, safety and whether the gift will outlast the week. A toy that is too advanced gets ignored and one that is too simple gets broken, so the age band on the box actually matters. Safety is non-negotiable for anything under three — small parts, sharp corners, cheap paint. Then there's usefulness: parents have been quietly steering children towards books, bicycles and building sets for as long as toys have existed, because those develop something. Had my parents bought me the games console I begged for at nine, I'd have spent that summer indoors instead of learning to swim at the Yunusobod pool. Children want the flashy thing; parents are weighing up the long-term consequences, and usually they're right.

blocks.text: Do we benefit from having friends with different personalities?

Enormously, yes. If all your friends think and react the way you do, you end up in a very comfortable echo chamber and never get told you're wrong. I've had the same cautious, quiet friend since school, and the friend who does me the most good is the loud, impulsive one who books a trip to Chimgan at nine in the evening. Had I only mixed with people like myself, I'd have spent my twenties indoors making lists. Different personalities also pick up the slack in a group: somebody organises, somebody calms everyone down, somebody remembers birthdays. A group of six identical people would be six people all waiting for someone else to take the initiative.
